summary: The Supreme Court of the United States held that notwithstanding the fact that polygamy is a person's religious belief, the Mann Act prohibits the transportation of women across state lines to participate in polygamy.
The Court held that the Commerce Clause allows the federal government to dissolve a public utility company that is not serving the local community properly.

The Court held that the United States federal government was empowered by Condemnation Act of August 1, 1888; the Public Buildings Act of 1926; and the United States Constitution to exercise its right of eminent domain over land containing buildings owned by a state or local government.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that a Jehovah's Witness minister could appeal his classification without first appearing at induction camp.
The Court held that attempting a second execution of a man in the electric chair, after the first attempt failed, did not constitute double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment.

The Court recognized the work-product doctrine, which holds that information obtained or produced by or for attorneys in anticipation of litigation may be protected from discovery under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
The Court held that the Hatch Act of 1939, as amended in 1940, does not violate the First, Fifth, Ninth, or Tenth amendments to U.S. Constitution.
The Court held that the Hatch Act of 1939 did not violate the Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court held that a preference for nepotism is an acceptable rational basis for a state policy.

The Court affirmed the conviction of Hans Max Haupt—father of Herbert Hans Haupt— for treason, and that after the Constitution's Treason Clause's two witness requirement is satisfied, it does not preclude the prosecution from entering out-of-court confessions into evidence.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of the National Labor Relations Act of 1935, also known as the Wagner Act.

In a dispute over the three-mile marginal belt along California's coast, the Court held that California did not own it and that the Federal Government had paramount rights and full dominion over its resources, including oil.

The United States Supreme Court held that the Sherman Act prohibits as per se violations all tying arrangements in which a product for which a seller has a legal monopoly, such as a patent, requires purchasers to buy as well a product for which the seller has no legal monopoly.

The Supreme Court of the United States found that courts have only limited scope of review over a Selective Service Board's classification of a Jehovah's Witness as a conscientious objector rather than a minister.

The Court ruled that specific provisions of the 1913 and 1920 California Alien Land Laws abridged the rights and privileges guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment to Fred Oyama, a U.S. citizen in whose name his father, a Japanese citizen, had purchased land.
The Court allowed prosecution of criminals for income tax evasion notwithstanding the Fifth Amendment.
The Court upheld the rights of communists to hold leadership positions in labor unions.
The Court held that a facially trivial implementation of a natural principle or phenomenon of nature is not eligible for a patent.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the war powers of the United States Congress extend beyond the end of hostilities allowing them to remedy problems caused by a war after it has ended.

In a challenge to a "released time" program letting public school class time be used for religious instruction, the Court struck down the Champaign, Illinois, program as unconstitutional because of the school system's involvement in administering and supporting the classes.

The Court held that patent cross-licenses between two competing manufacturers that fixed the prices of the licensed products, with one licensing others under similar price fixing, violated Sherman Act § 1, and that knowing licensees joined a hub-and-spoke conspiracy.

The Court held that a patent licensing program that fixed prices of many licensees and regimented an entire industry violated the antitrust laws, and later held that relief did not let compulsory-license licensees challenge the patents' validity.

The Court ruled that a New York Penal Law section banning publication of periodicals dealing in criminal deeds was applied so vaguely that it violated the First Amendment, as applied through the Fourteenth.
The Court held that jury verdicts must be unanimous for federal prosecutions.
The Court held that racially restrictive housing covenants (deed restrictions) cannot legally be enforced.
The Court affirmed the district court's ruling that the film studios' distribution scheme, involving studio-owned theaters and exclusive dealing arrangements, violated United States antitrust law.
The court held that a circuit court may order that an imprisoned person appear before it to argue an appeal.

The court held that a migratory divorce is entitled to res judicata when both parties participated in the action, both parties had the opportunity to contest personal jurisdiction, and the forum state does not allow the divorce to be collaterally attacked.

In a challenge by Japanese-American fishermen to a California law barring "aliens ineligible to citizenship" from getting fishing licenses, the Court held the restriction unreasonable and discriminatory against residents of Japanese ancestry.
The court held that the Full Faith and Credit Clause requires states to recognize a divorce granted in another state but not necessarily the incidences to that extraterritorial divorce.

The Court held that an ordinance banning sound amplification devices without the Chief of Police's permission was facially unconstitutional because it was a prior restraint on free speech in violation of the First Amendment.
The Court ruled that warrantless searches following arrests were unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Court held that a labor union's publication of a statement that advocated for its members to vote for a certain candidate for Congress did not violate the Federal Corrupt Practices Act, as amended by the 1947 Labor Management Relations Act.
The Court held that the Alien Enemies Act precluded judicial review of executive orders to remove foreign nationals from the United States during wartime.
The Court denied a federal district court jurisdiction to issue a writ of habeas corpus if the person detained is not within the territorial jurisdiction of the court when the petition is filed.
The Court upheld a Michigan law, which prohibited women from being licensed as a bartender in all cities having a population of 50,000 or more unless their father or husband owned the establishment.
The Court held that a state may create an employment right for its citizens that prevents their being denied employment because they are not members of a union.

The Court held that a Chicago "breach of peace" ordinance banning speech that stirred the public to anger, invited dispute, brought about unrest, or created a disturbance was unconstitutional under the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

The Court ruled that a petroleum conglomerate had illegally monopolized the American petroleum industry and ordered it to break itself up, while holding that antitrust law bans only "unreasonable" restraints on trade.

The Court held that lump sums paid in advance by publications to non-resident aliens are taxable income under the Revenue Act and are indistinguishable from "royalties" paid over time within the meaning of that Act.

The Court held that federal courts sitting in diversity should begin the running of the statute of limitations for a claim according to state law instead of according to the federal rules of civil procedure.
The court ruled that the tax violated the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of 28 U.S.C. §1332(e). §1332(e) treats citizens of United States territories as citizens of a state for the purpose of establishing diversity jurisdiction.

The Court affirmed the principle set forth in The West River Bridge Company v. Dix et al., 47 U.S. 507 (1848); that is, that intangible property rights are condemnable via the eminent domain power, and that just compensation must be given to the owners of such rights.

The Court held 6-3 that, while the Fourth Amendment was applicable to the states, the exclusionary rule was not a necessary ingredient of the Fourth Amendment's right against warrantless and unreasonable searches and seizures.
The court ruled that the use of a confession obtained through rigorous interrogation methods by law enforcement violates the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court, in a case about warrantless searches, held that police need not always be factually correct in conducting such a search, but the search must always be reasonable.
The Court held that warrantless searches immediately following an arrest are constitutional.

The Court ruled that Dennis did not have the right under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution to exercise free speech, publication and assembly, if the exercise involved the creation of a plot to overthrow the government.

The Court held that the Taft–Hartley Act's anti-communist oath requirement for labor union leaders did not violate the First Amendment, was not an ex post facto law or bill of attainder, and was not a prohibited test oath.

A Black man was refused admission to a state law school because the state constitution prohibited integrated education, and the Court ruled in his favor, reasoning that the racially separate law school was in fact unequal.
The Court prohibited racial segregation in state supported graduate or professional education.
The court held that for federal question jurisdiction to exist over a lawsuit seeking a declaratory judgment, the lawsuit must state a claim that raises a federal question.
It decided that US courts had no jurisdiction over German war criminals held in a US-administered prison in Germany.
Abolished segregation in railroad dining cars with an 8-0 ruling.

The Court ruled that a petroleum conglomerate had illegally monopolized the American petroleum industry and ordered it to break itself up, while holding that antitrust law bans only "unreasonable" restraints on trade.

In a hearing combining three federal cases, the Court held that the United States was not liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for injuries to armed forces members on active duty caused by the negligence of others in the armed forces.
The Court held that an agreement among competitors in interstate commerce to fix maximum resale prices of their products violates the Sherman Antitrust Act.

The Court held that a Maryland city violated the free exercise of religion by refusing a permit for Jehovah's Witnesses to meet in a public park when other religious and civic groups had received permits.

The Court held that a New York City ordinance requiring permits for public religious meetings on city streets was unconstitutional because it granted officials broad discretion to approve or deny permits without clear standards.
The Court held that a court will defer to a federal agency's findings of fact if supported by "substantial evidence on the record considered as a whole."

The court held that the Full Faith and Credit Clause prevents a third-party from challenging the validity of a divorce granted in a different state if that other state would not allow them to challenge the divorce.

The Supreme Court ruled that because the man had complete control of the money, his tax payment was correct and he could not get a refund—though he could still claim it as a loss on a subsequent tax return.

The Court held that "imitation jam", so labeled, was not a "misbranded" product under § 403 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938, 21 U.S.C. § 343, even though it did not meet federal regulations for being fruit jam.
The court held that the United States Court of Claims was an Article I tribunal.
The Court held that groups could sue to challenge their inclusion on the Attorney General's List of Subversive Organizations.

The Court ruled that Dennis did not have the right under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution to exercise free speech, publication and assembly, if the exercise involved the creation of a plot to overthrow the government.
The Court held that door-to-door solicitation could be restricted without violating the Due Process Clause, the First Amendment or the Commerce Clause.

The Court held that a municipal loyalty oath which required an oath and affidavit about one's beliefs and actions for the previous five years and which was enacted more than five years previous is not an ex post facto law nor a bill of attainder.

The Court held that a newspaper publisher who refused advertising from those who also advertised on a competing local radio station had attempted to monopolize trade in violation of § 2 of the Sherman Act and was properly enjoined.
The Court reversed the conviction of a scrap collector who sold spent bomb casings from an Air Force range he thought abandoned, holding that a crime requires criminal intent.

The court held that a sentence imposed pursuant to a plea agreement under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(c)(1)(C) is "based on" the defendant's Guidelines range so long as that range was part of the framework the district court relied on in imposing the sentence or accepting the agreement.

The Court held that a claim of conspiracy to fix uniform minimum prices and to eliminate competition throughout substantially all of the wrinkle finish industry of the United States by means of patent license agreements was, if proved, a violation of § 1 of the Sherman Act.

The Court held that an Ohio state court could exercise general personal jurisdiction over a foreign corporation on the basis of that company's "continuous and systematic" contacts with the state of Ohio.
The Court held that kidnapping of a defendant by State authorities for the purpose of taking a suspect from one jurisdiction to another for criminal trial, is constitutional.

The Court determined that the Alien Registration Act of 1940's authorization of deportation of legal residents for membership, even past, in communist parties did not violate the First Amendment, the Fifth Amendment, nor the constitution's Ex Post Facto Clause.
The Court upheld the convictions of five attorneys for contempt of court.

The Court ruled that states may constitutionally allow parties to require presidential elector candidates to pledge to vote for the party's nominees, and that denying the position to candidates who refused the pledge did not breach their rights.

The Court ruled that states may constitutionally allow parties to require presidential elector candidates to pledge to vote for the party's nominees, and that denying the position to candidates who refused the pledge did not breach their rights.

The Court upheld an Illinois law making it illegal to publish or exhibit any writing or picture portraying the "depravity, criminality, unchastity, or lack of virtue of a class of citizens of any race, color, creed or religion".

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a school district allowing students to leave a public school for part of the day to receive off-site religious instruction did not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court upheld a ruling that the dominant concrete block-making machine manufacturer violated antitrust laws through acquisitions, patent abuses and licensing vetoes, and approved compulsory reasonable-royalty licensing of its patents and compulsory sales of machines.

The Court held that the Federal Trade Commission has broad discretion to fashion cease and desist orders for Robinson–Patman Act violations, and that reviewing courts should not modify its remedy unless it bears no reasonable relation to the unlawful practices found.

The Court held that New York Education Law provisions letting a censor forbid commercial showing of films deemed "sacrilegious" were a restraint on freedom of speech and violated the First Amendment, overturning its earlier Mutual Film decision.
The Court limited the president's power to seize private property in a case arising when President Truman seized steel production facilities during the Korean War to head off a strike.
The Court held that cash contest prizes are taxable, and attributable to the most-recent thirty-six months ending with the close of the year in which it was received.
The Court ruled that a dual U.S./Japanese citizen could be convicted of treason against the United States for acts performed in Japan during World War II.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of placing the burden of persuasion on the defendant when they argue an insanity defense in a criminal trial.

The Court considered whether taxpayers' payment of a judgment against a corporation they had earlier liquidated was an ordinary business loss, and held it was a capital loss, agreeing with the Second Circuit.

The Court held that a person born in the United States, with both U.S. citizenship and a foreign citizenship obtained via an alien parent or parents, does not need to live in or return to the United States as an adult in order to retain U.S. citizenship.

The Court held that Oklahoma loyalty oath legislation violated the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution because it did not give individuals the opportunity to abjure membership in subversive organizations.

The Court held that exclusive output contracts used by four major companies, which foreclosed 75 percent of available outlets to competitors, fell within the Sherman Act's prohibitions and were an unfair method of competition under § 5 of the FTC Act.

The Court held that a lawful permanent resident, who departs from and returns to the country as a seaman on an American ship, retains procedural due process rights and cannot be deported under 8 CFR § 175.57(b) without a hearing.
The US Supreme Court confirmed that "the privilege against revealing military secrets... is well established in the law of evidence".
The Court held certain provisions of the Revenue Act of 1951 were constitutional, in particular sections related to an occupational tax on persons involved in gambling.

The Court held that a municipal ordinance used to penalize a Jehovah's Witnesses minister for preaching at a peaceful religious meeting in a public park, while other religious groups could hold services there, violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

The court held that a collective bargaining agreement may include a stipulation that employees are required to cross pocket lines, or the agreement may include a stipulation that employees cannot be forced to cross picket lines.
The Court upheld the prolonged immigration detention of an alien who, on confidential information and without a hearing, was denied admission to the United States.

The Court held that a New Hampshire city ordinance on permission to hold meetings in a public park did not violate the appellant's free exercise rights, even if his group was arbitrarily and unlawfully denied a license for a religious meeting.

The Court held that white-only pre-primary elections, such as those the Jaybird Democratic Association organized for county offices in Fort Bend County, were unconstitutional, finding for the black voters who sued.

The Court unanimously ruled that a cafeteria's segregating policies were illegal, in a case over the validity of 1872 and 1873 Acts that prohibited segregation in public places in the District of Columbia.

The Court held that a corporation offering equity stock shares to "key employees" was eligible for the transaction-based exemption from securities registration under Section 4(1) of the Securities Act of 1933.
The Court upheld, 7–2, the antitrust exemption first granted to Major League Baseball (MLB) three decades earlier in Federal Baseball Club v. National League.

In a suit by Arkansas against Texas over a foundation's contract with the University of Arkansas, the Court held that the suit was between two states and that the Foundation was not an indispensable party.

The Supreme Court of the United States held there was no basis for denying a petitioner's (a Jehovah's Witness) claim to ministerial exemption from military service, and his conviction for refusing to submit to his local board's induction order was reversed.

By a 7–2 margin the Court held that the provisions of the Securities Act of 1933 barring any waiver of rights under that statute took precedence over the Federal Arbitration Act's (FAA) requirement that arbitration clauses in contracts be given full effect by federal courts.
The Court held that administrative agencies in the Federal Government are obliged to follow their own regulations, policies and procedures.
The Court ruled that a mail order reseller was not required to collect a use tax unless it had sufficient contact with the state.
In a unanimous ruling, the court held that Mexican Americans and all other nationality groups in the United States have equal protection under the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution.

The Court ruled that U.S. state laws establishing racial segregation in public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, even if the segregated facilities are equal in quality.
The Court held that the Constitution prohibits segregated public schools in the District of Columbia.
The Court held that sale of natural gas at the wellhead was subject to regulation under the Natural Gas Act.
The court held that Congress may provide for the at-will removal of territorial offices, even if such officers exercise judicial functions.
By a 7–2 margin, the justices ruled that the exemption it had previously upheld for Major League Baseball was peculiar and unique to that sport and that it did not apply to boxing.
The court held that a Tribal nation's right of occupancy (or "aboriginal title") may be eliminated by the United States without any compensation.
The court held that state law, rather than federal admiralty law, should govern marine insurance contracts.
The Supreme Court of the United States upheld a draft board's rejection of Jehovah's Witness claim of conscientious objector status as lacking sincerity.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that willingness to fight in "theocratic" wars does not disqualify a Jehovah's Witness who would otherwise be eligible for exemption as a conscientious objector.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that a Jehovah's Witness was denied fair hearing because of failure to supply him with materials in his record.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a Jehovah's Witness was denied fair hearing because of failure to supply him with materials in his record.
The Court held that state laws regulating business are only subject to rational basis review and that courts need not contemplate all possible reasons for legislation.

The Court held that a non-citizen subject to a final order of deportation under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 could obtain judicial review by bringing an action for declaratory and injunctive relief under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The Court ruled that U.S. state laws establishing racial segregation in public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, even if the segregated facilities are equal in quality.
The Court expanded the rights of citizens to civilian trials, holding that an ex-serviceman cannot be court-martialed for crimes alleged during his military service.

The court held that, when an employer has committed an unfair labor practice, strikes in protest of that practice are protected by the National Labor Relations Act even when the collective bargaining agreement includes a no-strike clause.
The court held that a person given immunity from prosecution loses their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination, thus upholding the Constitutionality of the Immunity Act of 1954.
The Court ruled that the federal Smith Act superseded the Pennsylvania Sedition Act, even though the state law came first, in a case where a man was convicted of sedition under the state law.
United States Supreme Court held that a criminal defendant may not be denied the right to appeal by inability to pay for a trial transcript.

The Court upheld the constitutionality of a statute requiring organizations found to be controlled by the "world Communist movement" to register and disclose officers, funds, and membership, rejecting First and Fifth Amendment challenges.

The Court held that laws criminalizing the sale of non-obscene literature to adults because of its perceived unsuitability for children were unconstitutional under the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court ruled that involuntary blood samples, taken by a skilled technician to determine intoxication, do not violate substantive due process under the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution.
The Court ruled that professional football, unlike professional baseball, was subject to antitrust laws, declining to extend to football the exemption that baseball had received.

The Court held that the federal government must produce documents relied upon by government witnesses in federal criminal proceedings, in a case where a union president was convicted of filing a false non-Communist affidavit.

The Court held that United States citizen civilians outside of the territorial jurisdiction of the United States cannot be tried by a United States military tribunal, but instead retain the protections guaranteed by the United States Constitution, in this case, trial by jury.

The Court held that the power of the United States Congress is not unlimited in conducting investigations and that nothing in the United States Constitution gives it the authority to expose the private affairs of individuals.
The Court ruled that jailing an academic when he refused to answer questions about university lectures he had given was a violation of due process.

The Court, in a case on what counts as obscene material unprotected by the First Amendment, created a new test for obscenity, upheld the defendant's conviction and allowed some obscenity prosecutions, while drastically loosening obscenity laws.
The Court refused to stop the executive branch from handing United States Army soldier William S. Girard over to Japanese authorities for trial.
The Court held that perjury from a prosecution witness is a due process violation when the prosecutor knows the witness testimony is false.
The Court upheld the conviction of Junius Scales for violating of the Smith Act on the basis on his membership in the Communist Party of the United States (CPUSA).
Provided a basis for a broad reading of the "short and plain statement" requirement for pleading under Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

The Court declared that California did not violate the Due Process Clause by entering a judgment upon a Texas insurance company who was engaged in a dispute over a policy it maintained with a California resident.

The court held that when one is required to register one's presence, failure to register may be punished only when there is a probability that the accused party had knowledge of the law before committing the crime of failing to register.

The Court held that coordination between federal and state officials did not implicate double jeopardy, and that a defendant acquitted of a federal crime could be convicted of a state crime on the same evidence without violating due process.

The Court affirmed Congress's right to revoke United States citizenship as a result of a citizen's voluntary performance of specified actions, even in the absence of any intent or desire on the person's part to lose citizenship.
The Court ruled that it was unconstitutional to revoke citizenship as a punishment for a crime.

The Court ruled that a dual United States/Japanese citizen who had served in the Japanese military during World War II could not be denaturalized unless the United States could prove that he had acted voluntarily.
Unanimously, the Court overturned the conviction of a recovering New York drug addict who had been repeatedly solicited for drug sales by a fellow former addict who was working with federal agents.
The Court held that a taxpayer generally must pay the full amount of an income tax deficiency assessed by the Commissioner before challenging its correctness in a federal district court refund suit.
The Court held that the government violated the right to travel and First Amendment free speech rights when it suspended people's passports based on their political speech.
The Court held that one could not lawfully be arrested in one's home by officers breaking in without first giving one notice of their authority and purpose.
The Court held that the President's plenary removal authority does not include an officer of the United States who exercises quasi-judicial authority.
The Court held that the officers involved in the case did not take advantage of petitioner or overtake her will when eliciting the confession.

The Court limited criminal suspects' constitutional right to counsel before trial, refusing to overturn a subsequent conviction without a showing that the refusal of counsel had a coercive or prejudicial effect.

The Court held that a loyalty oath requirement for a property tax exemption violated the procedural due process rights of applicants who refused to sign, because it put the burden of proving their speech was not criminal on them rather than the state.
The Court denied the school board of Little Rock, Arkansas the right to delay racial desegregation for 30 months.
The court held that only parties to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's licensing proceedings are entitled to obtain judicial review of the Commission's licensing decisions.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the State of Arizona does not have jurisdiction to try a civil case between a non-Indian doing business on a reservation with tribal members who reside on the reservation, the proper forum for such cases being the tribal court.
The Court ruled that business may not deduct expenses they incurred for the "promotion or defeat of legislation" as "ordinary and necessary" business expenses on their federal income tax filing.
The Court held that exempting non-residents from a state tax on storing property in warehouses was constitutional.

The Court held that a Florida statute enacting the Uniform Law to Secure the Attendance of Witnesses, letting courts in two states agree to subpoena a witness, did not on its face violate the Privileges and Immunities or Due Process Clauses.

The Court expanded the circumstances in which federal courts should hold evidentiary hearings when presented with petitions for habeas corpus by state prisoners following denial of postconviction relief in state court.

The Court held that coordination between federal and state officials did not implicate double jeopardy, and that a defendant acquitted of a federal crime could be convicted of a state crime on the same evidence without violating due process.
The Court held that the Fifth Amendment's Double Jeopardy Clause did not bar a federal prosecution for a conspiracy that had already resulted in a state court conviction under state law.
The Court held that a retail chain's persuasion of a number of suppliers not to deal with a competitive retailer was a per se illegal boycott – under a hub-and-spoke conspiracy theory.

The Court ruled in favor of health inspectors who sought to enter a man's home to check for a rat infestation, reasoning that the search would benefit the public more than it intruded on his privacy interests.
The court held that where legal and equitable claims are joined in the same action, the legal claims must be tried by a jury before the equitable claims can be resolved.
The Court held that the Illinois law requiring trucks to have unique mudguards was unconstitutional under the Commerce Clause.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the actions of the House Un-American Activities Committee did not violate the First Amendment and, thus, the Court upheld Lloyd Barenblatt's conviction for contempt of Congress.

The Court held that the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia should have abstained from deciding the constitutionality of three barratry, champerty, and maintenance laws in the state of Virginia until state courts had had a reasonable chance to construe them.

The Court held that a prosecutor's knowing use of false testimony in a criminal case violates the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, even if it affects only the witness's credibility and not the defendant's guilt or innocence.

The Court held that a federal executive official who issues a press release about their official duties is absolutely immune from libel suits, so the acting director could not be sued over his press release about two former employees.

The United States Supreme Court held that "in the case of a lawful custodial arrest a full search of the person is not only an exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment, but is also a reasonable search under that Amendment."
The Court held that the First Amendment forbade state governments from compelling disclosure of an organization's membership lists through a tax-exemption regulatory scheme.

The Court held that a company that went beyond the Colgate doctrine by taking affirmative steps to induce adherence to its suggested prices formed a price-fixing combination among competitors, violating § 1 of the Sherman Act.

The Court overturned the ruling of a U.S. District Court, which had held that a law authorizing the Federal Government to bring civil actions against State Officials for discriminating against African-Americans citizens was unconstitutional.

The Court determined that the Federal Power Commission was authorized to take lands owned by the Tuscarora Nation by eminent domain under the Federal Power Act for a hydroelectric power project, upon payment of just compensation.
The Court held that a taxpayer generally must pay the full amount of an income tax deficiency assessed by the Commissioner before challenging its correctness in a federal district court refund suit.
The Court unanimously held that it is a violation of due process to convict a person of an offense when there is no evidence of his guilt.
The Court held the executor of a copyright holder's will is eligible to renew that copyright.

The court held that, after the Civil Rights Act of 1960 was signed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower on May 6, 1960, the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Alabama now had jurisdiction to hear a challenge against Alabama for violations of the Civil Rights Act of 1957.

The Court ruled that an interstate compact restricting convicted felons from holding union office was not preempted by federal labor law, did not violate due process, and was not an ex post facto law or bill of attainder.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of Section 1104 of the 1935 Social Security Act.
The court held that a court of admiralty has no inherent power, independent of any statute or rule, to order the taking of depositions for the purpose of discovery.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a Jehovah's Witness was denied fair hearing because of failure to supply him with materials in his record.
The court, in a 5–4 decision, upheld the trespassing conviction of six African-American men who were barred from a golf course because of their race.

The Court held the "silver platter doctrine", which allowed federal prosecutors to use evidence illegally gathered by state police, to be a violation of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court found an electoral district with boundaries created to disenfranchise African Americans violated the Fifteenth Amendment.
The Court ruled for the IRS and denied a taxpayer's claimed deduction on money he borrowed to buy a tax-deferred annuity.

The Court overturned the trespassing conviction of an African American law student who sat in a "whites only" bus terminal restaurant, holding that racial segregation in public transportation violated the Interstate Commerce Act.
By a 5–4 vote, the Court struck down an Arkansas law imposing disclosure requirements on public schoolteachers, reasoning that they were unconstitutionally overbroad.

The Court confirmed that federal district judges utilize, in an advisory (not as law) fashion, Federal Sentencing Guidelines, in cases involving conduct related to possession, distribution, and manufacture of crack cocaine.
In two cases involving limits on freedom of expression for motion pictures, the Court affirmed the right of local governments to engage in some form of censorship.

The Court considered federal civil rights law applied to constitutional violations by city employees and held that 42 U.S.C. § 1983 could be used to sue state officers who violated a plaintiff's constitutional rights.

The Court sustained the conviction of a housing administrator who refused to tell a congressional subcommittee whether he was a Communist Party member, upholding the conviction under the statute criminalizing refusal to answer pertinent questions from Congress.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the conviction of the petitioner, Carl Braden, based on his refusal to answer questions posed to him by the House Un-American Activities Committee, did not violate his First Amendment rights and was constitutional.

The Court unanimously held that a federal officer may not, without warrant, physically place themselves into the space of a person's office or home to secretly observe or listen and relate at the man's subsequent criminal trial what was seen or heard.
The Court decided that the Equal Protection Clause applies to private business that operates in a relationship to a government that is close to the point that it becomes a "state actor."
The Court held that asking a criminal defendant whether he had testified in previous trials violated his Fifth Amendment rights.
The Court held that denying a bar applicant's character and fitness because they would not answer questions about membership in the Communist Party did not violate the applicant's rights.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of an Alaskan law that imposed an annual tax on freezer ships operating in Alaskan waters, even if the fish onboard is canned and sold in another state.

The court held that the petitioner (Montana) was not a U.S. Citizen on the grounds that the petitioner did not earn citizenship through R.S. § 2172 as was argued, or R.S. § 1993 which provided citizenship to foreign-born children whose fathers were citizens.

The Court affirmed the Maryland State Supreme Court's decision that the state's Sunday closing laws did not have a religious purpose to aid religion and that the secular purpose of the legislation to set aside a day of rest and recreation did not violate the Establishment Clause.
The Court declared that a kosher butcher store had to abide by the state laws that banned them from selling on Sunday.

The Court held that blue laws, which prohibited most businesses from operating on Sundays, did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause nor the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.

In a 6–3 decision, the Court held that a Pennsylvania blue law forbidding the sale of various retail products on Sunday was not an unconstitutional interference with religion as described in the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court upheld the conviction of Junius Scales for violating of the Smith Act on the basis on his membership in the Communist Party of the United States (CPUSA).
The Court reversed the felony conviction of a lower-echelon official of the Communist Party USA (CPUSA).
The Court held that judges of the Court of Claims and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals were judges created under Article III of the Constitution (also known as Article III judges).
The Court ruled that the exclusionary rule, which bars prosecutors from using evidence obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment, also applies to the states.
The Court unanimously overturned a Missouri Supreme Court decision upholding the forfeiture of hundreds of magazines confiscated from a Kansas City wholesaler.
In a case where a man was convicted and sentenced to death in Alabama, the Court ruled unanimously that the absence of counsel at his arraignment violated his Fourteenth Amendment due process rights.

The Court overturned the convictions of three white men who conspired against black sawmill workers, holding that Congress lacked the power under the Thirteenth Amendment to intervene against racially motivated interference with labor contracts.
The Court unanimously ruled that Louisiana could not convict peaceful sit-in protesters who refused to leave dining establishments under the state's "disturbing the peace" laws.

The court held that due process does not require advance notice that the trial on the substantive offense will be followed by a habitual criminal accusation, but it does require a reasonable opportunity to defend against such an accusation.
The court held that a binding arbitration stipulation in a collective bargaining agreement constitutes a limited, implied no-strike clause over the matters subject to arbitration.
The Court vacated a lower appellate court decision, holding that federal courts should abstain from ruling on the constitutionality of a state tax issue that state courts should determine.
The court held that acquittals in criminal cases are final even if issued by mistake.

The Court held that redistricting qualifies as a justiciable question under the Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause, thus enabling federal courts to hear Fourteenth Amendment-based redistricting cases.
The court held that a transfer to a venue with personal jurisdiction is proper even if the court the case transferred from did not have personal jurisdiction.

The Court ruled that intensive and voluminous news coverage in the vicinity where the defendant was indicted and tried did not violate the Due Process or Equal Protection Clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Supreme Court ruled that a walk-out was protected activity even if workers did not present "a specific demand upon their employer to remedy a condition they found objectionable."
The Court held that a taxpayer recognizes a gain on the transfer of appreciated property in satisfaction of a legal obligation.
The court held that the Norris–LaGuardia Act prohibits injunctive relief as a remedy for the breach of a no-strike clause.
The court held that, when a union is liable for damages for violation of the no-strike clause, its officers and members are not liable for these damages.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that strongly-worded criticism of an ongoing grand jury investigation does not constitute a clear and present danger.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that corporate officers acting in their duties could be subject to sanctions under the Sherman Antitrust Act.
The Court ruled that it is unconstitutional for state officials to compose an official school prayer and encourage its recitation in public schools, due to violation of the First Amendment.
The Court held that judges of the Court of Claims and the Court of Customs and Patent Appeals were judges created under Article III of the Constitution (also known as Article III judges).
The Court struck down a California law that criminalized being addicted to narcotics, in a decision interpreting the Eighth Amendment to prohibit particular acts or conduct from being punished.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that block booking of movies—the offer of only a combined assortment of movies to an exhibitor—violates the Sherman Antitrust Act.
The court first ruled that state inmates had the right to file a writ of habeas corpus challenging both the legality and the conditions of their imprisonment.

The Court held that a federal district court's reservation of jurisdiction did not bar its review of a state court ruling, and it overturned Virginia's 1956 laws targeting the NAACP's litigation as violating the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

The Court held that the actions of the Rhode Island Commission to Encourage Morality in Youth, which involved pressuring distributors to stop selling certain publications, violated the First Amendment by creating an unconstitutional system of informal censorship.

The Court held that, under the accrual method, taxpayers must include as income in a particular year advance payments by way of cash, negotiable notes, and contract installments falling due but remaining unpaid during that year.
The Court ruled that the First and Fourteenth Amendments forbade state government officials from forcing a crowd to disperse when it was otherwise legally marching in front of a state house.

The Court expanded the circumstances in which federal courts should hold evidentiary hearings when presented with petitions for habeas corpus by state prisoners following denial of postconviction relief in state court.

The Court ruled that the Sixth Amendment requires states to provide attorneys to criminal defendants who cannot afford their own, extending the right to counsel from the federal government to the states.

The Court held that state prisoners were entitled to federal habeas relief even if they had not pursued a state-court remedy that was no longer available to them, unless they had deliberately bypassed the orderly procedure of state courts.
The Court held that a preliminary hearing where the defendant enters a plea is a critical stage in the criminal trial that attaches the Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
The Court held that under the Due Process Clause, the prosecution must turn over to a criminal defendant any significant evidence in its possession that suggests the defendant is not guilty.

The Court held that the duty of self-regulation imposed upon the New York Stock Exchange by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 did not exempt it from the antitrust laws nor justify its in denying petitioners the direct-wire connections without the notice and hearing which they requested.
The court upheld that the requirement of employees paying union fees as a condition of employment does not violate federal labor law, whether they formally join the union or not.
The Court held that the defendant Singer violated the antitrust laws by conspiring with two European competitors to exclude Japanese sewing machine competition from the US market.

The Court decided 8–1 in favor of the respondent, Edward Schempp, on behalf of his son Ellery Schempp, and declared that school-sponsored Bible reading and the recitation of the Lord's Prayer in public schools in the United States was unconstitutional.

The Court held that the Free Exercise Clause required the government to show a compelling interest and narrow tailoring before denying unemployment compensation to a woman fired because her job conflicted with her religion.

The Court held that when respondent George Fleuti, a Swiss national who had lived in the United States as a permanent resident since 1952, had briefly traveled from the United States to Mexico and then returned, he had not engaged in an "entry" within the meaning of the INA.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that service of process upon a party's designated agent does not invalidate personal jurisdiction that would otherwise be established, if the agent gives prompt notice to the party.
The Court held unconstitutional a Louisiana statute that required that the race of all candidates be listed on ballots.
The Court ruled that U.S. House districts must be approximately equal in population, in a challenge to the unequal population of congressional districts in Georgia.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that evidence of racial consideration cannot be elevated to prima facie proof when several plausible conflicting inferences that could be drawn from that evidence were "equally or more persuasive".
The Court limited state law on unfair competition when it prevents the copying of an item that is not covered by a patent.
Was a companion case to Sears, Roebuck & Co. v. Stiffel Co. that the Court decided on the same day.
The Court held that the freedom of speech protections in the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution limit the ability of public officials to sue for defamation.
The Supreme Court struck down a Birmingham, Alabama ordinance that prohibited citizens from holding parades and processions on city streets without first obtaining a permit.

The Court determined that the policy of United States federal courts would be to honor the Act of State Doctrine, which dictates that the propriety of decisions of other countries relating to their internal affairs would not be questioned in the courts of the United States.
The court held that only parties to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's licensing proceedings are entitled to obtain judicial review of the Commission's licensing decisions.
The Court extended the situations in which search warrants are required and reversed a robbery conviction that rested on evidence from a hotel room searched with only the desk clerk's permission.

The court held that rights of employees under a collective bargaining agreement are not automatically lost by the disappearance by merger of the employer, and, in appropriate circumstances, the successor employer may be required to arbitrate under the contract.
The Court held that when a case is transferred from a federal court in one state to a federal court in another, the choice of law should be that of the state in which the case was originally filed.

The Court held that a probable-cause hearing where a court decides whether there is sufficient evidence to present to a grand jury has a Sixth Amendment right-to-counsel requiring the appointment of a lawyer for the defendant.
The Court invalidated a law that stripped naturalized Americans of their citizenship as a result of extended or permanent residence abroad.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution does not allow the government to elicit statements from a person, without their attorney present, after their Sixth Amendment right to counsel is enlivened.

The Court held that a state cannot require an employee to take an unduly vague oath containing a promise of future conduct at the risk of prosecution for perjury or loss of employment, particularly where the exercise of First Amendment freedoms may thereby be deterred.
The Court extended the repair-reconstruction doctrine of Aro Mfg.

The court held that corporate shareholders have an implied private right of action to bring suit under Section 14(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for materially false or misleading proxy statements.
The Court ruled that the single-seat electoral districts of state legislative chambers must be roughly equal in population.
The Court, in one of a series of 1964 cases, ruled that state legislature districts had to be roughly equal in population.
The majority decision holds that the Fourteenth Amendment allows the federal government to enforce the first eight amendments on state governments.

The Court held that a search warrant affidavit may rest on hearsay, but the magistrate must be told the underlying circumstances relied on by the informant and those supporting the conclusion that the undisclosed informant was credible or reliable.

The Supreme Court of the United States reversed the convictions of five African Americans who were arrested during a protest of a privately owned amusement park by a park employee who was also a deputy sheriff.
The Court reversed the breach of peace and criminal trespass convictions of five African Americans who were refused service at a lunch counter of a department store.

The Court reversed the convictions of white and African American people refused restaurant service, holding that a Florida rule requiring separate lavatories for restaurants serving both races entangled the state in discrimination, violating the Equal Protection Clause.

By a 7–2 margin, the Court held that a seizure of the books was unconstitutional, since no hearing had been held on whether the books were obscene, and it reversed a Kansas Supreme Court decision that upheld the seizure.

The Court, in a case over criminal trespass convictions of twelve African American students at a private restaurant, vacated the Maryland Court of Appeals' judgment and remanded because the state law had changed.

The US Supreme Court held that due process prohibits retroactive application of any judicial construction of a criminal statute that is unexpected and indefensible by reference to the law that has been expressed prior to the conduct in issue.
The Court held that criminal suspects have a right to counsel during police interrogations under the Sixth Amendment.

The Court held that a contract calling for payment of patent royalties after the expiration of the licensed patent was misuse of the patent right and unenforceable under the Supremacy Clause, state contract law notwithstanding.

The Court reversed the Ohio Supreme Court, holding that the record did not show probable cause for a warrantless arrest, so evidence found in the search incident to that arrest was inadmissible and the conviction was vacated.
The United States Supreme Court ruled unanimously that a cohabitation law of Florida, part of the state's anti-miscegenation laws, was unconstitutional.

The Court held that using independent contractors to replace all maintenance workers without consulting the union bargaining representative of those employees violates the National Labor Relations Act.

The Court held that the Commerce Clause gave the U.S. Congress power to force private businesses to abide by Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, religion, or national origin in public accommodations.
The Court unanimously held that Congress acted within its Commerce Clause power when it forbade racial discrimination in restaurants, because such discrimination burdened interstate commerce.
The Court held that a state government cannot employ "breach of the peace" statutes against protesters engaging in peaceable demonstrations that may potentially incite violence.
The Court held that a state government cannot employ "breach of the peace" statutes against protesters engaging in peaceable demonstrations that may potentially incite violence.
In a dispute among three states over which could escheat intangible personal property such as uncashed checks, the Court ruled that authority lay with the state of the creditor's last known address.

In a case over government-operated film rating boards, the Court ruled that a board could only approve a film, not ban it, and had to approve a film within a reasonable time or go to court to stop its showing in theatres.

Dealt with an "interpretation test" permitted by the Louisiana Constitution of 1921 alleged to deprive Louisiana Negroes of voting rights in violation of 42 U.S.C. Section 1971(a) and the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments.

The Court ruled that the military draft exemption for conscientious objectors covered not only those who believed in a supreme being but also those whose sincere and meaningful beliefs held a place in their lives parallel to that of God.
The court held that lockouts are not considered unfair labor practices under the National Labor Relations Act of 1935.
In a diversity case about whether federal rules on service of process or state rules should govern, the Court ruled that federal courts shall apply the federal rule under the facts of the case.
The Court ruled that Virginia's partial elimination of the poll tax violated the Twenty-fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The court held that failure to provide notice of pending adoption proceedings to the adversely situated biological parent is a violation of due process.

The Court held that a court may consider post-acquisition evidence of the effect of a merger upon market competition when determining whether a merger violated antitrust law, but that consideration must not be conclusive on its own.

The Court ruled, by a 6–2 vote, that it is a violation of a defendant's Fifth Amendment rights for the prosecutor to comment to the jury on the defendant's declining to testify, or for the judge to instruct the jury that such silence is evidence of guilt.
The Court held that the comprehensive federal regulatory regime for trade on Indian reservations preempted a state income tax on that trade.
The Court ruled that civil forfeiture could not apply where the evidence used to invoke the forfeiture was obtained illegally.

The Court held that the Secretary of State was statutorily authorized to refuse to validate United States citizens' passports for travel to Cuba, and that this grant of authority was constitutionally permissible.

In a dispute over the three-mile marginal belt along California's coast, the Court held that California did not own it and that the Federal Government had paramount rights and full dominion over its resources, including oil.

The ruling of the Supreme Court struck down § 305(a) of the Postal Service and Federal Employees Salary Act of 1962, a federal statute requiring the Postmaster General to detain and deliver only upon the addressee's request unsealed foreign mailings of "communist political propaganda."
The Court upheld the rights of communists to hold leadership positions in labor unions.

The court held that the statute was unconstitutional, and that its effect was "to deny disadvantaged citizens... access to medical assistance and up-to-date information in respect to proper methods of birth control."

The United States Supreme Court overturned the fraud conviction of petitioner Billy Sol Estes, holding that his Fourteenth Amendment due process rights had been violated by the publicity associated with the pretrial hearing, which had been carried live on both television and radio.
The Court held that the Constitution neither prohibits nor requires that new interpretations of constitutional criminal rights have retrospective effect.

The Court ruled that people believed to be Communist Party members could not be required to register with the Subversive Activities Control Board, because the required information could be used to prosecute them and so violated their Fifth Amendment self-incrimination rights.
The Supreme Court struck down a Birmingham, Alabama ordinance that prohibited citizens from holding parades and processions on city streets without first obtaining a permit.
In a patent-license price-fixing case, the Court was evenly split and affirmed the lower court's decision without issuing an opinion, leaving the question inconclusive.
The court held that because bankruptcy courts sit in equity, they may order the forfeiture of property without seating a jury to find facts.

The Court clarified the nonobviousness requirement in patent law, confirming that non-obviousness is a question of law but holding that §103 required determining factual questions to resolve obviousness.
The Court held that statutory procedure in New York State that treated prisoners differently than non-prisoners in the civil commitment process were a violation of equal protection of the laws.
The Court held that protesters have a First and Fourteenth Amendment right to engage in a peaceful sit-in at a public library.

The Court rejected a challenge from the state of South Carolina to the preclearance provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which required that some states submit changes in election districts to the attorney general of the United States (at the time, Nicholas Katzenbach).
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure did not require courts to summarily dismiss fraud cases when the complaints were based on a thorough examination.
The Court held that regarding obscenity made a decade earlier in Roth v. United States (1957).
The Court held that a novel process for making a known steroid did not satisfy the utility requirement, because the patent applicants did not show that the steroid served any practical function.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that in order for a United States district court to have pendent jurisdiction over a state-law cause of action, state and federal claims must arise from the same "common nucleus of operative fact" and the plaintiff must expect to try them all at once.

In a dispute over timber cut and sold from Indian reservation land, the Court held that the tribes did not own the land, only had a right to occupy it, and could not cut and sell timber merely to sell it.
The Court held that crimes carrying possible penalties up to six months imprisonment do not require a jury trial if they otherwise qualify as petty offenses.

The Court held that "(w)hen an administrative agency is acting in a judicial capacity and resolves disputed issues of fact properly before it which the parties have had an adequate opportunity to litigate, the courts have not hesitated to apply res judicata to enforce repose."
The Court ruled that police must warn a person in custody of their constitutional rights before interrogation, or the person's statements cannot be used as evidence against them at trial.

The Court held that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) may sue in federal court to obtain a preliminary injunction to maintain the status quo against the consummation of a merger that the agency persuasively contends violates the antitrust laws.
The Court held that forcibly extracting and analyzing a suspect's blood sample was not compelled testimony and so did not violate the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

The Court ruled that Dennis did not have the right under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution to exercise free speech, publication and assembly, if the exercise involved the creation of a plot to overthrow the government.

The Court unanimously affirmed the First Amendment rights of state legislators and held that state legislators cannot lawfully limit a fellow legislator's right to express their views on local or national policy.

The Court held that the use of an undercover federal narcotics agent with a false identity did not violate the Fourth Amendment when he entered the petitioner's home by invitation to purchase marijuana.
The Court held 6–3 that the latter requires that merely negligent intrusions into the former by the media not be civilly actionable.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that law enforcement officers and other public employees have the right to be free from compulsory self-incrimination.

The court held in a plurality decision that the Self-incrimination Clause of the Fifth Amendment applied even to attorneys in a state bar association under investigation, and an attorney asserting that right may not be disbarred for invoking it.
The Court found in favor of the petitioner (Whitus), who had been convicted for murder, and as such reversed their convictions.
A federal "harmless error" rule must apply, instead of equivalent state rules, for reviewing trials where federally-protected rights had been violated.

When a court-appointed attorney sought to withdraw from a criminal appeal as frivolous, the Court ruled that the motion must come with a brief outlining possible grounds, the appellate court must independently review the case, and the defendant may appeal pro se or with other counsel.

The Court overturned the conviction of a newsstand clerk who sold paperback sex novels, ruling that written materials neither sold to minors nor foisted on unwilling audiences were constitutionally protected.
The Court upheld Clive Michael Boutilier's deportation from the United States under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 due to his history of homosexual activities.
The Court held that judicial review of a regulation's validity was inappropriate because the controversy was not ripe for adjudication.
The Court ruled that citizens of the United States may not be deprived of their citizenship involuntarily.
Set an important legal precedent that held that a state could not authorize invidious discrimination by private landlords without entangling itself in the ensuing discriminatory private decisions.
The Court held that the Interstate Commerce Commission has authority under the Interstate Commerce Act to promulgate railroad regulations with common carrier provisions.
The Court overruled a previous case (Frank v. Maryland, 1959) and established the ability of a resident to deny entry to a building inspector without a warrant.
The Court overruled a previous case (Frank v. Maryland, 1959) and established the ability of a commercial entity to deny entry to a fire inspector without a warrant or probable cause.
The Court held that laws banning interracial marriage violate the Equal Protection and Due Process clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The Court decided that the Compulsory Process Clause of the Sixth Amendment to the Constitution (guaranteeing the right of a criminal defendant to force the attendance of witnesses for their side) is applicable in state courts as well as federal courts.
The Court held that a pretrial identification not covered by the Sixth Amendment right to counsel should be excluded if it was so unnecessarily suggestive as to violate due process.

The Court held that a federal court cannot use the abstention doctrine to avoid a constitutional issue merely because it determines that the plaintiff is unlikely to receive the relief they requested.
The Court ruled that the government could not deprive people of constitutional rights, here freedom of association, even in the interests of national security.

The United States Supreme Court ruled 5-3 that in order for the taxpayer to be allowed to deduct the cost of his meals incurred while on a business trip, the trip must have required him to stop for sleep or rest.

The Supreme Court of the United States invalidated an Oregon statute for unconstitutionally intruding into the federal realm of foreign affairs even though the statute did not conflict with any federal treaty or statute.
The Court clarified the meaning and application of Rule 19 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
The Court upheld an appeals court decision to forbid segregation of public prisons.
The court held per curiam that after a successful effort to obtain an injunction under Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, attorney's fees under Section 204(b) are generally recoverable.
The Court ruled that local government districts had to be roughly equal in population.
The court held that a suit for breach of a collective bargaining agreement can be removed to federal court under federal question jurisdiction.
The Court ruled part of the Federal Kidnapping Act unconstitutional.
The Court ruled that material that is not obscene may nonetheless be harmful for children, and its marketing may be regulated.

The Court held that if a state law defines a crime more broadly than the common understanding of that crime, a conviction under that state law cannot be used as a sentencing enhancement under the federal Armed Career Criminal Act.

The Court held that an illegitimate child's right to recover for a deceased parent could not be denied merely because of illegitimacy, since such a law would violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court held that a defendant was deprived of his rights under the Confrontation Clause if a confession by his codefendant was introduced in their joint trial, regardless of whether the jury received instructions only to consider it against the confessor.
The Court held that a business in a privately owned shopping center cannot prevent labor picketing nearby with trespass laws.

The Court ruled that a criminal prohibition against burning a draft card did not violate the First Amendment's free speech guarantee, finding the law justified by a significant government interest unrelated to suppressing speech.
The Supreme Court ruled that the Menominee Indian Tribe kept their historical hunting and fishing rights even after the federal government ceased to recognize the tribe.

The Court ruled that a state statute giving the state unlimited challenges for cause against jurors who might have any objection to the death penalty violated the constitutional right to an impartial jury.

The Court ruled that police may constitutionally stop and frisk a person they reasonably suspect to be armed and involved in a crime, without probable cause, without violating the Fourth Amendment, if reasonable suspicion rests on specific and articulable facts.

The Court held that federal taxpayers have standing to seek relief from the courts for claims that federal tax money is being used for unconstitutional purposes in violation of the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) could not be withheld because of the presence of a "substitute father" who visited a family on weekends.
By a 6–3 margin the Court affirmed the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit's reversal of a district court denial of the petition.
The Court held that receiving a television broadcast does not constitute a "performance" of a work.

The Court held that the Civil Rights Act of 1866, as codified in 42 U.S.C. § 1982, barred both private and public racial discrimination in the sale or rental of property, a valid exercise of Congress's Thirteenth Amendment power.
The Court ruled that a Texas statute criminalizing public intoxication did not violate the Eighth Amendment protection against cruel and unusual punishment.
The Court held that Ohio had violated the equal protection rights under the Fourteenth Amendment of two political parties by refusing to print their candidates' names on the ballot.
The Court invalidated an Arkansas statute prohibiting the teaching of human evolution in the public schools.

The Court held an amendment of a city charter to discriminate against minorities, and constitute a real, substantial, and invidious denial of the equal protection of the laws under the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court ruled that the state could not pass judgment concerning religious doctrine or church law.
The Court expanded the rights of incarcerated litigants.
The Supreme Court struck down a Birmingham, Alabama ordinance that prohibited citizens from holding parades and processions on city streets without first obtaining a permit.

The Court held that criminal defendants could raise claims that evidence was obtained in violation of the Fourth Amendment in a collateral attack under the federal habeas corpus statute, overruling the Eighth Circuit's contrary decision.

The Court unanimously overturned a conviction for possessing obscene films found in a man's home and invalidated state laws forbidding private possession of obscene materials on First and Fourteenth Amendment grounds.

The Court held that a New York law criminalizing publicly mutilating, defacing, defiling, or casting contempt upon the U.S. flag by words or act was partly unconstitutional because it prohibited speech against the flag.
The Court invalidated state durational residency requirements for public assistance and helped establish a fundamental "right to travel" in U.S. law.
The Court affirmed the legality of deceptive interrogation tactics by the police.
An Illinois law that denied absentee ballots to inmates awaiting trial did not violate their constitutional rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court unanimously declared the Marihuana Tax Act unconstitutional in a challenge by a man arrested for marijuana possession who argued the act required self-incrimination, and it overturned his conviction.
The Court determined that when a defendant enters into a plea bargain, they waive their Sixth Amendment right to a trial by jury.

The Court held that radio broadcasters had First Amendment free speech rights that the FCC could partially restrict to serve the public interest in equitable use of scarce frequencies, so the Fairness Doctrine was constitutional.

The Court held that the government cannot punish inflammatory speech unless it is directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce it, and struck down Ohio's criminal syndicalism statute for broadly prohibiting mere advocacy of violence.

The Court held that the Qualifications of Members Clause of Article I of the US Constitution is an exclusive list of qualifications of members of the House of Representatives, which may exclude a duly elected member for only those reasons enumerated in that clause.

In a dispute over union authorization cards under the National Labor Relations Act, the Court upheld the NLRB's authority to order an employer that committed unfair labor practices to recognize and bargain with a union based solely on majority authorization cards.

The court held that police officers arresting a person at his home could not search the entire home without a search warrant, but that police may search the area within immediate reach of the person without a warrant.
In a double jeopardy case, the Court ruled that the Fifth Amendment's Double Jeopardy Clause applies to the states, and in doing so expressly overruled Palko v. Connecticut.

The Court held that the United States Selective Service System lacked statutory authority to punitively accelerate the induction of registrants declared "delinquent" for violating Selective Service regulations.

The court held that evidence withheld by the prosecution is only Brady material if there is a reasonable probability that the result of the proceeding would have been different, considering the context of the entire record.

The Court held that a merger of the Great Northern Railway Company and the Northern Pacific Railway Company did not violate antitrust laws due to the benefits of increased savings and efficient transportation outweighing the costs of decreased competition and job loss.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that power of states to pass laws interfering with interstate commerce is limited when the law poses an undue burden on businesses.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution requires an evidentiary hearing before a recipient of certain government welfare benefits can be deprived of such benefits.

The Court ruled, in a case about removing an unruly criminal defendant during trial, that a judge may remove a stubbornly defiant defendant from the courtroom after warning that continued disruption will lead to removal.
The Court held that "the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged."
The Court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause protects defendants from successive prosecutions by states and municipalities for offenses based on the same criminal conduct.
The Court held that "when an issue of ultimate fact has once been determined by a valid and final judgment, that issue cannot again be litigated between the same parties in any future lawsuit."
The Court held that a state can cap welfare based on the Aid to Families with Dependent Children at $250.00 per month regardless of the family's size or need.
The Court held that grants of tax exemption to religious organizations do not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court ruled that a recipient of postal mail has sole and unreviewable discretion to decide whether to receive further material from a sender, who has no constitutional right to send unwanted material into someone's home.
The Court refused to hold that large sentencing discounts and threats of the death penalty are sufficient evidence of coercion.
The Court ruled that a plea agreement was valid even if the defendant entered it to avoid the death penalty and based on a possibly mistaken belief that his confession would be admissible in court.
The Court ruled that actors could wear accurate military uniforms—regardless of the production's portrayal of the military—on First Amendment grounds.
The majority ruling, written by Justice Harlan, asserted that the burden of showing a lack of factual controversy rests upon the party asserting the summary judgment.
The Court held that to deny people living in federal enclaves the right to vote is a violation of their right to Equal Protection under the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court held that a search of a suspect's house is not "incident to the arrest" when the suspect's arrest took place outside.
The Court ruled that defendants have a Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial for offenses punishable by imprisonment for more than six months.

The Court held that the Fifth Amendment does not entitle a defendant in a criminal trial to refuse to provide pre-trial notice of some details of his alibi witnesses to the prosecution, and that the Sixth Amendment does not require a jury to have 12 members.

The Court held that the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause did not bar admitting a witness's prior inconsistent statements when the witness testified at trial and faced full cross-examination, or prior preliminary hearing testimony given with adequate opportunity for cross-examination.

The Court held that, if a person cannot afford to pay a fine, it violates the Equal Protection Clause to convert that unpaid fine into jail time to extend a person's incarceration beyond a statutory maximum length.

In a Selective Service case where the judge ordered an acquittal after a jury returned a guilty verdict, the Court held that the government had no power to appeal an acquittal, however wrong its legal basis.

The Court held that, if a person cannot afford to pay a fine, it violates the Equal Protection Clause to convert that unpaid fine into jail time to extend a person's incarceration beyond a statutory maximum length.

The Supreme Court of the United States affirmed that there are no constitutional barriers in place to prevent a judge from accepting a guilty plea from a defendant who wants to plead guilty, while still protesting his innocence, under duress, as a detainee status.
The Court held that where a trial judge abruptly declared a mistrial to keep a prosecution witness from incriminating himself, the Double Jeopardy Clause barred a second trial of the defendant.

The Court held that under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, an employer may not, in the absence of business necessity, refuse to hire women with pre-school-age children while hiring men with such children.

The Court ruled: A State's power to inquire about a person's beliefs or associations is limited by the First Amendment, which prohibits a State from excluding a person from a profession solely because of membership in a political organization or because of his beliefs.
