The Supreme Court of the United States held that requiring bar applicants, like Martin Stolar, to list every organization that they belonged to since age 17 is a violation of the First Amendment.

The United States Supreme Court held that United States federal courts were required to abstain from hearing any civil rights tort claims brought by a person who is currently being prosecuted for the underlying matters giving rise to those claims.
The Court held it is a violation of equal protection to convert a fine to jail time simply because the sentenced person cannot pay the fine.

In an employment discrimination case, the Court ruled that the company's employment requirements did not pertain to applicants' ability to perform the job and so unintentionally discriminated against black employees.
The Court held the National Firearms Act's registration requirements do not violate the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The court held that the United States Court of Claims was an Article I tribunal.

The Court held that recording conversations using concealed radio transmitters worn by informants does not violate the Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures, and thus does not require a warrant.
The Court declined to apply Chimel v. California retroactively and ruled that evidence from mistaken identity arrests can be admissible when other factors support probable cause.

The Court held that a person born outside the United States who received citizenship at birth through an automatic congressional grant could lose it for failing to meet reasonable residence requirements Congress imposed as a condition subsequent.
The Court held that busing was an appropriate remedy for the problem of racial imbalance in schools.
The Court held that the District of Columbia's abortion law banning the practice except when necessary for the health or life of the woman was not unconstitutionally vague.
The Court held that the lack of legal standards by which juries imposed the death penalty was not an unconstitutional violation of the Due Process Clause portions of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court held that a postal regulation that banned the sale of adult materials was constitutionally permissible.
A 6–3 court held that the federal statute governing the seizures was not in violation of the First Amendment as long as the government began forfeiture proceedings within 14 days of the seizure.
The Supreme Court of the United States decided that providing personal information at the scene of an accident does not infringe on one's Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
The Court held that a local city ordinance that made it a criminal offense for three or more persons to assemble on a sidewalk and "annoy" any passersby was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that Arizona's law suspending a driver's license was unconstitutional due to its conflict with the federal Bankruptcy Act under the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution.

The Court held that the First Amendment prevented the conviction of Paul Robert Cohen for the crime of disturbing the peace by wearing a jacket displaying "Fuck the Draft" in the public corridors of a California courthouse.

In a libel suit against a media company, the Court ruled that the actual malice standard applied to a private individual because the story was a matter of public concern, and that the evidence did not support the damages awarded.
The Court determined that state restrictions on welfare benefits for legal aliens but not for citizens violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court ruled that an implied cause of action existed for an individual whose Fourth Amendment protection against unreasonable searches and seizures had been violated by the Federal Bureau of Narcotics.
The Court held that juveniles in juvenile criminal proceedings were not entitled to a jury trial under the Sixth or Fourteenth Amendments.

The Court ruled that Pennsylvania's 1968 act and Rhode Island's 1969 act, which reimbursed private, mostly Catholic, schools for teachers' salaries, were unconstitutional because they violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court held that one-time construction grants to religious colleges and universities under Title I of the Higher Education Facilities Act of 1963 do not violate the Establishment or Free Exercise clauses of the First Amendment.

The Court unanimously reversed the conviction of Muhammad Ali for refusing military induction during the Vietnam War, finding the government had failed to properly specify why his conscientious objector application was denied.

The Court ruled that the First Amendment protected the right of The New York Times to print the classified Pentagon Papers, despite the executive branch's claimed need for secrecy and the President's effort to stop publication.
The Court held that imprisoned people have a right to access a law library.
The Court held that the administrators of estates cannot be named in a way that discriminates between sexes.

The Court ruled that the sentence of the defendant should be vacated because the plea agreement specified that the prosecutor would not recommend a sentence, but the prosecutor breached the agreement by recommending the maximum sentence.

The Court overturned the lower courts' decision to defer a soldier's habeas corpus petition seeking discharge as a conscientious objector until his court-martial ended, freeing the District Court to consider the petition.

The court held that the prosecution's failure to inform the jury that a witness had been promised not to be prosecuted in exchange for his testimony was a failure to fulfill the duty to present all material evidence to the jury, and constituted a violation of due process, requiring a new trial.
The Court declared a Jacksonville vagrancy ordinance unconstitutionally vague.

The Court held that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) may act against a company's “unfair” business practices even though the practice is none of the following: an antitrust violation, an incipient antitrust violation, a violation of the “spirit” of the antitrust laws, or a deceptive practice.
The Court held that the right to counsel in preliminary hearings announced by Coleman v. Alabama does not have a retroactive application.

The Court reversed a drive-in theater manager's obscenity conviction, holding that Washington citizens had no notice under the Sixth Amendment that the place where a film was shown was an element of the offense.

The Court struck down a Massachusetts law prohibiting the distribution of contraceptives to unmarried people for the purpose of preventing pregnancy, ruling that it violated the Equal Protection Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
The Court held that the fathers of children born out of wedlock had a fundamental right to their children.
The Court rejected a lawsuit by the Sierra Club seeking to block the development of a ski resort at Mineral King valley in the Sierra Nevada Mountains because the club had not alleged any injury.
The Court held that Amish children could not be placed under compulsory education past 8th grade.
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the Louisiana law that allowed less-than unanimous jury verdicts (9 to 12 jurors) to convict persons charged with a felony, does not violate the Due Process clause.

The Court held that state juries may convict a defendant of a felony by a less-than-unanimous verdict, affirming the Oregon Court of Appeals and finding Oregon's practice did not violate the Sixth Amendment right to trial by jury.

The Court ruled on the issue of whether the government's grant of immunity from prosecution can compel a witness to testify over an assertion of the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination.
The court held that a criminal defendant cannot be forced by law to testify before all other witnesses.
The Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel did not attach during a pre-indictment identification.

The Court determined a U.S. state violated due process by involuntarily committing a criminal defendant for an indefinite period of time solely on the basis of his permanent incompetency to stand trial on the charges filed against him.
The Court held that the accused cannot be subjected to actual imprisonment unless provided with counsel.

Petitioners challenged the constitutionality of the Uniform Commercial Code provisions of two states, Florida and Pennsylvania, which allowed for the summary seizure of a person's goods or chattels under a writ of replevin.
The Court held that a tip from a known informant can create enough reasonable suspicion to justify a patdown under Terry v. Ohio.

By a 5–3 margin, the Court reaffirmed the antitrust exemption that had been granted to professional baseball in 1922 under Federal Baseball Club v. National League, and previously affirmed by Toolson v. New York Yankees, Inc. in 1953.

The Court held that determinations of whether or not the right to a speedy trial has been violated must be made on a case-by-case basis, and set forth four factors to be considered in the determination.
The United States Supreme Court dismissed for lack of standing a claim in which the plaintiff accused the U.S. Army of alleged unlawful "surveillance of lawful citizen's political activity."

The Court ruled that a Chicago ordinance barring sidewalk protests near a school was a content-based restriction, since it treated labor-related protests differently, and held it unconstitutional for failing the higher standards for such restrictions.
The Court held that Central Connecticut State College's refusal to recognize a campus chapter of Students for a Democratic Society was unconstitutional.
The United States Supreme Court decided that arbitrary and inconsistent imposition of the death penalty violates the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments, and constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.
The court held that people facing parole revocation have due process rights under the Fourteenth Amendment.

In a case over a nontenured state university teacher not being rehired without a hearing, the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment did not require a hearing before nonrenewal unless the teacher showed a deprivation of a liberty or property interest.

In a case about the protections of the Speech or Debate Clause, the Court held that the clause's privileges and immunities for members of Congress also extend to Congressional aides, but not to activity outside the legislative process.

The Court held that the United States Attorney General has the right to refuse somebody's entry to the United States, as he has been empowered to do so in § 212(a)(28) of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952.

The Court ruled that a process claim directed to a numerical algorithm, as such, was not patentable because "the patent would wholly pre-empt the mathematical formula and in practical effect would be a patent on the algorithm itself."
The Court held that the trial court's failure to "have the jurors interrogated on the issue of racial bias" violated the petitioner's due process right under the Fourteenth Amendment.

In a patent-antitrust case, the Court held that the Government may challenge a patent's validity when the patent is directly involved in an antitrust violation, and that mandatory selling and compulsory patent licensing at reasonable charges are recognized antitrust remedies.
The Court ruled that the Constitution protected the right of pregnant women to choose to have an abortion before the point of fetal viability, striking down many state abortion laws.

The Court held that a state may not enforce its rules of evidence, such as rules excluding hearsay, in a fashion that disallows a criminal defendant from presenting reliable exculpatory evidence and thus denies the defendant a fair trial.

The Court held violative of the antitrust laws a single firm's refusal to deal with other firms that denied them access to a facility essential to engaging in business (a so-called essential facility).
The Court held that the federal Anti-Racketeering Act of 1934, known as the Hobbs Act, does not cover union violence in furtherance of the union's objectives.
The Court ruled that a particular section of a Texas Penal Code did not apply to mothers with out-of-wedlock children, in a dispute between the mother and the father of such a child.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that San Antonio Independent School District's financing system, which was based on local property taxes, was not a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a state could tax tribal, off-reservation business activities but could not impose a tax on tribal land, which was exempt from all forms of property taxes.

The Supreme Court of the United States holding that Arizona has no jurisdiction to impose a tax on the income of Navajo Indians residing on the Navajo Reservation if their income is wholly derived from reservation sources.

The Court ruled that Pennsylvania's 1968 act and Rhode Island's 1969 act, which reimbursed private, mostly Catholic, schools for teachers' salaries, were unconstitutional because they violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The majority opinion, authored by then-Associate Justice William Rehnquist, held that when claims of unconstitutional jury discrimination are brought on postconviction collateral review, they are subject to the timeliness requirement outlined in Rule 12(b)(2) Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure.

The court held that not every judicial proceeding that implicates a charge, claim, or defense based on an Act of Congress or a law made under its authority must be presided over by an Article III judge.
The Court decided that benefits given by the United States military to the family of service members cannot be given out differently because of sex.

In a consent search case, the Court ruled that knowledge of the right to refuse consent is a factor in whether consent was voluntary, but the state does not need to prove the person knew of that right under the Fourth Amendment.

The Court upheld a murder conviction notwithstanding a challenge that the evidence upon which guilt was based was obtained in violation of the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments of the United States Constitution.

The Court held that the land that had been the Klamath River Reservation and was incorporated into the Hoopa Valley Reservation in 1891 remained Indian country within the meaning of 18 U.S.C. §1151 despite the Act of June 17, 1892.
The high court ruled that California's state statutes criminalizing record piracy did not violate the Copyright Clause of the United States Constitution.

The Court held that the members of SCRAP—five law students from the George Washington University Law School—had standing to sue under Article III of the Constitution to challenge a nationwide railroad freight rate increase approved by the Interstate Commerce Commission (ICC).
The U.S. Supreme Court upheld a state court's injunction against the showing of obscene films in a movie theatre restricted to consenting adults.
The Court held that the First Amendment did not require that citizens be allowed to import obscene material for their personal and private use at home.

The Court, in a suit by black and Hispanic parents over segregation in Denver schools, found that the school board intentionally created and maintained segregated core city schools, so the entire district had to be desegregated.
The Court held that the search of an automobile by the United States Border Patrol without a warrant or probable cause violates the Fourth Amendment.

The court held that the Sixth Amendment does not grant a criminal defendant the right to have counsel present when the government uses a photo array to elicit an identification of the defendant from a witness.

The Court upheld an ordinance enacted in Pittsburgh that forbids sex-designated classified advertising for job opportunities, against a claim by the parent company of the Pittsburgh Press that the ordinance violated its First Amendment rights.

The Court upheld that states could make laws limiting the distribution of obscene material, provided that these laws were consistent with the Miller test for obscene material established by the Supreme Court in Miller v. California, 413 U.S. 15 (1973).
The Court declared a provision of the Food Stamp Act denying food stamps to households of "unrelated persons" to be a violation of the U.S. Constitution.
The Court held that the Hatch Act of 1939 does not violate the First Amendment, and its implementing regulations are not unconstitutionally vague and overbroad.
The Court prohibited state employees from engaging in partisan political activities.
The Court held that a state law restricting certain civil service jobs to citizens violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment because it "swep indiscriminately".
The Court found that the three New York State programs failed the primary effect prong of the Lemon test.

The Court held that an employer's refusal to hire a person because he is not a United States citizen is not employment discrimination based on "national origin" in violation of §703 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The United States Supreme Court held that "in the case of a lawful custodial arrest a full search of the person is not only an exception to the warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment, but is also a reasonable search under that Amendment."
The court held that each member of a class action must satisfy the amount-in-controversy requirement to remain attached to a lawsuit based on diversity jurisdiction.

The court held that a union seeking to justify a contractually prohibited work stoppage under Section 502 of the Labor Management Relations Act must present ascertainable, objective evidence supporting its conclusion that an abnormally dangerous condition for work exists.
The Court unanimously decided that the lack of supplemental language instruction in public school for students with limited English proficiency violated the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The Court ruled that the Fourth Amendment prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures was not violated when the police obtained voluntary consent from a third party who possessed common authority over the premises sought to be searched.
The court held that the Veterans' Administrations' allocation of greater educational benefits to combat veterans than conscientious objectors was consistent with the United States Constitution.
The Court held that a Massachusetts flag desecration law prohibiting "publicly treat[ing] contemptuously the flag of the United States" was unconstitutionally void for vagueness.

The Court held that the sovereign immunity recognized in the Eleventh Amendment prevented a federal court from ordering a state from paying back funds that had been unconstitutionally withheld from parties to whom they had been due.

The Supreme Court of the United States upheld a California law that prohibited an individual from running for an elected office as an independent candidate if they were registered with a political party within the 12 months prior to the primary election.
The Court held that it is unconstitutional to exclude minority party candidates from absentee ballots that include the major-party candidates.

The Court upheld the constitutionality of a residential zoning ordinance in Belle Terre, New York, allowing a restrictive definition of family that prevented unrelated college students from residing in a single-family dwelling.

The Court held that the Bank Secrecy Act, which required banks to record transactions and report certain high-dollar domestic and foreign transactions to the Treasury, did not violate the First, Fourth, or Fifth Amendments.

The Court held that granting widows a bonus property tax exemption not available to widowers does not violate the Equal Protection Clause because it has a "fair and substantial relation to the object of the legislation."
The court held that it is unconstitutional to prohibit incarcerated people from corresponding with law students and paralegals regarding prison conditions and potential attorney–client relationships.
The court held that police officers' interference with a strike was a violation of the First and Fourteenth Amendments.

The Court held that Oregon's statute allowing for the recoupment of costs related to court-appointed defense counsel did not violate either the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause or the Sixth Amendment's Assistance of Counsel Clause.

The Court interpreted the Equal Pay Act of 1963 and held that Corning Glass Works violated the Act by paying male night shift inspectors higher wages than female day shift inspectors performing the same work.

The Court held that pregnancy discrimination is not sex-based discrimination, and therefore the denial of insurance benefits for work loss resulting from a normal pregnancy does not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the hiring preferences given by the United States Congress does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
The court held that when other channels for communication exist, restricting physical access of the media to incarcerated people is not unconstitutional.
The Court held, 6–3, that convicted felons could be barred from voting beyond their sentence and parole without violating the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution.

The Court ruled that Georgia had gone too far in classifying the film Carnal Knowledge as obscene under the Miller standard, and it overturned the theatre manager's conviction for distributing obscene material.

In a case over a law exempting CIA funding from requirements that expenditures be audited and reported to the public, the Court held that a taxpayer's generalized, undifferentiated interest in government spending did not confer Article III standing.
The Court ruled that citizens do not have the right to challenge the constitutionality of members of Congress holding reserve commissions in the armed forces.
The Court held that, so long as they do not impose liability without fault, states are free to establish their own standards of liability for defamatory statements made about private individuals.

The Court, in a per curiam decision, ruled that a Washington state law that banned the display of the American flag adorned with additional decorations was unconstitutional as it violated protected speech.
The Court held that prisoners retained some due process rights when incarcerated.
The Court unanimously ordered President Richard Nixon to deliver tape recordings and other subpoenaed materials related to the Watergate scandal to a federal district court.

In a case over desegregation busing across district lines among 53 metropolitan Detroit school districts, the Court held that districts were not responsible for cross-district desegregation unless each had deliberately engaged in segregation.

The Court held that extensive state regulation of a public utility does not transform its acts into state action that is reviewable by a federal court under the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court upheld a federal statute granting female Naval officers four more years of commissioned service before mandatory discharge than male Naval officers.
The Court held that systematically excluding women from a venire, or jury pool, by requiring (only) them to actively register for jury duty violated the defendant's right to a representative venire.
The Court held that a public school must conduct a hearing before subjecting a student to suspension.
The Court held that it is a violation of the Fourth Amendment to detain an individual for an extended period of time without a probable cause hearing by a neutral magistrate.
The Court held that the Internal Revenue Service has exploratory as well as investigatory powers; the Service may issue a summons when the name of the taxpayer is unknown.

The Court held a Missouri trial court deprived a defendant of due process by failing to order a competency examination after he was hospitalized following an attempted suicide and as a result missed a portion of his trial for a capital offense.

The Court held that treaties and laws must be construed in favor of Native Americans, that the Supremacy Clause barred applying state game laws to the tribe, and that Congress showed no intent to subject the tribe to state hunting jurisdiction.

The Court held that employees in unionized workplaces have the right under the National Labor Relations Act to the presence of a union steward during any management inquiry that the employee reasonably believes may result in discipline.

The Court held that when state law lets a defendant plead guilty while keeping the right to judicial review of specified constitutional issues, the defendant may still pursue those claims in a federal habeas corpus proceeding.
The Court of Claims, later affirmed by an evenly divided Supreme Court, held that it was a fair use for libraries to photocopy articles for patrons engaged in scientific research.
The court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not prohibit an appeal by the government of a pretrial dismissal because the criminal defendant has yet not been put in jeopardy by a trial.
The Court held that both a Georgia statute prohibiting the release of a rape victim's name and its common-law privacy action counterpart were unconstitutional.

The Court unanimously held that a Social Security Act provision letting widows but not widowers collect special benefits while caring for minor children violated the equal protection right secured by the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
The court held that conspiracy to assault a federal officer, like the substantive crime of assaulting a federal officer, doesn't require knowledge that the victims were federal officers.
The Court struck down Utah's definitions of adulthood as a violation of the Equal Protection Clause: women reached adulthood at 18; men at 21.
The Court held that the EPA must approve a State Implementation Plan if it meets the criteria under the Clean Air Act.

The Court affirmed the American rule of attorney's fees, which makes each side of civil litigation responsible for their legal costs, regardless of which side prevails, unless Congress statutorily legislates otherwise.

The Court held that the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 gives federal courts jurisdiction to review decisions of the United States Department of Labor to proceed (or not) with prosecutions under the Act.
A unanimous court struck down a state statute requiring a defendant to prove the defense of provocation to downgrade a murder conviction to manslaughter.
The Court ruled that only those suffering direct loss from the purchase or sale of stock had standing to sue under federal securities law.

The Court established First Amendment protection for commercial speech in a challenge to government regulation of advertising, determining that such publications qualify as speech under the First Amendment.

The court held that shares of stock entitling a purchaser to lease an apartment in a co-op are not securities because the shares do not meet the investment contract criteria established in the Howey test.

The court held that receiving a song over a radio signal does not constitute a "performance," and therefore does not infringe upon the exclusive right to perform the copyrighted work publicly for profit.

The Court held that the Anti-Injunction Act does apply to state criminal proceedings initiated after a federal complaint is filed but before there has been a "proceeding of substance on the merits" in federal court.
The Court upheld Richmond, Virginia's annexation of land from surrounding counties.

In a Title VII employment discrimination case, the Court held that disparate impact plaintiffs did not need to prove bad faith to be entitled to backpay, and it expanded on the requirement that employment tests be job-related.
The Court reviewed the concept of judicial standing and affirmed that if the plaintiffs lacked standing, they could not maintain a case against the defendants.

The Court ruled that a state cannot constitutionally confine non-dangerous individuals who are capable of surviving safely in freedom by themselves or with the help of willing and responsible family members or friends.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Fourth Amendment's protection against the introduction of evidence obtained in an illegal arrest is not attenuated by reading the defendant their Miranda Rights.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that criminal defendants have a constitutional right to refuse counsel and represent themselves in state criminal proceedings.
The Supreme Court determined it was a violation of the Fourth Amendment for a roving patrol car to stop a vehicle solely on the basis of the driver appearing to be of Mexican descent.
The Court held that the Fourth Amendment prevented Border Patrol officers from conducting warrantless, suspicionless searches of private vehicles removed from the border or its functional equivalent.

The Court held that a criminal suspect's assertion of his right to remain silent after a Miranda warning does not preclude the police from re-Mirandizing him and questioning him about a different crime.
The Court held that a federal district court may not decline jurisdiction over a properly removed state case because it is backlogged, and that such a refusal may be reviewed by a writ of mandamus.
The Court held that a prophylactic injunction against non-culpable state executive officials was an overbroad interference by the Federal Courts in the state executive branches.
The Court decided that a warrantless arrest in public and consenting to a vehicle search did not violate the Fourth Amendment.

In a challenge to campaign finance limits under the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, the Court held that limits on election expenditures were unconstitutional because they contravened the First Amendment's protection of free speech.

The Court held that individuals have a statutorily granted property right in Social Security benefits, and the termination of such benefits implicates due process but does not require a pre-termination hearing.
The Court upheld Section 2805(a) of the California Labor Code against a Federal preemption challenge.
District attorneys or prosecutors were found to have full immunity from civil suits resulting from their government duties.
The Supreme Court of the United States determined that the U.S. Const., Amend. V protection against double jeopardy did not prevent a retrial of a defendant, who had previously requested a mistrial.
A sharply divided Court held that the plaintiff, whom the local police chief had named an "active shoplifter," suffered no deprivation of liberty resulting from injury to his reputation.
The Court upheld military regulations strictly forbidding partisan political activity on unrestricted areas of a military base, Fort Dix, against a First Amendment challenge.

The case involved Chicago families in housing projects who received Section 8 vouchers to move to the suburbs, and the Court ruled that the housing department had violated the Fifth Amendment and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
The Court held that the Fifth Amendment's self-incrimination clause did not protect a taxpayer or their attorney from being required to turn over workpapers prepared by the taxpayer's accountant.
The Court held that bank records are not subject to protection under the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court held that a state tax on personal property owned by tribe members inside reservations and a state sales tax on trade between two tribe members were preempted by the General Allotment Act.

By a 5–3 margin, the Court upheld the conviction of a Missouri man for selling heroin even though all the drug sold was supplied to him, he claimed, by a Drug Enforcement Administration informant who had, in turn, gotten it from the DEA.

The Court reversed the Court of Appeals, which had found a due process violation when a defendant unable to post bail was tried in prison clothes, and reinstated his conviction for assaulting his former landlord.

The Court determined that it is not necessary to provide full Miranda warnings to a person called to testify before a grand jury; and that false statements given during that testimony may not be suppressed in a subsequent prosecution for perjury.
The Court held that the Act of State doctrine does not apply to foreign acts that are "purely commercial."

The Court held that indigent individuals and organizations representing them lacked Article III standing to challenge an IRS revenue ruling giving favorable treatment to hospitals that limited non-emergency care for indigent patients.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the boundary between the states of New Hampshire and Maine was fixed by the 1740 decree of King George II of Great Britain.

Unanimously held the Wild and Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act of 1971, passed in 1971 by the United States Congress to protect these animals from "capture, branding, harassment, or death", to be a constitutional exercise of congressional power.
The court held that a guilty plea is not voluntary when the criminal defendant is not aware of all elements of the charge.

The Court determined that Maryland, which acted as a market participant rather than a regulator in its program to reduce abandoned cars, could favor its own citizens over out-of-state ones without violating the Dormant Commerce Clause.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Fair Labor Standards Act could not constitutionally be applied to state governments.
The Court ruled that private schools that discriminate on the basis of race or establish racial segregation are in violation of federal law.

In a case about prisoners' due process rights, the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause did not give a prisoner a right to a fact-finding hearing before transfer to a facility with significantly more unfavorable conditions.

The Court held that a non-lawyer jurist can constitutionally sit in a jail-carrying criminal case provided that the defendant has an opportunity through an appeal to obtain a second trial before a judge who is a lawyer.
The court upheld the decision by the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals ruling in favor of the respondent.
The Court held that once a school district remedies de jure racial discrimination they are not required to provide remedies for population shifts that are not caused by state discrimination.

The Court determined that the U.S. Congress has the power to abrogate the Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity of the states, if this is done pursuant to its Fourteenth Amendment power to enforce upon the states the guarantees of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court held that search of petitioner's offices for business records, their seizure, and subsequent introduction into evidence did not offend the Fifth Amendment's proscription that "o person... shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself."

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Massachusetts two-tier court system did not deprive Ludwig of his U.S. Const., Amend. XIV right to a jury trial and did not violate the double jeopardy clause of the U.S. Const., Amend. V.

The Court upheld the right to have an abortion in a challenge to a Missouri abortion statute, declaring unconstitutional its requirement of prior written consent from a parent for a minor or a spouse for a married woman.
The Court unanimously upheld a Massachusetts law requiring parental consent to a minor's abortion, where a judge could order consent for good cause if one or both parents refused.
The Court found Max Janis and Morris Levine guilty of illegal bookmaking activities in Los Angeles in a 5-3 ruling.
The Court limited which claims of Fourth Amendment violations could be made by state prisoners in habeas corpus petitions in federal courts.

The Court allowed the United States Border Patrol to set up permanent or fixed checkpoints on public highways leading to or away from the Mexican border and that the checkpoints are not a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

The Court held that a prisoner claiming an Eighth Amendment violation under § 1983 must allege acts or omissions sufficiently harmful to show deliberate indifference to serious medical needs, and that medical malpractice alone is not cruel and unusual punishment.
The Court ruled that statutory or administrative sex classifications were subject to intermediate scrutiny under the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

In a suit by a fired teacher against his school district, the Court held that the district was primarily a local entity beyond the Eleventh Amendment's reach, and remanded the case for the district court to examine whether he would have been fired anyway.

In a challenge to a New York law requiring reporting and storage of Schedule II drug prescription information, the Court reversed the district court's decision that had held the statutes unconstitutional.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that states could not discriminate against another state's articles of commerce.
Explained how the holding of a case should be viewed where there is no majority supporting the rationale of any opinion.

The Court held that a Social Security provision requiring widowers, but not widows, to have received at least half their support from the deceased spouse was invidious discrimination against female wage earners and violated Fifth Amendment due process.

The court held that Congress's abrogation of standard habeas corpus procedure in the District of Columbia's local court system was not an unconstitutional suspension of the writ because the District had an adequate post-conviction alternative.
The Court held that the Seventh Amendment did not require a jury trial to enforce civil penalties for violating a federal "public rights" statute, so an administrative agency could enforce them.

The Court held that American Indians convicted on reservation land were not deprived of equal protection, because the federal criminal statutes rested on political membership in an Indian tribe or nation rather than on impermissible racial classifications.
The Court upheld the disciplinary corporal punishment policy of Florida's public schools by a 5-4 vote.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that New Hampshire could not constitutionally require citizens to display the state motto upon their license plates when the state motto was offensive to their moral convictions.

The Court rejected unmarried biological fathers' equal protection and due process challenges to immigration preference provisions that excluded their illegitimate children, and upheld the provisions, citing Congress' exceptionally broad power to admit or exclude noncitizens.

The Court held the search of letters or envelopes from foreign countries falls under the border exception to the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution, which prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures.
The court ruled on whether state governments have the authority to deny permanent immigrants access to tuition assistance or loans for higher educational institutions.

The Court held that under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, an employer may discharge an employee who observes a seventh-day sabbath, and that the employee is not entitled to equal employment opportunity protection.
The Supreme Court held that the identification procedures used against Brathwaite did not violate the Constitution of the United States.

The Supreme Court of the United States unanimously struck down a North Carolina law prohibiting the sale of apples in closed containers marked with any apple grade other than the United States Department of Agriculture grade. However, displaying the USDA grade was not required.
The Supreme Court ruled states are not required to treat abortion in the same manner as potential motherhood.
The court held that, although the Constitution protects a woman’s right to choose an abortion, it does not require the government to subsidize the exercise of that right.

The Court held that, absent exigency, the warrantless search of double-locked luggage just placed in the trunk of a parked vehicle is a violation of the Fourth Amendment and not justified under the automobile exception.
The Court overturned United States v. Arnold, Schwinn & Co., 388 U.S. 365 (1967), which held that vertical restraints on the territory a product could be sold in were per se illegal.

The Court held that a state prisoner who failed to raise a federal constitutional claim at trial or on appeal as state rules required, without showing cause and prejudice, could not raise it later in federal habeas corpus proceedings.
The Court held that the death penalty for rape of an adult was grossly disproportionate and excessive punishment, and therefore unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
The court held that an absentee and unwed father has no substantive due process right to intervene in an adoption of the child.
The Court held that foreign states could sue for treble damages in U.S. courts, because they should be recognized as "persons" under the Clayton Act.
The court held that a prosecutor may threaten a defendant with more serious charges in order to induce a guilty plea and file those new charges if the defendant does not comply.
The Court held that Wisconsin statutes requiring noncustodial parents to obtain a court order before receiving a marriage license violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that a defendant cannot be sentenced under the punishments of both 18 U.S.C. 2113 (d) and 18 U.S.C. 924 (a) for armed robbery.
The Court held that a Georgia state statute authorizing criminal conviction upon the unanimous vote of a jury of five was unconstitutional.
The Court held the Double Jeopardy Clause does not bar the federal prosecution of a Native American (Indian) who has already been prosecuted by the tribe.
The Court ruled that trial judges may instruct a jury not to draw any inference of guilt from a defendant's refusal to testify, even when the defendant objects to the instruction.
The Supreme Court held that the judge was immune from being sued for issuing the order because it was issued as a judicial function.
The United States Supreme Court held that a court cannot impose rulemaking procedures on a federal government agency.

The Court held that the title owner that acquired depreciable real estate as if the owner were a mere conduit or agent was indeed the owner and, for Federal income tax purposes, had the legal right to take tax deductions associated with depreciation on the building.
It held the Tennessee state law prohibiting religious ministers holding elected office violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.
The United States Supreme Court held that corporations have a First Amendment right to make contributions to ballot initiative campaigns.

In a dispute over the three-mile marginal belt along California's coast, the Court held that California did not own it and that the Federal Government had paramount rights and full dominion over its resources, including oil.
The Supreme Court sustained a law passed by the governing body of the Santa Clara Pueblo that explicitly discriminated on the basis of sex.
The court held that a parent allowing a child to overstay an agreed parenting plan in another state does not establish minimum contacts for the purpose of personal jurisdiction over that parent.
The Court held that the state-allowed re-sale provision did not constitute state action, and thus, the plaintiff did not possess a colorable federal due process claim.

The Court held that state prisoners are entitled to notice, an adversarial hearing, and counsel before their involuntary transfer to state mental hospitals for treatment under the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

The Court held that solicitation of prospective litigants by nonprofit organizations that engage in litigation as a form of political expression and political association constitutes expressive and associational conduct entitled to First Amendment protection.

The Court held that firefighters can not enter a burned premises (in this case, a furniture store) to retrieve evidence of arson barring a search warrant, evidence of exigent circumstances, evidence of abandonment, or consent.

The Court held that when an appellate court reverses a conviction for insufficient evidence, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second prosecution, so the only just remedy is to order an acquittal rather than allow a new trial.
The court held that jeopardy attaches in a jury trial when the jury is empaneled and sworn because the defendant has an interest in retaining a chosen jury.
The Supreme Court of the United States upheld a Maryland law prohibiting oil producers and refiners from operating service stations within its borders.

In a challenge to the Tellico Dam's construction over the endangered snail darter, the Court ruled for the plaintiffs and upheld an injunction, finding the dam's operation would conflict with Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act.
The Court ruled that an invention that departs from the prior art only in its use of a mathematical algorithm is patent eligible only if there is some other "inventive concept in its application."
The Supreme Court of the United States held that states could not discriminate against another state's articles of commerce.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that lands designated as a reservation in Mississippi are "Indian country" as defined by statute, although the reservation was established nearly a century after Indian removal and related treaties.
The Court refused to recognize a "right of access", under the First Amendment, to interview particular prisoners.

The United States Supreme Court overturned the United States District Court for the Western District of North Carolina's decision that the Price Anderson Act violated equal protection by treating victims of nuclear accidents differently from the victims of other industrial accidents.
The Supreme Court ruled in the city's favor.

The court held that where a warrant affidavit contains a statement, necessary to the finding of probable cause, that is demonstrated to be both false and included by an affiant knowingly and intentionally, or with reckless disregard for the truth, the warrant is not valid.
The Court held Minnesota's retroactive alteration of a private pension agreement violated the Contract Clause.
The Court upheld affirmative action, allowing race to be one of several factors in college admission policy.

In a case about the legal immunity of federal officials sued on constitutional grounds, the Court held that they were entitled only to qualified immunity, except for duties where absolute immunity could be shown to be essential.
The Court held that sentencing authorities must have the discretion to consider at least some mitigating factors, rather than being limited to a specific list of factors.

In a 5–4 decision, the Court held that to claim the protection of the Fourth Amendment, a defendant must demonstrate that they have a reasonable expectation of privacy in the place or belonging that is subjected to a search.
The court held that nonmutual offensive issue preclusion is available in federal court, but only if it would be fair.
The Court upheld IRSTooltip Internal Revenue Service regulations limiting how taxpayers could write down inventory value.
The court held that railroad pensions were not subject to division upon divorce because they were not community property.

The Court held that a Texas law, the Texas Optometry Act, which prohibited optometrists from using trade names for commercial purposes and which requires that 4/6 of the members of the Texas Optometry Board be members of the Texas Optometric Association is constitutional.

The Court held that Montana, not the United States in trust for the Crow Tribe, held title to the Big Horn Riverbed under the Equal Footing Doctrine, and that the Tribe could not regulate nonmember hunting and fishing on nonmember-owned fee-simple land within its reservation.
The court held that federal patent law does not preempt state contract law so as to preclude enforcement of the contract.
The Court held that Alabama statutes imposing alimony obligations on husbands but not on wives violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court ruled that U.S. states lack sovereign immunity from private lawsuits filed against them in the courts of another state.
The Court held that police may not stop motorists without any reasonable suspicion to suspect crime or illegal activity to check their driver's license and auto registration.
The Court held that a state may refuse to hire a non-citizen as a public school teacher if they could be but do not wish to become a citizen.
The Court invalidated a Louisiana statute allowing a conviction upon a nonunanimous verdict from a jury of six for a petty offense.
The Court held that the United States Congress may enact legislation governing wildlife on federal lands.
The Court upheld a Georgia law that barred fathers of illegitimate children from bringing wrongful death claims without imposing the same burden on mothers.

The Court held that a New York law, which allowed unwed mothers, but not unwed fathers, a veto over the adoption of that couple's children, was discriminatory, and violated the equal protection clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court held that an administrative agency of the United States government, seeking enforcement of its orders, cannot withdraw its petition or the transcript of the administrative hearing once these have been submitted to the appropriate court.

The Court considered the constitutionality of conditions of confinement in federal short-term detention facilities and found that, although pre-trial detainees' treatment is constrained by the Constitution, all the challenged policies passed constitutional scrutiny.
The court held that parolees do not have a reasonable expectation of due process.
The Court held that, where two statutes criminalize the same act and those statutes have different maximum penalties, the maximum penalty of the statute the prosecutor chose to charge under applies.

The Court held that a state statute requiring each major political party to have a State Committee of two persons from each county did not violate party members' First and Fourteenth Amendment freedom of association regarding purely internal party decisions.
The Court held that the Fourth Amendment guarantee against unreasonable search and seizure applies to Puerto Rico.

In a land dispute, the Court held that 25 U.S.C. § 194 applied only to individuals and not to a state, that federal law governed the tribe's right to possession, and that state law determined how that applied to the natural movement of a river's boundaries.
The Court decided an issue of Federal statutory hearing rights.

The Court held that the installation and use of a pen register by the police to obtain information on a suspect's telephone calls was not a "search" within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution, and hence no search warrant was required.

The court held that, absent exigency, the warrantless search of personal luggage merely because it was located in an automobile lawfully stopped by the police, is a violation of the Fourth Amendment and not justified under the automobile exception.

The Court determined that the defendant's arrest in El Paso, Texas for a refusal to identify himself after being seen and questioned in a high-crime area was not based on a reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing and thus violated the Fourth Amendment.
The Court held that statements made by a Senator in newsletters and press releases were not protected by the Speech or Debate Clause.

The United States Supreme Court held that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits racial discrimination by private employers, does not condemn all private, voluntary, race-conscious affirmative action plans.
The Court ruled 8-1 that teenagers do not have to secure parental consent to obtain an abortion.
The Court held that a ban on the sale of a commodity already in a commercial inventory is not a taking when there is no requirement to surrender the commodity to the government.
The Court ruled that a warrant could not be used to search an unnamed individual unless the warrant mentioned that unnamed parties were involved or exigent circumstances were shown to exist.
The court held that national labor unions are not liable for the actions of local union members who engage in wildcat strikes unless they provoke the strikes.

The Court held that citizenship cannot be taken away without intent to relinquish it, overturned portions of a federal act making certain actions conclusive proof of such intent, and ruled intent may be shown by a preponderance of the evidence.

In a case on spousal privilege in the law of evidence, the Court held that the witness-spouse alone has a privilege to refuse to testify adversely, and it upheld the petitioner's conviction based on his wife's testimony.
The Supreme Court ruled that Henry Kissinger was not required under the Act to turn over transcripts of phone conversations he made as an adviser to President Richard Nixon.

The Court held that a printer's employee who deduced the identities of takeover target companies and traded in their stock without disclosing his knowledge had not violated § 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 or SEC Rule 10b-5.

The Court held that a taxpayer who wants to question Internal Revenue Service agents about their motives for issuing a summons may do so if they can point to "specific facts or circumstances plausibly raising an inference of bad faith."

The Court upheld a life sentence with the possibility of parole under Texas' three strikes law for a felony fraud crime, where the offense and two prior offenses involved about $230 of fraudulent activity.

The Court held that state prisoners are entitled to notice, an adversarial hearing, and counsel before their involuntary transfer to state mental hospitals for treatment under the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
The Court held that public defenders cannot be fired solely based on their political affiliation.

The Court struck down a New York statute allowing warrantless entry into a private home to make a felony arrest, because the Fourth Amendment draws a firm line at the house's entrance absent exigent circumstances.

The court held that a municipality has no immunity from liability under Section 1983 flowing from its constitutional violations and may not assert the good faith of its officers as a defense to such liability.

The court held that the fact that a plaintiff may bring a suit against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) does not prevent them from seeking a remedy under Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that disproportionate effects alone, absent purposeful discrimination, are insufficient to establish a claim of racial discrimination affecting voting.
The majority upheld Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 against a challenge to its constitutionality.

The Court, clarifying what counts as interrogation under Miranda, held that interrogation includes not just direct questioning but also its functional equivalent, meaning police words or actions reasonably likely to elicit an incriminating response.
The Court held that a death sentence could not be granted for a murder when the only aggravating factor was that the murder was found to be "outrageously or wantonly vile."
The Court determined "seizure" occurs when an officer uses displays of authority to detain a person.

In a diversity action asking whether state law or Federal Rule 3 determined when an action commenced for tolling the state statute of limitations, the Court found no conflict because not applying the federal rule would not thwart its purpose.

In a dispute over the three-mile marginal belt along California's coast, the Court held that California did not own it and that the Federal Government had paramount rights and full dominion over its resources, including oil.

The Court affirmed the California Supreme Court's decision in a free speech dispute between a shopping center and several local high school students who wished to canvass signatures for a petition against a U.N. General Assembly resolution.

The Court held that the test for determining whether a zoning ordinance or governmental regulation will be considered a taking is whether such action “substantially advances” a legitimate state interest.

The Court considered whether living organisms can be patented and held that human-made bacteria could be patented under U.S. patent law because such an invention was a "manufacture" or "composition of matter".
The Court held that individual states, when acting as producers or suppliers rather than as market regulators, may discriminate preferentially against out-of-state residents.
The Court found unjustified and unconstitutional an Illinois law that banned residential picketing but exempted labor disputes, because its distinction was based on the subject matter of a protest.
The Court held that a jury must be allowed to consider lesser included offenses, not just capital offense or acquittal.
The Court reversed a district court's suppression of evidence in the criminal prosecution of an Ohio businessman charged with tax evasion.

The Court held, consistent with Witherspoon v. Illinois, that a Texas requirement that jurors swear that mandatory imposition of a death sentence would not interfere with their consideration of factual matters such as guilt or innocence was unconstitutional.
The Court ruled that "automatic standing" to bring a Fourth Amendment claim based merely on possession of a seized item lacks constitutional merit.

The Supreme Court of the United States holding that Arizona's taxes that were assessed against a non-Indian contractor that was working exclusively for an Indian tribe on that tribe's reservation were preempted by federal law.

The Court, in a case on patent misuse and the 1952 patent law amendments, held that supplying an unpatented product especially adapted for a patented process and lacking substantial non-infringing use was unlawful contributory infringement.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that states participating in Medicaid are not required to fund medically necessary abortions for which federal reimbursement was unavailable as a result of the Hyde Amendment, which restricted the use of federal funds for abortion.

The Court held that Congress did not violate separation of powers by letting the Sioux Nation pursue a previously adjudicated claim, and that taking the Black Hills land set aside for the tribe required just compensation, including interest.
The United States Supreme Court held that the U.S. Congress could constitutionally use its spending power to remedy the effects of past discrimination.

After a murder case ended in three mistrials and the judge closed the fourth trial to the public and press, the Court ruled the closure violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments, which implicitly guarantee the press access to public trials.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that individuals who bribed a judge for an injunction were not protected by judicial immunity and therefore could be held liable for the damages resulting from the injunction.

The Court held that a provision of the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 letting the federal government appeal certain criminal sentences after they are imposed did not violate the Fifth Amendment's Double Jeopardy Clause.

The court held that Congress can repeal or modify a statutorily defined formula for annual cost-of-living increases to the compensation of federal judges, but Congress must act with respect to any particular increase before the increase takes effect.
The Court held that a company (in this case, the Upjohn company) could invoke the attorney–client privilege to protect communications made between company lawyers and non-management employees.

The Court found no violation of the equal protection or commerce clauses in a Minnesota state statute banning retail sale of milk in plastic nonreturnable, nonrefillable containers, but permitting such sale in other nonreturnable, nonrefillable containers.
The court held that because Fedorenko lied on his visa application, his visa and citizenship were invalid.
The Court limited the jurisdiction of federal courts to review state court factual determinations under 28 USC § 2254(e).
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a state could allow the broadcast and still photography coverage of criminal trials.
The Court held that the Federal Reserve's amendment to Regulation Y, which lowered regulatory burdens on well-managed banks did not exceed the Board's statutory authority.
The Court held that controlling the execution of a physical process, by running a computer program did not preclude patentability of the invention as a whole.
The court declined to issue a firm holding because the equal-protection claim at issue was not properly raised.

The U.S. Supreme Court held that trial judges in criminal proceedings must, upon proper request of the defendant, inform the jury of his right against self-incrimination, and that its execution may not be used against him.
The Court held a Louisiana Head and Master law, which gave sole control of marital property to the husband and indicated the husband's dominance over the wife in the marriage, unconstitutional.

The Court held that Montana, not the United States in trust for the Crow Tribe, held title to the Big Horn Riverbed under the Equal Footing Doctrine, and that the Tribe could not regulate nonmember hunting and fishing on nonmember-owned fee-simple land within its reservation.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that Indiana's denial of unemployment compensation benefits to petitioner violated his First Amendment right to free exercise of religion.
The Court held that the Eleventh Amendment prohibits a federal court from ordering state officials to obey state law.

It was held that, based on the Fourth Amendment, a police officer may not conduct a warrantless search of a third party's home in an attempt to apprehend the subject of an arrest warrant, absent consent or exigent circumstances.
The court held that Section 301 of Taft-Hartley Act did not create liability for damages for unionists for breach of no-strike clauses.
The Court held that, per Miranda v. Arizona (1966), the state may not force a defendant to submit to a psychiatric examination solely for the purposes of sentencing.
The Court held that once a defendant invokes his Fifth Amendment right to counsel, police must cease custodial interrogation.
The Court ruled in favor of Maryland, which had challenged a Louisiana tax law on natural gas extracted within the state as violating the Commerce Clause.
The court held that whether prison conditions constitute cruel and unusual punishment must be proven with objective proof of the excessive harms caused directly by the challenged conditions.

The Court held for Fourth Amendment purposes, a warrant to search for contraband founded on probable cause implicitly carries with it the limited authority to detain the occupants of the premises while a proper search is conducted.
The Court held that the practice of requiring only men to register for the draft was constitutional.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of a statute that prohibited depositing unstamped "mailable matter" in a mailbox approved by the United States Postal Service.
The court held that federal law precluded a state court from dividing a military pension pursuant to state community property laws.
The Court upheld the right of the executive branch to revoke a citizen's passport for reasons of national security and the foreign policy interests of the U.S. under the Passport Act of 1926.

The Court held that when a police officer has made a lawful custodial arrest of the occupant of an automobile, the officer may, as a contemporaneous incident of that arrest, search the passenger compartment of that automobile.
It was decided that cities could regulate billboards, and that municipal governments could not treat commercial outdoor advertising more harshly than noncommercial messages.
The Court held that a severance tax in Montana does not violate the Commerce Clause or the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution.

The Court held that when the U.S. government provides an "open forum," it may not discriminate against speech that takes place within that forum on the basis of the viewpoint it expresses—in this case, against religious speech engaged in by an evangelical Christian organization.
The Court upheld a state law as constitutional that excluded aliens from positions as probation officers.
The Court held that it is not a violation of the Fourth Amendment for an arresting officer to accompany the arrested at all times, regardless of where they go.

The Supreme Court of the United States holding that an Indian tribe has the authority to impose taxes on non-Indians that are conducting business on the reservation as an inherent power under their tribal sovereignty.
The Court held that the fact that one of the jurors in a murder trial had applied to work for the prosecutor did not violate the defendant's constitutional right to a fair jury trial.

The Court held that an organization may sue in its own right if directly injured, such as through a "drain on the organization's resources," and that "testers" who sought to determine whether a company violated the law may have standing in their own right.

The Court held that the petitioner was entitled to have his discrimination complaint adjudged by Illinois's Fair Employment Practices Commission (FEPC), which had dismissed it for its own failure to meet a deadline.
The justices unanimously upheld an ordinance passed by a Chicago suburb that imposed licensing requirements on the sale of drug paraphernalia by a local record store.

In a case over the burden of proof for terminating parental rights for permanent neglect, the Court reversed and vacated the lower ruling, holding that states must show at least clear and convincing evidence to sever parental rights irrevocably.
The court held that a one-year statute of limitations for establishing paternity denies illegitimate children the equal protection of law.

The Court held that a trade union that refused to unload cargo from the Soviet Union in protest against the invasion of Afghanistan had engaged in a secondary boycott, an unfair labor practice under the National Labor Relations Act.

The Court held that the Minnesota Charitable Solicitation Act, which imposed registration and reporting requirements on religious organizations that solicit more than 50% of their funds from nonmembers, violated the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.
The Court held that aggravating circumstances in the death penalty context must meaningfully narrow the number of people eligible for the death penalty.
The court was asked to decide if a legal warrantless search of an automobile allows closed containers found in the vehicle (specifically, in the trunk) to be searched as well.
The Court confirmed the application of and set out a test for contributory trademark liability under § 32 of the Lanham Act (15 U.S.C. § 1114).

The Court considered whether Puerto Rico could by statute give a political party the power to fill an interim vacancy in its Legislature, and it upheld the Puerto Rico Supreme Court's decision that this did not violate the Constitution.
The Court held that distinguishing bounty benefits based on the length of time a person has resided in a state violates the Equal Protection Clause.

The Supreme Court of the United States struck down both a state statute denying funding for education of undocumented immigrant children in the United States and an independent school district's attempt to charge an annual $1,000 tuition fee for each student to compensate for lost state funding.

The Court rejected a doctors' society's defense that its maximum-fee arrangement for patients under certain health insurance plans was necessary and beneficial, finding the price fixing was not truly necessary and the justifications failed.
The court held that the exclusion of the press and public from a trial is prohibited by the First Amendment unless the exclusion is motivated by a compelling state interest.
The Court held that a president "is entitled to absolute immunity from damages liability predicated on his official acts."
The court held that the United States Court of Claims was an Article I tribunal.

The Court held that, in a state's calculation of income tax for a corporation from another state, the state cannot include income from the intangible assets of subsidiary corporations that have on connection with the state.

The Court held that a governmental action amounting to a permanent physical occupation of property effects a regulatory taking to the extent of the occupation, regardless of any important public benefit or minimal economic impact on the owner.
The Court held that an at-large election system for a large rural county with a large black population violated the Equal Protection Clause.
The Supreme Court held, in a 9–0 decision, that the Sherman Act did not invalidate a California law prohibiting the importing of spirits not authorized by the brand owner.
The Court unanimously ruled that the First Amendment did not protect the sale or manufacture of child sexual abuse material, also known as child pornography, and that states could outlaw it.

The court ruled that the imposition of the death penalty under the felony murder rule when the defendant did not intentionally kill the victim constituted cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment of the United States constitution.
The Court determined the constitutionality of deporting aliens who might give testimony in criminal alien smuggling prosecutions.
The Court ruled that a state's broad power to regulate economic activities does not include the power to prohibit peaceful advocacy of a politically motivated boycott.
The United States Supreme Court decided that a Nebraska statute forbidding commercial exportation of water from Nebraska was unconstitutional in that it violated the dormant commerce clause.

The Court held that a lawful permanent resident returning from a brief trip abroad is entitled to due process protections in exclusion proceedings under the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Supreme Court, in an 8–1 decision, ruled that Massachusetts' law violated the Establishment Clause as it delegated powers normally reserved to the government to non-government entities and would allow decisions to be made along religious lines, effectively advancing religious purposes.

The Court held that prosecutors may use a suspect's refusal to submit to a blood-alcohol test as evidence of guilt and that the introduction of such evidence at trial does not violate the suspect's Fifth Amendment privilege against self incrimination.

The Court held that the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 made it unlawful for an employer to discriminate by age against employees or potential employees aged 40 to 70, except where age is a bona fide occupational qualification or the differentiation rests on reasonable non-age factors.

The Court held that using a beeper to help officers follow a car on a single trip violated no legitimate expectation of privacy, so it was no search or seizure and needed no warrant under the Fourth Amendment.

The Court held that Title 42 U.S.C. § 1983 did not authorize a convicted state defendant to assert a claim for damages against a police officer for giving perjured testimony at the defendant's criminal trial.

In a Fourth Amendment case about warrantless searches and seizures, the Court ruled that police may approach a person based on their behavior but, absent more, cannot detain or search that person without a warrant.

The court held that, when punishing an employee for engaging in an unprotected strike, an employer may not consider their status as a union official when deciding the degree of discipline to inflict but may consider their role in the actual strike.
The Court held that Ohio's filing deadline for independent candidates was unconstitutional.
The Court held that the plaintiff, Adolph Lyons, lacked standing to challenge the Los Angeles city police department's use of chokeholds.
The Court reversed the lower courts' decision that had favored an assistant district attorney who was fired after circulating a questionnaire about management practices to her fellow prosecutors.
The Court held that a state statute regulating economic aspects of nuclear generating plants was not preempted by the federal Atomic Energy Act of 1954.
The court held that incarcerated people do not have a due process right to choose the prison in which they are held, even if they are transferred to a prison across the ocean.

The Court held that the religion clauses of the First Amendment did not prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from revoking the tax exempt status of a religious university whose practices are contrary to a compelling government public policy, such as eradicating racial discrimination.
The Court held that a local government could imprison or jail someone for not paying a fine only if a hearing showed that the person could have paid it but willfully chose not to.
In an antitrust case the U.S. government brought under Section 8 of the Clayton Act against banks and their holding companies over shared board members, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit.
The court ruled that the law was not in violation of the Contract Clause or the Equal Protection Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
In a Fourth Amendment case about probable cause, the Court overruled two earlier decisions and replaced the Aguilar–Spinelli test with a "totality of the circumstances" test.
The United States Supreme Court affirmed its abortion rights jurisprudence.
The Court held that it does not violate the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution for a trained police dog to sniff a person's luggage or property in a public place.
The Court held that aggravating circumstances in the death penalty context must meaningfully narrow the number of people eligible for the death penalty.
The Court held that the one-house legislative veto violated the constitutional separation of powers.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the United States is accountable in money damages for alleged breaches of trust in connection with its management of forest resources on allotted lands of the Quinault Reservation.

The court held that the mere existence of a biological link between an unwed father and a child does not merit protection under the Due Process Clause regarding adoption; the unwed father must earn rights under that clause by coming forward and contributing to the child's development.

The Court overturned a mandatory sentence of life in prison without parole, given to a man with a seventh nonviolent felony conviction for writing a check from a fictitious account, as cruel and unusual punishment.
In a 5–4 decision, the Court upheld the statute.
The Court held California may properly require respondent to obtain a state license in order to sell liquor for off-premises consumption.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that government funding for chaplains was constitutional because of the "unique history" of the United States.

In a death penalty case where the defendant argued psychiatrists could not accurately predict future dangerousness, the Court ruled that such psychiatric predictions could be presented to a jury during the sentencing phase of a capital trial.
The Court extended Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968) to allow searches of car compartments during a stop with reasonable suspicion.

In a dispute where 7-Eleven franchisees sued in California state court and the parent company invoked arbitration clauses, the Court held that the Federal Arbitration Act applied to contracts executed under state law.

The Court held that the Eighth Amendment does not require a state appellate court, as an invariable rule, to proportionally compare a death sentence with penalties in similar cases before affirming it, even if the prisoner requests it.

The Court held that a city can pressure private employers to hire city residents, but using that power to bias private contractors against out-of-state residents may be challenged under the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article Four.

The court held that a gun owner's acquittal on criminal charges involving firearms does not preclude a subsequent in rem forfeiture proceeding against those firearms when that subsequent proceeding is civil rather than criminal.
The Court decided that opening up reservation lands for settlement by non-Indians does not constitute the intent to diminish reservation boundaries.
The Court held that its decision in Edwards v. Arizona (1980) should not be applied retroactively.

The United States Supreme Court held that a state could assert personal jurisdiction over the publisher of a national magazine which published an allegedly defamatory article about a resident of another state, and where the magazine had wide circulation in that state.

The United States Supreme Court held that a court within a state could assert personal jurisdiction over the author and editor of a national magazine which published an allegedly libelous article about a resident of that state, and where the magazine had wide circulation in that state.

The Court held the analysis of the tying issue must focus on the hospital's sale of services to its patients, rather than its contractual arrangements with the providers of anesthesiological services.
The Court held that purchases in the United States by an out-of-state corporation did not establish general personal jurisdiction.
The Court rejected the consideration of racial bias in child custody proceedings, holding it unconstitutional under the 14th Amendment.
The court held that a finding of prejudice in ineffective assistance of counsel claims cannot be based entirely on an inference.

The United States Supreme Court held that prisoners in administrative segregation pending the investigation of crimes committed within the prison had no Sixth Amendment entitlement to counsel prior to the initiation of adversary judicial proceedings against them.
