The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Equal Protection Clause prohibited the state of Texas from barring noncitizens from applying for commission as a notary public.

The United States Supreme Court held that a state could use eminent domain to take land that was overwhelmingly concentrated in the hands of private landowners and redistribute it to the wider population of private residents.

In a case about the exclusionary rule for evidence gathered through Fourth Amendment violations, the Court ruled that evidence law enforcement would inevitably have discovered through legal means remained admissible.

The court held that accepting a first plea bargain that is later rescinded does not create a right to have that first bargain specifically enforced when the criminal defendant accepts a second, less-beneficial plea bargain.

The Court held that a parent company is incapable of conspiring with its wholly owned subsidiary for purposes of Section 1 of the Sherman Act because they cannot be considered separate economic entities.

The Court considered a challenge to the EPA's 1981 change in its definition of "source" under the Clean Air Act, overturned the lower court's decision, and ruled for Chevron because courts should broadly defer to the agency.
By a 7-2 majority, the Court ruled that undocumented immigrant workers were “employees” covered by the National Labor Relations Act of 1935 (NLRA).

The Court held by a 5–4 majority that restrictions upon travel to Cuba established as part of the Cuban Assets Control Regulations in 1963 did not violate the freedom to travel protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
The court held that a tax on a class of goods with the purpose or effect of protecting or encouraging local business violates the Dormant Commerce Clause.
Specifically prohibited sleeping in Lafayette Park and the National Mall at issue.

The Court ruled that a person in police custody following a misdemeanor traffic offense was entitled to the protections of the Fifth Amendment pursuant to the decision in Miranda v. Arizona 384 U.S. 436 (1966).
The Court held that a New Jersey state gaming law requiring union leaders to be of good moral character was not preempted by the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA).
The Court held that prison inmates have no privacy rights in their cells protected by the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The court held that a ban on contact visits for pretrial detainees is not unconstitutional.
In a case about associative freedom and a Minnesota antidiscrimination law, the Court held that the Minneapolis branch of the United States Jaycees could not bar women from becoming voting members.
The Court held that use of an electronic beeper device to monitor a can of ether without a warrant constituted an unlawful search.
The Court determined that citizens do not have standing to sue a federal government agency based on the influence that the agency's determinations might have on third parties.

The Court declined to award the costs of the substitute facility, holding that the Fifth Amendment does not require consequential damages when the market value of the condemned property is ascertainable and when there is no showing of manifest injustice.
The Court held that if the author of a work authorizes derivatives, the terms negotiated in exchange for that grant stand even if the grant is later rescinded.
In a dispute over an off-airport parking company's registered trademark, the Court affirmed the registration as more than a descriptive trademark.
The Court ruled that wanted posters create reasonable suspicion to detain and identify suspects that match descriptions contained in those posters.

In a case about a school official's search of a student's purse after she was caught smoking, the Court held that the Fourth Amendment applies in schools but requires only reasonable suspicion, and ruled the search constitutional.
The Court held that a three-day delay in searching a motor vehicle under government control did not violate the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Court held that the Congress has the power under the Commerce Clause of the Constitution to extend the Fair Labor Standards Act, which requires that employers provide minimum wage and overtime pay to their employees, to state and local governments.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment required the state to provide a psychiatric evaluation to be used on behalf of an indigent criminal defendant if he needed it.

In a dispute between a brokerage firm and a former client, the Court held unanimously that the Federal Arbitration Act required state-law claims to be arbitrated when the parties had contracted to do so, even with parallel federal claims in court.
The Supreme Court of the United States clarified how long police are permitted to stop vehicles as part of an investigatory stop before it violates the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The Court held that compelled surgical intrusion into a person's body to obtain evidence implicates privacy and security expectations so greatly that it would be unreasonable under the Fourth Amendment, even if it would likely produce evidence of a crime.

The Court held that a federal agency's decision to not take an enforcement action is presumptively unreviewable by the courts under section 701(a)(2) of title 5, United States Code, which is part of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a state cannot tax out-of-state insurance companies at a greater rate than domestic insurance companies under the Privileges and Immunities Clause of Article Four of the United States Constitution.

The Court held that under the Fourth Amendment, an officer pursuing a fleeing suspect may not use deadly force to prevent escape unless there is probable cause that the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury.

An evenly split Court upheld per curiam a lower court's decision that the display of a privately sponsored nativity scene on public property does not violate the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.
The court held that the Fifth Amendment's Grand Jury Clause is not violated if a federal defendant is found guilty by a trial jury without having found "all" parts of an indictment proved.
The Court permitted the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to withhold the identities and institutional affiliations of researchers who worked on Project MKUltra.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that an Indian tribe is not required to obtain the approval of the Secretary of the Interior in order to impose taxes on non-tribal persons or entities doing business on a reservation.

The Supreme Court of the United States unanimously invalidated the criminal disenfranchisement provision of § 182 of the Alabama Constitution as a violation of the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The Court held that a motor home was subject to the automobile exception to the search warrant requirement of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution because the motor home was readily movable.

The Court held that The Nation's quoting and summarizing of President Ford's forthcoming memoir was not fair use, rejecting its public-interest argument because the right of first publication was important enough to favor Harper & Row.

The Court held that states can require an advertiser to disclose certain information without violating the advertiser's First Amendment free speech protections as long as the disclosure requirements are reasonably related to the State's interest in preventing deception of consumers.
The Court held that States cannot tax tribes without express Congressional approval.
The Court held that tribal court remedies must be exhausted before tribal court jurisdiction can be challenged in federal court.
The court held that a prosecutor in a capital case must never tell the jury that jurors are not deciding whether the defendant will die.

The court held that to fall within the collateral order exception to the final judgment rule, an order must conclusively determine the disputed question, resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits of the action, and be effectively unreviewable on appeal from a final judgment.
The Court held that due process required that prison disciplinary decisions to revoke good-time credits must be supported by "some evidence."
The court ruled that the purchase of the magazines was not a seizure, and Macon was found guilty of the sale of obscene materials.
The Court held that the right to petition does not provide absolute immunity to petitioners; it is subject to the same restrictions as other First Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that though portions of a law against obscenity and prostitution might be invalid, it would not be invalidated as a whole unless severing unconstitutional provisions would result in an unworkable law.
The Court decided whether a dominant firm's unilateral refusal to deal with a competitor could establish a monopolization claim under Section 2 of the Sherman Act.

The Court held that an attorney's curt letter to a court employee, followed by the attorney's refusal to apologize for sending the letter, did not justify suspending the attorney from practicing law in federal court.
The court held that the government's interest in securing military bases justified excluding people who had been ordered not to reenter.
The Court held that a state statute providing employees with an absolute right not to work on their chosen Sabbath violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court held that a credit reporting agency could be liable in defamation if it carelessly relayed (i.e. published) false information that a business had declared bankruptcy when in fact it had not.
The court held that the National Labor Relations Board's policy of affording employees a right to resign without paying union dues is not facially unlawful.

Discussed whether copies of copyrighted works could be regarded as stolen property for the purposes of a law which criminalized the interstate transportation of property that had been "stolen, converted or taken by fraud" and holding that they could not be so regarded under that law.

The Court, addressing Congress' power to abrogate states' Eleventh Amendment immunity, held that Congress may abrogate it only by making its intention unmistakably clear in the language of the statute.

The Court held that New York City's program sending public school teachers into parochial schools to provide remedial education to disadvantaged children under Title I caused excessive church-state entanglement and violated the Establishment Clause.

The Court, applying rational basis review, struck down a city zoning ordinance as applied to a group home for intellectually disabled people, while declining to treat intellectually disabled people as a quasi-suspect or suspect class.
By a 5–3 margin it upheld the lower court, requiring that the dealer arbitrate its claim before a panel in Tokyo, as stipulated in the contract.

The Court ruled that, under the dual sovereignty doctrine, the Fifth Amendment's double jeopardy clause did not bar one state from prosecuting and punishing someone already convicted and sentenced for the same act in another state.
The Court ruled unanimously that the government does have the power to control intrastate wetlands as waters of the United States.

The Court held that a defendant's conviction must be reversed if members of their race were systematically excluded from the grand jury that indicted them, even if they were convicted following an otherwise fair trial.

The United States Supreme Court reversed the lower court's finding and overturned the petitioner's conviction, on the grounds that it was fundamentally unfair for the prosecutor to comment during the court proceedings on the petitioner's silence invoked as a result of a Miranda warning.
The court held that misjoinder under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 8(b) is subject to harmless error analysis, and it is not reversible error per se.

In a dispute over a utility's billing-envelope newsletters, the Court held that a state commission order forcing the utility to carry a rival group's message was unconstitutional, since the right to speak includes the right not to carry messages one disagrees with.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that localities may impose regulations prohibiting adult theaters from operating within certain areas, finding that the regulation in question was a content-neutral time/place/manner restriction.
The Court held that a person has no reasonable expectation of privacy under the Fourth Amendment when police look for a vehicle identification numbers after they have developed reasonable suspicion.
The court held that prison staff are not generally liable for the use of excessive force during prison disturbances such as a hostage situation where a guard is taken.
The Court clarified its earlier Monell decision and established that municipalities can be held liable even for a single decision that is improperly made.
A Jewish Air Force officer was denied the right to wear a yarmulke when in uniform on the grounds that the Free Exercise Clause applies less strictly to the military than to ordinary citizens.

In an antitrust case over whether Matsushita and other Japanese television manufacturers had a horizontal agreement, the Court held that evidence must tend to exclude the possibility of independent action to survive summary judgment.
The court held that a city's conditioning of an entity's franchise renewal of the settlement of a labor dispute is preempted by the National Labor Relations Act.

The Court held, in a case about the Sixth Amendment right to counsel in police interrogation, that once an accused claimed counsel at a plea hearing or other proceeding, a later waiver during police questioning was invalid unless the accused initiated the communication.
The Court held the Due Process Clause requires state supreme court justices to recuse themselves from cases in which they have a direct, personal, substantial, and pecuniary interest in the outcome.
The Court held that the rule from Lockett v. Ohio (1978) dictated that mitigating evidence not be subject to limitations based on relevance.
The Court unanimously held that an unloaded handgun is a “dangerous weapon” within the meaning of federal bank robbery laws.
The Court determined that citizens do not have Article III standing to challenge the constitutionality of a state statute in federal court unless they possess a "direct stake" in the outcome.
The Court ruled that a prosecutor's use of peremptory challenges to exclude jurors solely because of their race in a criminal case violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court held that aerial observation of a person's backyard by police, even if done without a search warrant, does not violate the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

The Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit and remanded, in a First Amendment dispute over restrictions on cable franchising, holding that the disputed factual issues needed fuller development before the legal issues could be decided.

In a land claim brought by a terminated tribe, the Court held that federal policy did not preclude applying a state statute of limitations to the claim, and it remanded to the Fourth Circuit to decide whether South Carolina's statute applied.
The Court ruled that a government program requiring the use of a Social Security number did not violate the First Amendment.
The Court held that, pursuant to the Eagle Protection Act, American Indians were prohibited from hunting eagles.
The Court held that a manufacturer cannot be held liable in tort for purely economic losses resulting from a defective product that causes damage only to itself and not to persons or other property.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that there was an exception to the "virtually per se rule of invalidity" of the dormant commerce clause.
The Court held that a party moving for summary judgment need show only that the opposing party lacks evidence sufficient to support its case.

The Court rejected the prosecution's argument that a habeas petition raising ineffective assistance of counsel was a back-door Fourth Amendment claim, holding the two issues were distinct and the petition could go forward.

The Court upheld the common law rule that the insane cannot be executed, ruling that a petitioner is entitled to a competency evaluation and an evidentiary hearing in court on their competency to be executed.

The Court held that the "cause and prejudice" rule applies to appeals, so a person ordinarily cannot file a habeas petition to review a constitutional problem that their lawyer did not complain about in their initial appeal.
The Court reversed a lower court's decision and stated that the lower court should not have heard the case until after the Ohio Civil Rights Commission had concluded their investigation.
The Court reversed a lower court's decision that the change in the statutory definition of a household violated the appellee's due process rights.

The Court unanimously found that official discrimination and racial campaign appeals, combined with a multimember districting scheme, impaired black voters' ability to elect their candidates, invalidating North Carolina General Assembly districts.

The United States Supreme Court held that claims of partisan gerrymandering were justiciable, but failed to agree on a clear standard for the judicial review of the class of claims of a political nature to which such cases belong.

The Court upheld the constitutionality of a Georgia sodomy law criminalizing oral and anal sex in private between consenting adults, reasoning that the Constitution did not confer a fundamental right to engage in homosexual sodomy.

In a 5–4 decision, the Supreme Court held that the Puerto Rico government (law) could restrict advertisement for casino gambling from being targeted to residents, even if the activity itself was legal and advertisement to tourists was permitted.
The Court held that a regression analysis does not have to account for every possible factor that could influence salary in order to be considered as evidence of discrimination.
The Court upheld the suspension of a high school student who delivered a sexually suggestive speech at a school assembly.
The Court held that the closure was aimed at non-expressive activity and its incidental burden on speech was not subject to any First Amendment scrutiny.

The Court struck down the Gramm–Rudman–Hollings Act as an unconstitutional usurpation of executive power by Congress, because the law empowered Congress to terminate the Comptroller General for specified reasons.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Fourth Amendment does not prohibit a State from proving charges with the evidence discovered during an inventory search.
The Court held that a suspect's awareness of the crimes about which he may be questioned is not relevant to his waiver of his Fifth Amendment rights.
The Court held that where police reasonably believe their warrant was valid during a search, execution of the warrant does not violate respondent's Fourth Amendment rights.
The Supreme Court's decision effectively overturned the existing laws restricting gaming/gambling on U.S. Indian reservations.

The Court held that in a criminal case the requirement that the prosecution prove each element of a crime beyond a reasonable doubt applies only to elements of the offense, not to justification, so states could place the burden of proving justification on the defense.
The Court held that the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution requires the police to have probable cause before they can seize items in plain view.
The court held that the prosecutor may offer a plea bargain to a defendant in exchange for the defendant's promise not to sue the state under Section 1983, and that contract may be enforceable.
The Court decided that the standard for withholding of removal, which was set in INS v. Stevic, was too high a standard for applicants for asylum to satisfy.
In a Fifth Amendment Takings Clause case, the Court upheld a Pennsylvania statute that limited coal mining causing subsidence damage to buildings, dwellings, and cemeteries.
The Court found that the plan did not violate the protection against discrimination on the basis of sex in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
The Court, in a case over a search of a state hospital doctor's office during a workplace misconduct investigation, ruled that public employees retain their Fourth Amendment rights.

The Court held, 5–4, that the Confrontation Clause of the Constitution's Sixth Amendment barred the admission, in a joint trial, of a non-testifying codefendant's confession incriminating the defendant, even if the defendant's own confession was admitted against him.

The court held that a sales-tax scheme that taxes general interest magazines, but exempts newspapers and religious, professional, trade, and sports journals, violates the First Amendment's freedom of the press guarantee.
The death sentence of Warren McCleskey for armed robbery and murder was upheld.
The Court held that Jewish people can file racial discrimination suits.

The Court barred the widow of a serviceman killed while piloting a helicopter on a United States Coast Guard rescue mission from bringing her claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act (the "FTCA" or the "Act").

The U.S. Supreme Court held that a statute ordering the escheat of fractional interests in real property which had been bequeathed to members of the Oglala Sioux tribe was an unconstitutional taking which required just compensation.

The Court determined that the Bail Reform Act of 1984 was constitutional, which permitted the federal courts to detain an arrestee prior to trial if the government could prove that the individual was potentially a danger to society.

The court held that a regulation preventing inmates from marrying without permission violated their constitutional right to marry because it was not logically related to a legitimate penological concern, but a prohibition on inmate-to-inmate correspondence was justified by prison security needs.

In a dispute over mandatory arbitration of private securities fraud claims, the Court held that Wilko v. Swan did not apply to claims under the 1934 Act, reversing the Second Circuit, and also held that RICO claims were arbitrable.
The court held that the complete destruction of the value of property constituted a "taking" under the Fifth Amendment even if that taking was temporary and the property was later restored.

The court ruled that the prison regulations were not a violation of the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment of the U.S. Constitution to deprive an inmate of attending a religious service for "legitimate penological interests."
The United States Supreme Court held that an ordinance prohibiting all "First Amendment activities" in the Los Angeles International Airport was facially unconstitutional due to its overbreadth.

The Court considered a Louisiana law requiring creation science to be taught whenever evolutionary science was taught in public schools, and ruled that it violated the Establishment Clause because it was intended to advance a particular religion.
The Court held that the respondent's rights under the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment were not violated by his exclusion from the competency hearing.
The Court held that criminal defendants have a constitutional right to testify on their own behalf.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a mandatory death penalty for a prison inmate who is convicted of murder while serving a life sentence without possibility of parole is unconstitutional.

The Court held that juror testimony could not be used to discredit or overturn a jury verdict, even if the jury had been consuming copious amounts of alcohol, marijuana, and cocaine throughout the course of the trial.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of a federal statute that withheld federal funds from states whose legal drinking age did not conform to federal policy.
The Court ruled unanimously that federal courts have the power to enforce extraditions based on the Extradition Clause of Article Four of the United States Constitution.

The Court held that a state tax on using motor vehicles on the highway is unconstitutional when the amount of the tax is not calculated to be proportional to highway use and when the tax treats in-state and out-of-state road users differently.
The court decided that the exemption of religious organizations from the prohibition of religious discrimination in employment in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act is constitutional.

The United States Supreme Court decided that the federal statute criminalizing mail fraud applied only to the schemes and artifices defrauding victims of money or property, as opposed to those defrauding citizens of their rights to good government.

The Court ruled that a government employee's extremely critical remark about the President, made on a matter of public interest by someone with no policymaking role and little public interaction, was protected by the First Amendment, though direct threats would not be.
The court held that the standard of proof in a paternity action need not be higher than the preponderance of the evidence.

In a 6–3 decision, the Court held that officers are entitled to qualified immunity from civil damages if they can demonstrate that a "reasonable officer" could have believed that their actions did not violate the United States Constitution, even if that belief was incorrect.

The Court held that a serviceman could not file a tort action against the federal government even though the government secretly administered doses of LSD to him as part of an experimental program, because his injuries were found by the lower court to be service-related.

The Court ruled a California Coastal Commission regulation which required private homeowners to dedicate a public easement along valuable beachfront property as a condition of approval for a construction permit to renovate their beach bungalow unconstitutional.
The court decided that the warrantless search of a probationer's residence based on "reasonable grounds" in accordance with a state probation regulation did not violate the Fourth Amendment.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the former presiding officers of the New Jersey legislature did not have Article III standing to appeal a case, as that standing had passed on to their legislative successors.
The Court held that the two jury polls and the supplemental charge did not unlawfully pressure the jury to give a death sentence.
The Court held that defense witnesses can be prevented from testifying under certain circumstances, even if that hurts the defense's case.
The Court held that parodies of public figures, even those intending to cause emotional distress, are protected by the First and Fourteenth Amendments to the U.S. Constitution.

The Court ruled that courts must review the Board of Immigration Appeals's decision to deny motions to reopen immigration proceedings—the name of the procedural device used to present new evidence to immigration officials—for abuse of discretion.

The U.S. Supreme Court found the "display clause" of the code banning the display of certain protest signs to be facially unconstitutional, as the U.S. government did not have a compelling interest in protecting foreign governments from insults.
The court held that Freedom of Association under the First Amendment does not create a right to strike.

The Court ruled on the applicability of the Free Exercise Clause to the practice of religion on Native American sacred lands, specifically in the Chimney Rock area of the Six Rivers National Forest in California.
The Court ruled that section 310(b)(1) of the Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act of 1982 (TEFRA) does not violate the Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The United States Supreme Court held that before admitting evidence of extrinsic acts under Rule 404(b) of the Federal Rules of Evidence, federal courts should assess the evidence's sufficiency under Federal Rule of Evidence 104(b).
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Fourth Amendment does not prohibit the warrantless search and seizure of garbage left for collection outside the curtilage of a home.

The Court held that a federal court's dismissal of a civil action on the ground that it should be heard in a foreign court, under the doctrine of forum non conveniens, does not preclude the plaintiff from filing the same action in a state court that applies different forum non conveniens rules.

The court held that, notwithstanding the right to choice of counsel, the trial court has significant discretion to deny a criminal defendant's waiver of a conflict of interest with their chosen lawyer.
The Court held that a convicted person may use habeas corpus to challenge their conviction if they later learn that the prosecution racially discriminated in jury selection.
The Court held that the United States may be liable for negligence when federal employees violate mandatory duties imposed by statute or regulation, even in the context of a regulatory program.
The Court clarified and extended the protections provided under Edwards v. Arizona.
The Court held that the federal statute governed the District Court's decision whether to give effect to the forum-selection clause.
The Court held that a state notice-of-claim statute could not be applied to a civil rights suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 in state court.

The Court held that an attempted Hobbs Act robbery does not qualify as a "crime of violence" under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A) because no element of the offense requires proof that the defendant used, attempted to use, or threatened to use force.
The Supreme Court held that the FTCA's intentional tort exception did not apply.

The Court determined that a cause of action would not be implied for the violation of rights where the U.S. Congress had already provided a remedy for the violation of rights at issue, even if the remedy was inadequate.
The Supreme Court of the United States upheld the ordinance by the town of Brookfield, Wisconsin, preventing protest outside of a residential home.
The Court held that government contractors are immune from liability for design defects in military equipment.
The Court ruled that when officers conduct an unlawful search followed by a lawful one, evidence seized in the second search is admissible if that search is genuinely independent of the earlier one.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of the Adolescent Family Life Act.
The Court determined the Independent Counsel Act was constitutional.
The U.S. Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a minor on grounds of "cruel and unusual punishment."
In a case over a family accused of enslaving two men on their farm, the Court held that the jury had been improperly instructed on the nature of involuntary servitude and remanded for a new trial.

The Court held that the placement of a screen between a defendant and the witnesses testifying against him, making it impossible for the witnesses to see him during their testimony, violated the Confrontation Clause.
The United States Supreme Court held that agencies should not be presumed to have the power to promulgate retroactive rules unless that power is expressly authorized by Congress.
The Court held that police officials do not need a warrant to observe an individual's property from public airspace.

The United States Supreme Court held that the minority set-aside program of Richmond, Virginia, which gave preference to minority business enterprises (MBE) in the awarding of municipal contracts, was unconstitutional under the Equal Protection Clause.

In a challenge to a Texas statute exempting religious publications from state sales tax, the Court overturned an appellate court's decision that the exemption was constitutional and remanded the case.
The Court held that a state anti-plug molding law preempted because it partially duplicated and therefore interfered with the balance Congress had struck by federal patent law.

The court held that a state government agency's failure to prevent child abuse by a custodial parent does not violate the child's right to liberty for the purposes of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The court held that the plain statement rule of Michigan v. Long applies to federal habeas proceedings originating from state court judgments.

The Court invoked the one person, one vote principle emanating from the Equal Protection Clause; extending the principle in Reynolds v. Sims to municipal government, the Board's structure was ruled to be unconstitutional.

By a 5–4 margin it upheld the mail fraud conviction of an Illinois man and resolved a conflict among the appellate circuits over which test to use to determine if a defendant was entitled to a jury instruction allowing conviction on a lesser included charge.
The Court upheld an ordinance imposing age limits on teen dance halls, ruling that gathering for recreational dancing is not an "expressive association" under the First Amendment.
The Court held that, when determining how much business a corporation has done in a state for tax purposes, the Dormant Commerce Clause requires only that the formula be rational.
The Court decided states may impose taxes on non-tribal commercial activity that takes place on tribal land.

An accounting firm denied an employee partnership allegedly because she did not fit the partners' idea of how a woman should look and act, and the Court held that this constituted sex discrimination under Title VII since the employer failed to prove it would have denied her anyway.

The Court determined that an objective reasonableness standard should apply to a civilian's claim that law enforcement officials used excessive force in the course of making an arrest, investigatory stop, or other "seizure" of their person.
The court held that a civil sanction is criminal punishment and can activate the Double Jeopardy Clause if it serves the traditional goals of punishment: retribution or deterrence.
The Court held that investors’ claims under the Securities Act of 1933 can be resolved through arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act.
The Court held that, if a criminal defendant received a sentence after a guilty plea but withdrew that plea and was convicted at trial, the judge may hand down a more severe sentence.
The Court held that testimony in the form of a victim impact statement is admissible during the sentencing phase of a trial only if it directly relates to the "circumstances of the crime."
The court held that the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986 (SARA) rendered states liable for monetary damages in federal court.
The Court held that States and their officials acting in their official capacity are not persons when sued for monetary damages under the Civil Rights Act of 1871.
The Court held that the due-process rights of a man who claimed to be a child's biological father had not been violated.
The Court held, 5–4, that burning the flag of the United States is protected speech under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, as doing so counts as symbolic speech and political speech.

In a libel case brought by a public figure, the Court held that departure from responsible reporting alone was not enough for damages, but that reckless disregard for the truth, including ignoring obvious sources, could support damages for actual malice.
The Court found that the city had a substantial interest in limiting excessive noise and the regulation was "content neutral".
The Court held that capital defendants do not have a constitutional right to counsel in state collateral postconviction proceedings.

The court held that, in general, the Seventh Amendment entitles a person who has not submitted a claim against a bankruptcy estate to a jury trial when sued by the bankruptcy trustee over an issue where the jury trial right attaches.

The Court upheld the death penalty for mentally disabled offenders because the Court determined executing the intellectually disabled was not "cruel and unusual punishment" under the Eighth Amendment.

The Court instructed a lower court to reevaluate the compatibility of a resolution of the State University of New York that prohibited private commercial enterprises from operating in SUNY facilities with the First Amendment.
The Supreme Court in Webster allowed for states to legislate in an aspect that had previously been thought to be forbidden under Roe v. Wade (1973).

The Court considered holiday displays on public property in downtown Pittsburgh and held that the county violated the Establishment Clause by displaying a nativity scene in the courthouse, because its primary effect was to advance religion.
The court held that a city's conditioning of an entity's franchise renewal of the settlement of a labor dispute is preempted by the National Labor Relations Act.

The Court held that neither common law evidentiary privilege, nor First Amendment academic freedom protects peer review materials that are relevant to charges of racial or sexual discrimination in tenure decisions.
The Court held that state courts have concurrent jurisdiction to decide civil claims brought under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO).

In a case about determining childhood Social Security disability benefits, the Court ruled that substantial parts of the SSI program's regulation on childhood disability were inconsistent with the Social Security Act's "comparable severity" standard.

The majority opinion authored by Associate Justice Thurgood Marshall held that the "demand notes were securities within the meaning of section 3(a)(10) of the 1934 Act" and "rejected the application of the Howey and Landreth Timber tests to note transactions".
The Court determined that Fourth Amendment protections do not apply to searches and seizures by United States agents of property owned by a nonresident alien in a foreign country.

The Court held that the Fourth Amendment permitted a properly limited protective sweep during an in-home arrest when the officer reasonably believed, based on specific and articulable facts, that the area harbored a person posing a danger to those at the scene.
The court held that the receiving court must apply the choice-of-law rules of the court where the case originated after a change of venue between federal district courts.
The United States Supreme Court held that an action by an employee for a breach of a labor union's duty of fair representation entitled him to a jury trial under the Seventh Amendment.
The Court held that the state could deny unemployment benefits to a person fired for violating a state prohibition on the use of peyote even though the use of the drug was part of a religious ritual.

The Court held that it would not be a violation of the Fourth Amendment for state police departments to allow officers conducting an inventory search discretion in which closed containers they choose to open.

The Court ruled that a confession given at the police station was admissible, even though the suspect had been arrested illegally in his home without a warrant, because it was made outside the home after Miranda warnings.

In a 7–2 decision, the court held that a person staying as a guest in the house of another had a legal expectation of privacy, and that a warrantless entry into that house to arrest the person tainted the arrest and the individual's subsequent statements.

The Court held that the First Amendment allows states to outlaw possessing child pornography, not just distributing it, found Ohio's law not overbroad given a narrowing interpretation, and ordered a new trial.

The Court held that the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments do not require mandatory appellate review of death penalty cases, and that next-friend suits require a prior relationship and an appellant unable to litigate his own cause.

The Court held that a successor copyright owner (one who obtains ownership later on, such as the heirs of a copyright owner who dies) has the exclusive right to permit the creation and exploitation of derivative works, regardless of potentially conflicting agreements by prior copyright holders.

The Court ruled that parents' payments toward their sons' missionary expenses for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints could not be treated as "charitable contributions" under the tax regulation.

The Court held that that: "the Double Jeopardy Clause bars a subsequent prosecution if, to establish an essential element of an offense charged in that prosecution, the government will prove conduct that constitutes an offense for which the defendant has already been prosecuted."
The court held that restitution obligations constitute "debts" within the meaning of § 101(11), and are therefore dischargeable under Chapter 13 of the Bankruptcy Code.

The Court unanimously held that a state court may constitutionally exercise personal jurisdiction over a non-resident served with process while temporarily visiting the state, though the justices disagreed on the reasoning.
The Court concluded that Indian tribes could not prosecute Indians who were members of other tribes for crimes committed by those nonmember Indians on their reservations.
The U.S. Supreme Court reversed, saying the letterhead was truthful, and the First Amendment favored disclosure over concealing information.
The Court held that the Fourth Amendment does not prohibit the warrantless seizure of evidence which is in plain view.
The Court held that the Court's decision in American Trucking Associations, Inc. v. Scheiner did not apply retroactively.
The Court held that undercover police agents did not need to give Miranda warnings when talking to suspects in jail.
By a 5–4 decision invalidated a federal law against flag desecration as a violation of free speech under the First Amendment.
The majority opinion ruled that anonymous tips can provide reasonable suspicion for a traffic stop provided that police can factually verify the circumstances asserted by the tip.

In a case under the Militia Clauses of Article I, Section 8, the Court held that Congress may authorize National Guard members to be ordered to active federal duty for training abroad without the governor's consent or a declared national emergency.
The Court held that police sobriety checkpoints met the Fourth Amendment standard of reasonable search and seizure, and so were constitutional under the federal Constitution.

The Court held that, of several incriminating statements a drunk-driving suspect made in police custody, only his confused answer about when he turned six was inadmissible, as it was testimonial; the others were admissible.

The Court held that 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(1) of United States patent law exempted premarketing activity conducted to gain approval of a device under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act from a finding of infringement.
The Court rejected the argument that a separate opinion privilege existed against libel.
The Court held that the First Amendment forbids a government entity from basing its decision to promote, transfer, recall, or hire low-level public employees based upon their party affiliation.

In a 5–4 decision, the Court affirmed the earlier ruling of the Supreme Court of Missouri and ruled in favor of the State of Missouri, finding it was acceptable to require "clear and convincing evidence" of a patient's wishes for removal of life support.
The Court held that intermediate scrutiny should be applied to equal protection challenges to federal statutes using benign racial classifications for a non-remedial purpose.

The Court upheld two important aspects of the capital sentencing scheme in Arizona—judicial sentencing and the aggravating factor "especially heinous, cruel, or depraved"—as not unconstitutionally vague.

The Court held that the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause, which provides criminal defendants with the right to confront witnesses against them, did not bar the use of one-way closed-circuit television to present testimony by an alleged child sex abuse victim.
The Court held that suits against the government were subject to the same presumption of equitable tolling as are suits against private parties.
The Court reversed the conviction of John L. Cheek, a tax protester, for willful failure to file tax returns and tax evasion, who was convicted again during retrial.
The court held that the three prong test for the issuance of a subpoena in United States v. Nixon does not apply to subpoenas issued by a grand jury.
The Court held that an Indian tribe was not subject to state sales taxes on sales made to tribal members but was liable for state taxes on sales to non-tribal members.
The court held that a plaintiff challenging government action that does not regulate their own conduct must show that they are within the statute's "zone" of protection to have Article III standing.

The Court, in a case about the standard of review for an allegedly coerced confession, ruled the confession involuntary, held that the harmless error rule applied, and found its use as evidence was not harmless.

The Court re-examined the Batson Challenge against race-based peremptory strikes and expanded it, allowing defendants and other parties to question peremptory challenges in jury selection regardless of race, under the Equal Protection Clause.
The Supreme Court held that United States federal courts will enforce forum selection clauses so long as the clause is not unreasonably burdensome to the party seeking to escape it.

The Court held that a fleeing suspect is not "seized" under the terms of the Fourth Amendment unless the pursuing officers apply physical force to the suspect or the suspect submits to officers' demands to halt.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Federal Arbitration Act requires enforcement of an arbitration clause to compel arbitration of statutory Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 claims.
The Court held that the petitioner, Bryan Lankford, had been unconstitutionally sentenced to death in violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court upheld Department of Health and Human Services regulations prohibiting employees in federally funded family-planning facilities from counseling a patient on abortion.

The court held that the Bankruptcy Code's Section 522(f) allows a judicial lien to be eliminated even when a state's bankruptcy policy has defined exempt property to exclude property encumbered by a judicial lien.
The Court held that a prosecutor may dismiss jurors who are bilingual in Spanish and English from juries that will consider Spanish-language testimony.

The Court held that police may search an automobile and containers within it when they have probable cause to believe contraband or evidence is inside, and it overruled earlier precedents that required a warrant for containers alone.
The Court held that peremptory challenges may not be used to exclude jurors on the basis of race in civil trials.

The Court held that a state statute allowing prejudgment attachment of a defendant's real property without prior notice or hearing, extraordinary circumstances, or a bond requirement violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

The United States Supreme Court held that individuals are eligible to file for relief under the reorganization provisions of chapter 11 of the United States Bankruptcy Code, even if they are not engaged in a business.

The Court held that the right to counsel secured by the Sixth Amendment and the right to counsel protected by Miranda v. Arizona are separate and distinct, such that invoking one does not implicitly invoke the other.
The Court overturned a per se rule imposed by the Florida Supreme Court that held consensual searches of passengers on buses were always unreasonable.

The Court considered whether a Missouri constitutional provision requiring state judges to retire at age 70 conflicted with the federal ADEA and the Equal Protection Clause, and it upheld the provision.

The Court ruled that a state has the constitutional authority to ban public nudity, even as part of expressive conduct such as dancing, because doing so furthers a substantial government interest in protecting morality and order.
The Court held that the First Amendment freedom of the press did not exempt journalists from generally applicable laws, in a case where newspapers published a source's name despite promising not to.

The Court held that a petitioner was barred from raising federal constitutional claims in federal habeas court because he had procedurally defaulted them in state habeas proceedings by filing his notice of appeal three days late.

The Court held that the Eleventh Amendment prevents tribes from filing lawsuits against the United States because they are not party to the Constitution; therefore, the United States must sue itself as a trustee for the tribe under United States v. Minnesota.

The Court held that testimony in the form of a victim impact statement is admissible during the sentencing phase of a trial and, in death penalty cases, does not violate the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause of the Eighth Amendment.
The Supreme Court of the United States decided the characteristics of inferior officers of the United States for the purposes of the Appointments Clause.

In a federal felony trial where a magistrate judge supervised jury selection, the Court ruled that a defendant must affirmatively object, and that merely acquiescing to the magistrate's involvement is not enough to reverse a conviction.

The Court ruled that the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause allowed a state to impose a life sentence without the possibility of parole for the possession of 672 grams (23.70 oz) of cocaine.

The court held that a "substantial likelihood of material prejudice" test for a restriction of lawyer speech about an ongoing proceeding satisfies the First Amendment, but the test must not be void for vagueness.

The Court confirmed that the Attorney General of the United States has broad discretion to reopen deportation (now called "removal") proceedings, as well as other adjudications heard before immigration courts.

The United States Supreme Court ruled that a Guatemalan man seeking asylum in the United States of America as a result of forced conscription in a guerrilla army did not establish persecution on account of political opinion, a legal requirement for asylum.
The Court on a 7–2 vote held that the use of excessive physical force against a prisoner may constitute cruel and unusual punishment even though the inmate does not suffer serious injury.
The Court held that expenditures incurred by a target corporation in the course of a friendly takeover are nondeductible capital expenditures.

The Court ruled that a person's rights of association and due process, as granted under the First Amendment and Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution, cannot be infringed upon if such an association has no bearing on the case at hand.
The court held that the United States Court of Claims was an Article I tribunal.

The Court held that a court of appeals may review an interlocutory order issued by a district court acting in its appellate capacity in a bankruptcy matter, when such review is authorized under 28 U.S.C. § 1292.
The Court held that principles of agency were relevant to interpreting the concept of "employee".

The court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act does not confer upon parents a private right to sue a state for not making "reasonable efforts" towards family reunification under that act, and they cannot sue for that under Section 1983.
The Court held that "a…offense and a conspiracy to commit that offense are not the same offense for double jeopardy purposes."

The Court held unanimously that New Kent County's freedom of choice plan did not adequately comply with the school board's responsibility to determine a system of admission to public schools on a non-racial basis.

The Court overturned a Nebraska man's conviction for receiving child sexual abuse material through the mail, ruling that postal inspectors had implanted the desire to do so through repeated written entreaties, which amounted to entrapment.

The Court held that a cause-and-prejudice standard, rather than Fay v. Noia's deliberate bypass standard, is the correct standard for excusing a habeas corpus petitioner's failure to develop a material fact in state-court proceedings.
The Court ruled that the federal courts do not have the supervisory power to require prosecutors to present exculpatory evidence to the grand jury.

The court held that private citizens are not entitled to qualified immunity from Section 1983 suits over misusing an unconstitutional public process merely because they presumed the process was constitutional.
The Court held that a Tennessee law that restricted political campaigning within 100 feet (30 m) of a polling place did not violate the First Amendment.

The court held that, to prove that a public official has committed extortion in violation of the Hobbs Act by accepting a payment, the government is not required to show that the official took an "affirmative act" to induce the payment.
The Court held that an Alabama law imposing a fee (of $72 per ton) on out-of-state hazardous waste being disposed of in-state violated the Dormant Commerce Clause.

The Court held that Hawaii laws effectively prohibiting write-in voting did not violate the First or Fourteenth Amendment, reasoning that getting nominated under Hawaii's election laws was relatively easy.

The Court held that an equipment manufacturer lacking significant market power in the primary equipment market could still have enough market power in the repair parts aftermarket to be liable under antitrust laws for exclusionary conduct there.

The Court held that a group of American wildlife conservation and other environmental organizations lacked standing to challenge regulations jointly issued by the Secretaries of the Interior and Commerce.

The Court held that the respondent's forcible abduction from a foreign country, despite the existence of an extradition treaty with said country, does not prohibit him from being tried before a U.S. court for violations of American criminal laws.

The Court held that, notwithstanding the traditional exception to diversity jurisdiction prohibiting federal courts from hearing domestic relations cases, federal courts may hear money damages suits between former spouses.
The Court held that, if a company is in multiple and independent lines of business in and outside a state, then that state may tax the company's income from in-state activities only.
The Court upheld Proposition 13, California's constitutional amendment that capped property taxes and limited reassessments to when property changes ownership.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a criminal defendant cannot make peremptory challenges based solely on race.
The Court permitted the federal government to induce shifts in state waste policy through other means.

The Supreme Court of the United States unanimously invalidated Saint Paul, Minnesota's Bias-Motivated Crime Ordinance and reversed the conviction of a teenager for burning a cross on the lawn of an African-American family.
In a suit by a smoker against tobacco companies, the Court held that the Surgeon General's warning did not preclude lawsuits by smokers against tobacco companies on the basis of several claims.
The Court held that schools may not sponsor clerics to conduct even non-denominational prayer.

The court held that the 8+1⁄2 year delay between Doggett's indictment and actual arrest violated his Sixth Amendment right to a speedy trial, arguing that the government had been negligent in pursuing him and that Doggett had remained unaware of the indictment until his arrest.

Resulted in an eight to one ruling that the eight public universities in Mississippi had not sufficiently integrated and that the state must take affirmative action to change this under the Equal Protection Clause.
The Court held that Two Pesos, Inc. infringed upon the trademark of Taco Cabana, Inc. by copying the design of their restaurants.

In a case about the 1990 Census, the Court held that the President is not an "agency" under the Administrative Procedure Act, so the Act does not authorize judicial review of actions Congress delegated to the President.

The Court upheld the right to have an abortion as established by the "essential holding" of Roe v. Wade (1973) and issued as its "key judgment" the restoration of the undue burden standard when evaluating state-imposed restrictions on that right.
The Court held that a seizure of property like that which occurs during an eviction, even absent a search or an arrest, implicates the Fourth Amendment.

The court decided whether a portion of a dwelling unit exclusively used as a principal place of business for any trade or business of a taxpayer would allow a deduction to the taxpayer's income taxes under Internal Revenue Code Section 280A(c)(1)(A).

The court held that only a natural person may qualify for in forma pauperis (IFP) treatment in federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1915, and that the term "person" as used in § 1915 does not include artificial entities.

The Court determined that a question of whether the Senate had properly tried an impeachment was political in nature and could not be resolved in the courts if there was no applicable judicial standard.
The court held that Section 1985(3) of The Civil Rights Act of 1871 does not provide a federal cause of action against persons obstructing access to abortion clinics.

The Court held that failure to make an objection under Collins v. Lockhart did not constitute undue prejudice required by Strickland v. Washington, because the error did not cause a fundamentally unfair trial, as opposed to merely a different outcome of the case.
The Court held that claims of actual innocence do not, by themselves, provide a basis for federal habeas relief.
The Supreme Court of the United States rejected the assertion that attempted monopolization may be proven merely by demonstration of unfair or predatory conduct.
The court held that severance is not automatically required in every case where co-defendants desire to make mutually antagonistic defenses.

The court held that the Interstate Agreement on Detainers's statute of limitation for bringing a case against an incarcerated person who gives notice to a forum state that they are incarcerated in another state begins after the notice letter has been received by the forum state's prosecution.

The majority opinion authored by Associate Justice Thurgood Marshall held that the "demand notes were securities within the meaning of section 3(a)(10) of the 1934 Act" and "rejected the application of the Howey and Landreth Timber tests to note transactions".

The Supreme Court ruled that the Immigration and Naturalization Service's regulations regarding the release of alien unaccompanied minors did not violate the Due Process Clause of the United States Constitution.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a ban by the city of Cincinnati, on the distribution of commercial material via news racks, violated the First Amendment.

The Court held that, when a state uses a consistent narrowing definition for a broad term like "utter disregard," the broad term can function as a valid aggravating circumstance under the Fourteenth Amendment.
The court held that a disparate treatment claim cannot succeed unless the employee's protected trait had a determinative influence on the employer's decisionmaking.

The Court held that federal courts deciding whether to grant habeas relief for unconstitutional trial error should assess such claims using the harmless error standard from Kotteakos v. United States.

The Court held that Fifth Amendment Miranda v. Arizona arguments can be raised again in federal habeas corpus proceedings, even if a criminal defendant had a fair chance to argue those claims in state court.

In a dispute over the three-mile marginal belt along California's coast, the Court held that California did not own it and that the Federal Government had paramount rights and full dominion over its resources, including oil.

The court held that a first-time offender could accrue multiple convictions and trigger penalties "n the case of his second or subsequent conviction" under the Armed Career Criminal Act, specifically 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1), a provision of the Armed Career Criminal Act.

The Court held that the government was not entitled to a presumption that a source was confidential under Exemption 7(D) of the Freedom of Information Act whenever the source gave information to the FBI during a criminal investigation.

The Court held that the exchange of a gun for drugs constituted "use" of the firearm for purposes of a federal statute imposing penalties for "use" of a firearm "during and in relation to" a drug trafficking crime.

The Court unanimously held that, when a police officer who is conducting a lawful patdown search for weapons feels something that plainly is contraband, the object may be seized even though it is not a weapon.
In a unanimous decision, the court concluded that it was.
The Court held that a court reporter is not absolutely immune from damages liability for failing to produce a transcript of a federal criminal trial.
The United States Supreme Court held that enhanced penalties for hate crimes do not violate criminal defendants' First Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that an ordinance passed in Hialeah, Florida, forbidding the unnecessary killing of "an animal in a public or private ritual or ceremony not for the primary purpose of food consumption", was unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that Congress specifically abrogated treaty rights with the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe as to hunting and fishing rights on reservation lands that were acquired for a reservoir.

The court held that a school must continue to provide an interpreter under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act even if the child elects to attend a religious school; to do so does not violate the Establishment Clause.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that imprisoned people do not need to be actively experiencing injuries from their confinement conditions before challenging them as cruel and unusual punishment.

The United States Supreme Court held that federal courts cannot require that a plaintiff exhaust his administrative remedies before seeking judicial review when exhaustion of remedies is not required by either administrative rules or statute.
The U.S. Supreme Court decided on June 21, 1993.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that if a defendant was competent to stand trial, they were automatically competent to plead guilty, and thereby waive the panoply of trial rights, including the right to counsel.
The Court upheld the decision of the West Virginia state court awarding $19,000 in compensatory damages and $10 million in punitive damages to the plaintiff.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution applies to civil forfeiture cases.

The Court ruled that redistricting based on race, here a snake-like majority-minority North Carolina district drawn solely on race, must meet strict scrutiny under the Equal Protection Clause and violated the Fourteenth Amendment.

In a double jeopardy case, the Court overruled an earlier decision, revived the traditional Blockburger standard, and held that subsequent convictions for offenses containing the same elements violated the Double Jeopardy Clause.

The Court held that foreign companies acting in foreign countries could nevertheless be held liable for violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act if they conspired to restrain trade within the United States, and succeeded in doing so.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that, in certain circumstances, a court may order that parents be reimbursed for unilaterally withdrawing disabled children from schools that do not comply with the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, the Court held that a determination about whether a work environment is hostile or abusive requires a consideration of all relevant circumstances.

The Court held that commissioned military officers, who are appointed by the president of the United States by and with the advice and consent of the United States Senate, may be assigned to act as military judges without the need to be confirmed a second time by the Senate.

The court held that the comprehensive administrative review scheme established by the Federal Mine Safety and Health Amendments Act of 1977 implicitly precludes federal district court jurisdiction over pre-enforcement challenges to the Act and its regulations.
The Court ruled that the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) could apply to enterprises without economic motives; anti-abortion protesters could thus be prosecuted under it.
The Court held that there is no substantive due process violation that creates liability under Section 1983 when the police arrests someone for conduct that is not unlawful.

In a dispute over attorneys' fees under the Copyright Act of 1976, the Court held that such awards are discretionary and that the same standards apply to a prevailing plaintiff and a prevailing defendant.
The Court held that peremptory challenges based solely on a prospective juror's sex are unconstitutional.

In a securities fraud case, the Court held that private civil liability under Rule 10b-5 does not extend to aiders and abettors who do not themselves engage in a manipulative or deceptive practice, so private plaintiffs could not bring such suits.

The Court considered whether an officer's undisclosed opinion that a questioned person was a suspect mattered for Miranda custody, and held unanimously that such a subjective view was irrelevant, reversing and remanding.
The United States Supreme Court held that an Executive Order to shut down the Philadelphia Naval Base was not subject to judicial review.
The United States Supreme Court ruled that the crime of possessing an unregistered machine gun requires knowledge that the firearm is a machine gun under the National Firearms Act.

The Court held that a public hospital did not need to determine what a nurse actually said in criticizing a supervisor's staffing practices, if it reasonably believed what she said and reasonably believed it could be disruptive, and it vacated the appeals court ruling.
In a dispute over whether a state could impose minimum water flow requirements on a proposed hydropower dam under section 401 of the Clean Water Act, the Court ruled in favor of the state.
The Court ruled that an uncounseled misdemeanor conviction, which resulted in a punishment other than imprisonment, can be used to enhance a sentence for a subsequent offense.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that a prison official's "deliberate indifference" to a substantial risk of serious harm to an inmate violates the cruel and unusual punishment clause of the Eighth Amendment.

The Court held that that, where a capital defendant's future dangerousness is at issue, and the only alternative sentence available is life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, the sentencing jury must be informed that the defendant is ineligible for parole.
The Court held that the FCC's statutory authority to "modify" requirements did not allow it to set aside the requirement that common carriers file tariffs with fixed terms and prices.
The Court held that an amendment to the Oregon state constitution disallowing judicial review of the size of punitive damages was a violation of due process.

The Court held that a §1983 plaintiff seeking damages for an allegedly unconstitutional conviction or imprisonment must prove the conviction or sentence was reversed, expunged, declared invalid by a state tribunal, or called into question by a federal writ of habeas corpus.

In a dispute over FCC must-carry rules for cable television operators, the Court held in the first ruling that cable companies were First Amendment speakers, and in the second held the rules were not restrictions of their free speech rights.

The Court considered a First Amendment challenge by antiabortion protesters to a Florida state court injunction limiting their demonstrations outside an abortion clinic, and it affirmed in part and reversed in part.

The United States Supreme Court held that a fine for contempt that could not be purged by compliance with the order of the court was a criminal contempt, and it could not be assessed without a jury trial.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, the Court held that government prosecutors need not prove evidence of an overt act in furtherance of the conspiracy when prosecuting individuals under the drug conspiracy statute codified at 21 U.S.C. § 846.
The Court considered whether the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey was an "arm of the state" entitled to Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity and held that it was not.
The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, which had found federal child pornography laws unconstitutionally vague, because the relevant sections could be interpreted in a constitutional way.
The Court held that under Federal Rules of Evidence Rule 801(d)(1)(B), a prior consistent statement is not hearsay only if the statement was made before the motive to fabricate arose.
The United States Supreme Court expanded the ability to reopen a case in light of new evidence of actual innocence.
The Court held that Amtrak is a government agency and is thus subject to the First Amendment.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that allowing the judge to impose a death sentence and making the jury recommendation non-binding even when it calls for life imprisonment is constitutional.
The Court held that a color could meet the legal requirements for trademark registration under the Lanham Act, provided that it has acquired secondary meaning in the market.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that Congress may not retroactively require federal courts to reopen final judgments.
The court held that an order from the Board of Immigration Appeals denying deferral of removal in a withholding only proceeding is not a final order of removal.
The Court held that a prosecutor has an affirmative duty to disclose evidence favorable to a defendant pursuant to Brady v. Maryland and United States v. Bagley.
The Court struck down the Gun-Free School Zones Act of 1990 (GFSZA), determining that it was not a valid exercise of Congress's power to regulate interstate commerce.

The Court ruled that states cannot impose qualifications for prospective members of Congress stricter than those the Constitution specifies, invalidating 23 states' congressional term limit provisions.

The Court held that the traditional, common-law-derived "knock and announce" rule for executing search warrants must be incorporated into the "reasonableness" analysis of whether the actual execution of the warrant is/was justified under the 4th Amendment.
The Court reversed a district court ruling that had required Missouri to correct intentional racial discrimination in Kansas City schools by funding salary increases and remedial education programs.

The court held that a petitioner who makes a timely challenge to the constitutionality of the appointment of an Officer of the United States is entitled to a decision on the merits of the question under the Appointments Clause.

The Court held that racial classifications, imposed by the federal government, must be analyzed under a standard of "strict scrutiny", the most stringent level of review, which requires that racial classifications be narrowly tailored to further compelling governmental interests.
The court held that a statute creates a liberty interest for incarcerated people only if it imposes "atypical and significant hardship" in relation to the ordinary incidents of prison life.
The court held the trial judge's refusal to submit the question of "materiality" to the jury was unconstitutional.

The Court held that lying to an investigator is not obstruction of justice merely because the investigator would then testify before a grand jury; the accused must specifically intend to influence such proceedings directly.
The Court upheld a state's restriction on lawyer advertising under the First Amendment's commercial speech doctrine.

The Court upheld a public school district's random drug testing of student-athletes, holding that although the tests were Fourth Amendment searches, they were reasonable given the schools' interest in preventing teenage drug use.
The Court held that "direct evidence" of legislative purpose could demonstrate a racial motive supporting a claim under Shaw v. Reno.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) does not apply in custody rulings for Miranda.

The Court held that when a bankruptcy court remanded a removed action to state court because of a timely-raised removal defect or lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, the removal statute barred a court of appeals from reviewing the order.

The Court interpreted a federal statute imposing a mandatory five-year term for "using" a firearm in a drug trafficking crime, ruling that "use" means "active employment" of a firearm, not mere possession, and remanded the cases.

In a dispute over whether software copyright covers a program's user interface such as menus, the Court, split evenly with one justice recused, left the lower court's decision affirmed without setting national precedent.

The Court held a defendant's immediate appeal of an unfavorable qualified immunity ruling on a motion to dismiss does not deprive the court of appeals of jurisdiction over a second appeal, also based on qualified immunity, immediately following denial of summary judgment.
The Court held that the innocent owner defense is not constitutionally mandated by Fourteenth Amendment Due Process in cases of civil forfeiture.

The Court held that under the Constitution's Census Clause, Congress is granted with the authority to conduct an "actual enumeration" of the American society, chiefly for the purpose of allocating congressional representation among the states.
The Court ruled that states could moderate national banks if doing so does not prevent or largely interfere with the national bank's ability to exercise its powers.

The Court held that Article One of the U.S. Constitution did not give the United States Congress the power to abrogate the sovereign immunity of the states that is further protected under the Eleventh Amendment.

The Court reversed an Oklahoma court decision holding that a defendant is presumed to be competent to stand trial unless he proves otherwise by the second highest legal standard of proof, that of clear and convincing evidence, ruling that to be unconstitutional.
The court held that the burden of proof for selective prosecution rests with the defendant, who must show the government declined to prosecute similarly situated suspects of other races.

The Court held that a complete ban on the advertising of alcohol prices was unconstitutional under the First Amendment, and that the Twenty-first Amendment, empowering the states to regulate alcohol, did not lessen other constitutional restraints of state power.
The Court held that a state constitutional amendment in Colorado preventing protected status based upon homosexuality or bisexuality violated the Equal Protection Clause.
The Court held that appellate courts should review probable cause determinations for warrantless searches de novo.
"declared that any traffic offense committed by a driver was a legitimate legal basis for a stop."
The Court ruled that North Carolina's congressional redistricting plan, challenged as a racial gerrymander, violated the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Supreme Court, in a plurality opinion, held that race was the predominant factor in the creation of the districts and that under a strict scrutiny standard the three districts were not narrowly tailored to further a compelling governmental interest.
The Court created a psychotherapist-patient privilege in the Federal Rules of Evidence.
The court held that in rem civil forfeitures are not "punishment" for purposes of the Double Jeopardy Clause.
The court held that Bounds v. Smith did not create an abstract, freestanding right for incarcerated people to access a law library or legal assistance.
The Court held that the New York state rule applied.
The Supreme Court of the United States struck down the long-standing male-only admission policy of the Virginia Military Institute (VMI) in a 7–1 decision.
The Court concluded that AEDPA's provisions changed the standards governing the granting of habeas corpus petitions but did not violate the Suspension Clause.

In a challenge to provisions of the Cable Television Consumer Protection and Competition Act of 1992, the Court held that sections 10(b) and 10(c) violated the First Amendment, while upholding section 10(a) as consistent with it.
The Court held that the United States Government had breached its contractual obligations.

The Court held that the Fourth Amendment does not require police officers to inform a motorist at the end of a traffic stop that they are free to go before seeking permission to search the motorist's car.

The Court held that federal jurisdiction predicated on diversity of citizenship can be sustained even if there did not exist complete diversity at the time of removal to federal court, so long as complete diversity exists at the time the district court enters judgment.

The Court ruled for a mother whose parental rights were terminated and who could not afford record preparation fees, holding that a court may not bar an appeal in parental rights cases because of a party's financial means.

The Court concluded that Federal Rule of Evidence 403 required the trial court to accept a defendant's stipulation to a prior conviction, an element of the charged crime, over the prosecution's objection.

The Court held that a provision escheating to the tribe, upon the owner's death, small fractional interests in an allotment (under two percent and earning less than $100 in five years) worked an unconstitutional taking.

The Court unanimously held that under federal law, U.S. employers must not engage in workplace discrimination such as writing bad job references, or otherwise retaliating against former employees as a punishment for filing job discrimination complaints.
