The court ruled in a 6–3 decision that "floating buffer zones" preventing protesters approaching people entering or leaving the clinics were unconstitutional, though "fixed buffer zones" around the clinics themselves remained constitutional.
The Court held that officers could order passengers out of a car during a traffic stop, extending Pennsylvania v. Mimms.

In a dispute over whether St. Louis police sergeants and lieutenants were owed overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Court held that it should defer to the Secretary of Labor's interpretation of the regulations.
The Court held that Article III required standing for each stage of litigation, rather than just when a complaint is filed.
The court, in a per curiam opinion, "dismissed the writ of certiorari as improvidently granted."

The Court held that people who have been released from incarceration in programs that are equivalent to parole have the same rights as people on parole; they are entitled to a hearing before the government can return them to incarceration.

In a dispute over FCC must-carry rules for cable television operators, the Court held in the first ruling that cable companies were First Amendment speakers, and in the second held the rules were not restrictions of their free speech rights.
The Court held that state governments may prohibit candidates from being listed on the ballot for more than one party.
The Court held that the Fourth Amendment does not allow a blanket exception to the knock-and-announce rule for investigations of drug-related felonies.

In a case about tribal courts' authority over civil disputes between nonmembers on public highways in Indian Country, the Court held that, absent Congressional authorization, tribal courts could not adjudicate such matters on state-maintained highways crossing reservation land.
It held that members of the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals were "inferior officers" under the Appointments Clause.
The Court held that a spouse that is not a participant in an ERISA account cannot will part or all of it before distribution of the pension plan.

The court held that the rule of Simmons v. South Carolina, that a capital defendant has the right to have their jury informed of their parole ineligibility where their future dangerousness is put at issue, does not apply retroactively to cases on federal habeas corpus review.

The Court overruled its earlier decision and held that it did not violate the Establishment Clause for a state-sponsored education program to let public school teachers instruct at religious schools, if the material was secular and neutral and no excessive entanglement existed.

The Court held that the Coeur d'Alene Tribe could not maintain an action against the state of Idaho to press its claim to Lake Coeur d'Alene due to the state's Eleventh Amendment immunity from suit, notwithstanding the exception recognized in Ex parte Young.
The Court held the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996's amendments to Title 28, Section 2254 of the United States Code applies to cases filed after the Act's effective date.

The court held that a government-imposed fee that forced fruit growers to contribute to collective product advertising for the sale of their fruits was an economic policy that did not trigger First Amendment scrutiny.

In an insider trading case, the Court held that a person may be liable under Rule 10(b)-5 for misappropriating confidential information, and that the SEC did not exceed its rulemaking authority in adopting Rule 14e-3(a).
The Court unanimously held that a right to assisted suicide was not protected by the Due Process Clause.

The Court ruled that New York's ban on physician-assisted suicide was constitutional, holding that preventing doctors from assisting even terminally ill or suffering patients was a legitimate state interest within the state's authority.
The Court held individual members of Congress do not automatically have standing to litigate the constitutionality of laws affecting Congress as a whole.

The Court unanimously ruled that the indecency provisions of the 1996 Communications Decency Act, which regulated materials distributed via the Internet, violated the First Amendment's guarantee of freedom of speech.
The court held that certain interim provisions of the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act violated the Tenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court held that vertical maximum price fixing was not inherently unlawful, thereby overruling a previous Supreme Court decision, Albrecht v. Herald Co., 390 U.S. 145 (1968).
The court held that 18 U.S.C. 666(a)(1)(B) does not require the Government to prove the bribe in question had a demonstrated effect upon federal funds.
The court held that the government may levy a remedial civil penalty after a criminal punishment without violating the Double Jeopardy Clause's prohibition on multiple punishments.
The Court ruled that the Fifth Amendment does not protect the right of those being questioned by law enforcement officials to deny wrongdoing falsely.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that banks had prudential standing to challenge regulations that permitted credit unions to enroll unaffiliated members.
The Supreme Court granted certiorari on appeal from the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit, which had ruled in the tribe's favor, saying they occupied Indian Country.

The Court unanimously held that a district court conducting coordinated pretrial proceedings in multiple cases by designation of the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation under 28 U.S.C. § 1407(a) has no authority to reassign a transferred case to itself for the actual trial of the case.

The court decided unanimously local legislators are entitled to the same absolute immunity from civil liability under Section 1983 for their legislative activities as are federal, state and regional legislators regardless of motive or intent.
The Court ruled that debt arising from a medical malpractice judgment, attributable to negligent or reckless conduct is dischargeable under the Bankruptcy Code.
The Court held that property damage during a no-knock warrant is irrelevant as long as law enforcement has reasonable suspicion that knocking and announcing would be a dangerous move.
The court held that the Bruton rule does not allow the admission of an out-of-court confession by a defendant to be entered against a jointly-tried co-defendant with the defendant's name redacted.
The court held that Ohio's clemency procedure is constitutional because the minimum required by the Due Process Clause is notice and an opportunity to be heard.
The Supreme Court issued a ruling with regard to the highly controversial matter of polygraph, or "lie-detector," testing.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that if there is to be an award of statutory damages in a copyright infringement case, then the opposing party has the right to demand a jury trial.
The Court upheld the validity of laws relating to U.S. citizenship at birth for children born outside the United States, out of wedlock, to an American parent.
The court held that a law is not invalid when a president signs it after Congress has adjourned, so long as it is signed within 10 days.

The Court held that a federal court of appeals has an inherent power to recall its mandate, but in habeas corpus cases that power may be exercised only in extraordinary circumstances, given the emphasis on finality of criminal judgments.

The Court held that 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b) did not apply to a petition that raises only a competency to be executed claim and that respondent did not, therefore, need authorization to file his petition in the District Court.
The court held that state-owned public television networks are not required to invite minor-party candidates with few supporters to major-party debates because the networks are not public forums.
The court held that the Declaratory Judgment Act cannot be used to seek an advance ruling on a collateral issue.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a Native Nation is entitled to sovereign immunity from contract lawsuits, whether made on or off reservation, or involving governmental or commercial activities.

In a dispute between two states over jurisdiction of Ellis Island, which was expanded by federal land reclamation, the Court ruled that roughly 83% of the island was part of New Jersey rather than New York.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the indirect liability of a parent corporation under CERCLA is to be determined by its control over a subsidiary's facility, rather than the relationship between the corporation and subsidiary.

The court held that, in death-penalty cases, the constitution does not require juries to be informed of a lesser-included offense that may suit the facts without being death-eligible when the proposed alternative is not a lesser-included offense under state law.

The Court was asked to rule on whether a particular statute with the phrase “carries a firearm” should be interpreted so as to be limited to carrying a firearm only on one's person or interpreted more broadly to include carrying a firearm in a vehicle.
The court held that interest earned on client funds held in IOLTA accounts is the "private property" of the client for Takings Clause purposes.

The court held that a Social Security disability claimant seeking court reversal of an agency decision denying benefits may appeal a district court order remanding the case to the agency for further proceedings.

In a case about a teacher's sexual harassment of a student, the Court held that a school district may be liable, but damages under Title IX require that an official with authority had actual knowledge and was deliberately indifferent.

The Court held that asset forfeiture is unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause when it is grossly disproportional to the gravity of the defendant's offense, striking down the federal government's forfeiture.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the death of an attorney's client does not terminate attorney–client privilege with respect to records of confidential communications between the attorney and the client.

The Court held that the line-item veto under the Line Item Veto Act of 1996 violated the Presentment Clause, because it impermissibly let the president unilaterally amend or repeal parts of statutes duly passed by Congress.
The Court held that the Coal Industry Retiree Health Benefit Act (Coal Act) constituted an unconstitutional regulatory taking of property which required the Act to be invalidated.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that reproduction does qualify as a major life activity according to the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA).
The court held that concern with foreign prosecution is beyond the scope of the Self Incrimination Clause.
The court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not preclude retrial on a prior conviction allegation in noncapital sentencing proceedings.
The Court held that employers are liable if supervisors create a hostile work environment for employees.

The court held that "an employer is vicariously liable for actionable discrimination caused by a supervisor, but subject to an affirmative defense looking to the reasonableness of the employer's conduct as well as that of a plaintiff victim."
The Court determined what constituted being "on sale" for the purposes of barring the grant of a patent for an invention.

The Court ruled that the Fourth Amendment prohibits a police officer from further searching a vehicle which was stopped for a minor traffic offense once the officer has written a citation for the offense.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the NCAA's receipt of dues payments from colleges and universities which received federal funds, was not sufficient to subject the NCAA to a lawsuit under Title IX.
The court held that a state may tax the revenue of a government contractor received from work for the federal government.

The Court ruled that the IDEA's related services provision required public school districts to fund continuous, one-on-one nursing care for disabled children, despite the school district's arguments about the cost of the services.
The Court held that the Daubert standard applies to expert testimony from non-scientists.
The Court ruled that the Ojibwe retained certain hunting, fishing, and gathering rights on the ceded land.

The Court held that, absent exigency, a warrantless search of a passenger's container capable of holding the object of a search supported by probable cause did not violate the Fourth Amendment, being justified under the automobile exception.

The Court considered Fifth Amendment self-incrimination rights in federal sentencing and ruled that pleading guilty does not waive the privilege at sentencing, and that courts cannot draw an adverse inference from silence when finding facts affecting the sentence's severity.

In a dispute over a customs classification regulation, the Court held that Chevron deference was appropriate for regulations issued by Customs on behalf of the Treasury, and rejected the importer's argument that the regulation applied only to customs officers.
In an immigration dispute, the Court determined that federal courts had to defer to the Board of Immigration Appeals's interpretation of the Immigration and Nationality Act.
Unanimously held the entrance of a third-party not directly involved in aiding a search warrant into a private household unconstitutional.

The Court held that the omission of an element of an offense with which a defendant is charged and convicted should be evaluated under the "harmless error" standard that the Court previously described in the 1967 case Chapman v. California.
The Court held that a law cannot be so vague that a person of ordinary intelligence can not figure out what is innocent activity and what is illegal.
The Court held that appeals from the USPTO Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences are to be reviewed for whether the Board's conclusions are supported by "substantial evidence" under the APA.

The Supreme Court stated that the equitable remedies authorized by the Judiciary Act of 1789 are limited to remedies that were available in courts of equity at that time, particularly from the Lord Chancellor in the English Court of Chancery.
The Court decided that mitigating measures should be taken into account when determining whether one's impairment constitutes a disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA).

The Court held that under the Americans with Disabilities Act, people with mental disabilities have the right to live in the community rather than institutions if professionals deem it appropriate, they do not oppose it, and it can be reasonably accommodated.
The Court held the United States Congress may not use its Article I powers to allow people to sue a state in that state's own courts without the state's consent.

The Court held that the plaintiff residents in the area of South Carolina's North Tyger River had standing to sue an industrial polluter, against whom various deterrent civil penalties were being pursued.

The Court determined that the US Congress's enforcement powers under the Fourteenth Amendment to the US Constitution did not extend to the abrogation of state sovereign immunity under the Eleventh Amendment over complaints of discrimination that is rationally based on age.

The Court unanimously decided that scheduling of a trial date outside the 180-day period of Article III of the Interstate Agreement on Detainers Act (IAD) by a defendant's counsel waived the defendant's right to dismissal on the ground that the trial did not occur within that period.
The Supreme Court of the United States upheld the Driver's Privacy Protection Act of 1994 (DPPA) against a Tenth Amendment challenge.
The Court decided an appellant who was the defendant in a criminal case cannot refuse the assistance of counsel on direct appeals.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that their earlier decision in Buckley v. Valeo (1976), upholding federal limits on campaign contributions also applied to state limits on campaign contributions to state offices.

In a challenge to Hawaii's voting rules, the Court ruled that the state could not restrict eligibility to vote in elections for the Board of Trustees of the Office of Hawaiian Affairs to persons of Native Hawaiian descent.

The Court unanimously held that certain state regulations regarding oil tankers and oil barges are preempted under the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution in deference to the extensive body of federal regulations affecting these classes of vessels.
The Court ruled that the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act did not give the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) the authority to regulate tobacco products as "drugs" or "devices."

The court held that the Federal Arbitration Act's venue provisions are permissive, allowing a motion to confirm, vacate, or modify to be brought either in the district where the award was made or in any district proper under the general venue statute.
The court held that product design is not inherently distinctive trade dress.
The Court held that public universities may subsidize campus groups by means of a mandatory student activity fee without violating the students' First Amendment rights.

The Court determined that a police officer may not legally stop and frisk someone based solely on an anonymous tip that describes a person's location and appearance, but does not furnish information as to any illegal conduct.
The court held that an ordinance banning public nudity did not violate the free speech rights of a nude entertainment establishment's operator, employees, or customers.
The Court applied the ruling of Minnesota v. Dickerson to luggage, which held that police may not physically manipulate items without a warrant without violating the Fourth Amendment.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Anthony Kennedy, the Supreme Court held that the provision at issue only bars evidentiary hearings by state prisoners in federal habeas proceedings if "there is lack of diligence, or some greater fault, attributable to the prisoner or his counsel".

The court held that due process requires a party to be given an opportunity to respond and contest their personal liability for a fee award after being made a party and before the entry of a judgment against them.
The Court held that under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, a certificate of appealability must be issued by a circuit Justice of judge before an appeal can proceed.
The Court held that a county's policy of requiring employees to schedule time off to avoid accruing time off was not prohibited by the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The Court found unconstitutional parts of the Violence Against Women Act of 1994, which let victims of gender-motivated violence sue attackers in federal court, because they exceeded Congress's powers under the Commerce Clause and the Equal Protection Clause.

The Court ruled that the scope of the federal bribery statute 18 U.S.C. § 666(b), which applied to organizations that received "benefits in excess of $10,000 under a Federal program", included funds received through Medicare.
The Court held that a search warrant is always required unless there are exceptional circumstances.
The Court held that a private person may not bring suit in a federal court on behalf of the United States against a State (or state agency) under the False Claims Act.

The Court struck down Section 505 of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which required that cable television operators completely scramble or block channels that are "primarily dedicated to sexually-oriented programming" or limit their transmission to the hours of 10 pm to 6 am.

The court held that because an owner-occupied residence not used for any commercial purpose does not qualify as property "used in" commerce or commerce-affecting activity, arson of such a dwelling is not subject to federal prosecution under the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970.
The Court held that a federal automobile safety standard pre-empted a stricter state rule.
The Supreme Court of the United States struck down a Washington state law that allowed any third party to petition state courts for child visitation rights over parental objections.
The Court held that the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 does not provide a remedy for coverage determinations by health maintenance organizations.
The Court held, 5–4, that a defendant charged with robbery under 18 USC § 2113(a) was not entitled to a jury instruction to consider the lesser offense of larceny under 18 USC § 2113(b).
The Court ruled that a policy permitting student-led, student-initiated school prayer at high school football games violates the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment.

The Court unanimously struck down, under the federal preemption doctrine, a Massachusetts law that barred state agencies from buying goods and services from companies doing business with Myanmar (Burma).
The Court upheld the requirement that the Miranda warning be read to criminal suspects and struck down a federal statute that purported to overrule Miranda v. Arizona (1966).

In a case about aggravating factors in crimes, the Court ruled that the Sixth Amendment jury trial right prohibited judges from enhancing sentences beyond statutory maxima based on facts not decided by a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
The United States Supreme Court held that California's blanket primary violates a political party's First Amendment freedom of association.
In a 5–4 decision, the Supreme Court ruled that opposition to homosexuality is part of BSA's "expressive message" and that allowing homosexuals as adult leaders would interfere with that message.

The Court ruled 6–3 that the right to free speech was not violated by a Colorado law limiting protest, education, distribution of literature, or counseling within eight feet of a person entering a healthcare facility.
The Court ruled that it was permissible for states to make loans to religious schools under Chapter 2 of the Education Consolidation and Improvement Act of 1981.

The Court struck down the law, finding the Nebraska statute criminalizing "partial birth abortion" violated the Due Process Clause of the United States Constitution, as interpreted in Planned Parenthood v. Casey and Roe v. Wade.
The Court held that the petition did not toll.
The Court held unanimously that, under the federal mail fraud statute, "property" did not include state video poker licences, because such transactions were not a vested right or expectation.
The Court held, 6–3, that police may not conduct vehicle searches, specifically ones involving drug-sniffing police dogs, at a checkpoint or roadblock without reasonable suspicion.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that public policy considerations do not require courts to refuse to enforce an arbitration award ordering an employer to reinstate an employee truck driver who twice tested positive for marijuana.

In a dispute over a Florida statewide recount of undervotes in the 2000 presidential election, the Court held that no constitutional recount could be conducted in the remaining time, and that the recount violated the Equal Protection Clause.

The Court held that the Corps of Engineers' use of the "migratory bird rule" to extend Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting authority to isolated waters, including isolated wetlands, exceeded the authority granted by that section.

The Court upheld a Bureau of Prisons regulation that reduced prisoners' sentences for completing a substance abuse program, even though the statute restricted the credit to those who did not commit a firearm-aided felony.
The Court rejected a challenge to Washington state's civil commitment statute for sexual predators, following earlier cases that had upheld civil commitment statutes.

The case concerned the denial of a business license for an adult store selling sexually explicit materials, and the Court dismissed it because the store had withdrawn its application to renew the license.
The Court held that the sport-association can be sued as a state actor because its actions and history have been "entangled" with state action.
A unanimous Court held that they are not exempt.

In a case about the government's power to limit a person's control of their home pending a search warrant, the Court held the search was not unconstitutional because police reasonably needed to prevent destruction of evidence.
The Court considered whether the federal FDCA pre-empted a state-law fraud-on-the-FDA claim, and it decided to reject the lawsuit attempt.
The Supreme Court decided that Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act was unconstitutional, insofar as it allowed states to be sued by private citizens for money damages.
The Court concluded that the law did not always apply to federal flood control facilities.
The Court held that federal common law governs the preclusive effect of a judgment entered in a federal court sitting in diversity.
The Court held that an attempt by the state of Missouri to influence Congressional elections in favor of candidates who supported term limits was unconstitutional.

The Court ruled that congressional restrictions barring Legal Services Corporation attorneys from representing clients seeking to challenge existing welfare law violated the First Amendment's free speech guarantees.
The Court held unanimously that the exemption did not apply.
In a trademark dispute, the Court determined that a functional design could not be eligible for trademark protection and established a presumption that a patented design is inherently functional.

The court held that the courts of appeal must give deferential review to decisions of district courts under the Sentencing Guidelines on the question of consolidation of a defendant's prior convictions.
The Court found Medical University of South Carolina's policy regarding involuntary drug testing of pregnant women to violate the Fourth Amendment.
The Court held that the exemption was limited to the specific listing of professions contained in the text.
The Court held that state statutes having a ‘connection with’ ERISA-governed benefit plans are preempted by ERISA.
The Court held that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel is offense-specific and does not always extend to offenses that are closely related to those where the right has been attached.
The Court upheld the provision because the companies were still able to pursue a claim in state court.
The court held that wages are to be taxed on the year they were actually paid.
The Court decided that a regulation enacted under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 did not include a private right of action allowing private lawsuits based on evidence of disparate impact.
The Court held that a person's Fourth Amendment rights are not violated when the subject is arrested for driving without a seatbelt.
The Court ruled, in a 5–4 decision, that a defendant sentenced under that Act could not challenge previous convictions on appeal that were used to increase his new sentence.

The Court held that a prisoner could not challenge his current sentence on the ground that it was enhanced by an unconstitutional prior conviction, basing its decision on a reading of the statute rather than the Sixth Amendment.
The Court held that the tribe waived its sovereign immunity when it agreed to a contract containing an arbitration agreement.

The Court held that there was no due process violation for lack of fair warning when courts broadened pre-existing common law limitations on what acts constitute a crime under a more broadly worded statute to include additional acts.

The Court rejected the common-law medical necessity defense to crimes under the federal Controlled Substances Act, regardless of their legal status under state laws, such as California's, that recognize a medical use for marijuana.

In a case over a media defendant's broadcast of a taped conversation of a labor official discussing a teachers' strike, which had been recorded in violation of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, the Court held the broadcast was legal.

The Court concluded that a secret understanding to violate an arrangement under the Act still constituted a violation, rejecting an argument that oral contracts were categorically excluded from the provision's coverage.

The Court held that an award of attorney's fee to a "prevailing party" under the Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Award Act of 1976 must be to a party that has received a judgment on the merits or a court-ordered consent decree.
The Court held the Navajo Nation's imposition of a hotel occupancy tax upon nonmembers on non-Indian fee land within its reservation is invalid.

The Court ruled for a golfer whose circulatory condition impaired his ability to walk, who sued the PGA Tour under the ADA to be allowed to use a golf cart in its qualifying tournament despite its walking requirement.
The Court held that Booth still had a mechanism of administrative review, and thus his claim was premature.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the boundary between the states of New Hampshire and Maine was fixed by the 1740 decree of King George II of Great Britain.
Addressed Rule 11(a) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and whether the failure to sign a notice of appeal requires a court to dismiss the appeal.
In a case about the extent of New York v. Belton and automobile searches, the Court unanimously dismissed the case because the Florida state courts' decision was not final.

The Court reversed the Texas courts in a case about whether sentencing instructions given to a Texas jury adequately emphasized mitigating factors for intellectually disabled defendants, finding the instructions insufficient.

The Court held that an affiliated group's product liability loss must be figured on a consolidated, single-entity basis; a conglomerate cannot aggregate the product liability loss of its subsidiaries and report that sum as its product liability loss.
The Court held that front pay is not an element of compensatory damages under the Civil Rights Act of 1991 and thus is not subject to the damages cap imposed by the Act.

The court ruled that the use of thermal imaging devices to monitor heat radiation in or around a person's home, even if conducted from a public vantage point, is unconstitutional without a search warrant.
The Court upheld the validity of laws relating to U.S. citizenship at birth for children born outside the United States, out of wedlock, to an American parent.
The Court held that a public school's exclusion of a club from its limited public forum based solely on the club's religious nature was impermissible viewpoint discrimination.
The case concerned how far RICO reached certain corporation-individual organizations, and the Court unanimously decided to apply the Act to respondent Don King.
The Court, addressing when Chevron deference should be applied, determined that it applies when Congress delegated authority to the agency generally to make rules carrying the force of law.

In a dispute over ownership of lands submerged under Lake Coeur d'Alene and the St. Joe River, the Court held that the United States, not Idaho, held title, in trust for the Coeur d'Alene Tribe as part of its reservation.

In a challenge to a federal limit on party spending for congressional campaigns, the Court held that the party committee's expenditures, made independently of a specific candidate, did not violate FECA's contribution limits and were protected by the First Amendment.

The Court held that a newspaper publisher, in licensing back issues for electronic databases such as LexisNexis, could not license the works of freelance journalists contained in those newspapers, affirming the writers' copyright privileges.

The Court held that a Massachusetts ban on tobacco advertising and sales near schools and playgrounds, challenged by a tobacco company on First Amendment grounds, was overbroad and also preempted by federal law.
The Court held that a claimant does not waive his right to challenge a regulation as an uncompensated regulatory taking by purchasing property after the enactment of the regulation challenged.

The Court held that the rule from Cage v. Louisiana, which found certain jury instructions on reasonable doubt unconstitutional, was not made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court.

The court ruled narrowly that section 241 of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (8 U.S.C. § 1231) contains an implicit time limitation and did not authorize indefinite detention of foreigners that no other country would accept.

The Court held that the discovery rule (that a federal statute of limitations begins to run when a party knows or has reason to know that she was injured) does not apply to the two-year statute of limitations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that Indian tribes were liable for taxes on gambling operations under 25 U.S.C. §§ 2701–2721.
The court held that the police search of a probationer supported by reasonable suspicion and pursuant to a probation condition satisfied the requirements under the Fourth Amendment.
The Court held that for the first time that utility patents may be issued for crops and other flowering (sexually reproducing) plants under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
The court held that to afford due-process notice, the government must attempt to provide actual notice, but it is not required to succeed in providing actual notice.

The Court reversed the decision by the Court of Appeals to grant a partial summary judgment in favor of the respondent, Ella Williams, that had qualified her inability to perform manual job-related tasks as a disability.

The Court unanimously reaffirmed that the Fourth Amendment required courts to judge the reasonableness of a traffic stop by the totality of the circumstances rather than examining each of an officer's reasons for the stop individually.
The Court upheld the Kansas Sexually Violent Predator Act (SVPA) as consistent with substantive due process.

The United States Supreme Court held in favor of Owasso Independent School District that students scoring each other's tests and calling out the grades do not violate the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974 (FERPA).

The Court held that for complaints in employment discrimination cases, a plaintiff is not required to allege specific facts that establish a prima facie case as required by the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework.
The court held that prisoners alleging assaults by prison guards must meet §1997e(a)'s exhaustion requirement before commencing a civil rights action.

The Court held Congress's authorization of evictions of tenants from public housing where a tenant's invitee into the housing engaged in drug-related activity and the tenant did not know about it was constitutional.

The Supreme Court of the United States denied an award of back pay to an undocumented worker, José Castro, who had been laid off for participating in a union organizing campaign at Hoffman Plastics Compounds plant, along with several other employees.

The Court struck down two overbroad provisions of the Child Pornography Prevention Act of 1996 because they abridged the freedom to engage in a substantial amount of lawful speech, rejecting a bid to widen categorically unprotected speech.
The Court held a spouse in a tenancy by the entirety possesses an individual right in their own estate to the level to constitute "rights to property" for the purpose of a lien.

In a case about reasonable accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Court held that a requested accommodation such as a transfer can be unreasonable if it would violate the employer's seniority system.

In a challenge by two adult stores operating under one roof to a Los Angeles zoning ordinance restricting adult businesses, the Court ruled in favor of the city and reversed the lower court's decision.

The Court held that the FCC can require state commissions to set the rates charged by incumbents for leased elements on a forward-looking basis untied to the incumbents' investment and that the FCC can require incumbents to combine elements of their networks at the request of entrants.
The Court ruled that the Child Online Protection Act was unconstitutional because it violated the First Amendment's guarantee of freedom of speech.
The Court upheld the Alabama Supreme Court's ruling that counsel (a lawyer) must be provided for the accused in order to impose a suspended prison sentence.
The Court upheld a death sentence despite the defendant's argument that he should not be sentenced to death because he was suffering from drug-induced psychosis when he committed the crimes.
The court held that patent issues raised in a counterclaim do not give rise to Federal Circuit jurisdiction.

The Court determined that Kansas' Sexual Abuse Treatment Program (SATP) served a vital penological purpose and determined that allowing minimal incentives to take part in the SATP does not equal compelled self-incrimination as prohibited by the Fifth Amendment.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a corporation organized under the laws of a British overseas territory is considered a "citizen or subject of a foreign state" for purposes of federal court jurisdiction.

The Court held that a town ordinance making it a misdemeanor to engage in door-to-door advocacy without first registering with town officials and getting a permit violated the First Amendment as applied to religious proselytizing, anonymous political speech, and handbill distribution.
The court decided that punitive damages may not be awarded in private lawsuits brought under § 202 of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) and § 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.

In a case over a drug interdiction search on a Greyhound bus, the Court held that officers need not advise passengers of their right to refuse consent, and that the search was reasonable because the passengers voluntarily consented.

The Court ruled that the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act of 1974, which bars federal funding of schools that release education records to unauthorized persons, creates no right enforceable under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 6–3 that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishments, but that states can define who has an intellectual disability.
The court held that the federal Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) did not preempt an Illinois medical-review statute.
The Court held that the use of certain statistical techniques in the United States census does not violate 13 U.S.C. §195 or the Census Clause of the Constitution.

The United States Supreme Court applied the rule of Apprendi v. New Jersey to capital sentencing schemes, holding that the Sixth Amendment requires a jury to find the aggravating factors necessary for imposing the death penalty.
The Court held that Brady v. Maryland did not require prosecutors to disclose impeachment evidence during plea bargaining.
The Court upheld an Ohio program that used school vouchers.

The Court ruled that qualified immunity did not apply to a lawsuit challenging the Alabama Department of Corrections's use of the "hitching post," a punishment in which inmates were immobilized for long periods.

In a 5–4 decision, the court ruled that Minnesota's announce clause, which forbade candidates for judicial office from announcing their views on disputed legal and political issues, was unconstitutional.
The Court considered whether a law saying a government agent "shall" act by a given date limited the agent's power to act afterward, and held that the agent could still act after the date.
The Supreme Court disagreed and allowed the statute to remain in effect.

The Court unanimously held that the Fair Housing Act imposed liability without fault on a corporate employer under traditional agency principles, normally making the corporation vicariously liable but not its officers or owners.
The Court held that that, under the Federal Trademark Dilution Act, a claim of trademark dilution requires proof of actual dilution, not merely a likelihood of dilution.

In a dispute over deteriorated Fort Apache buildings held in trust for an Indian tribe, the Court affirmed the appellate court, holding that the federal government used the trust property and therefore had a duty to maintain it.
The court held that due process does not require the opportunity to prove a fact that is not material to a state's statutory scheme.

The Court held that habeas corpus relief was unavailable for a claim that a sentence under California's three strikes law was an unconstitutionally disproportionate punishment barred by the Eighth Amendment's ban on cruel and unusual punishments.
The court held that local governments are "persons" who may be sued via qui tam actions under the False Claims Act.

The court held that mental anguish damages resulting from the fear of developing cancer may be recovered under the Federal Employers' Liability Act by a railroad worker suffering from the actionable injury asbestosis caused by work-related exposure to asbestos.

The Court held, 5–4, that any state statute banning cross burning on the basis that it constitutes prima facie evidence of intent to intimidate is a violation of the First Amendment to the Constitution.

The United States Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause usually limits punitive damage awards to less than ten times the size of the compensatory damages awarded and that punitive damage awards of four times the compensatory damage award is "close to the line of constitutional impropriety".

The court held that in deciding whether the physician-shareholders should be considered employees for purposes of coverage under the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), the common law element of control is the main guidepost.

The Court held that the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 was narrowly targeted at sex-based overgeneralization and was a valid exercise of congressional power under Section 5 of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court held that a police officer does not deprive a suspect of constitutional rights by failing to issue a Miranda warning.
The Court held that a federal administrative agency approved public utility tariff preempted a state public utilities commission rate order under the filed rate doctrine.

The United States Supreme Court imposed stringent limits on the right of a lower court to order the forcible administration of antipsychotic medication to a criminal defendant who had been determined to be incompetent to stand trial for the sole purpose of making them competent and able to be tried.

The United States Supreme Court ruled that the United States Congress has the authority to require public schools and libraries receiving E-Rate discounts to install web filtering software as a condition of receiving federal funding, as required in the Children's Internet Protection Act of 2000.

In a challenge to the University of Michigan's undergraduate affirmative action admissions policy, the Court ruled that the point system awarding 20 points to underrepresented minorities was unconstitutional because it prevented individualized assessment of diversity contributions.

The Court held that a student admissions process that favors "underrepresented minority groups" did not violate the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause so long as it took into account other factors evaluated on an individual basis for every applicant.

The Supreme Court of the United States invalidated a California law that required any insurance company wishing to do business in the state to publish information regarding insurance policies held by persons in Europe from 1920 through 1945.
The court held that an arbitrator must determine whether the contracts forbid class arbitration.

The Court found that a three-judge district court panel failed to consider all the relevant factors when assessing whether Georgia's 2001 State Senate redistricting plan caused retrogression of black voters' effective exercise of the franchise under Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act.
The Court ruled that U.S. state laws criminalizing sodomy between consenting adults are unconstitutional.
The Court held that California's retroactive extension of the statute of limitations for sexual offenses committed against minors was an unconstitutional ex post facto law.
The United States Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of most of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (BCRA), often referred to as the McCain–Feingold Act.
The Court unanimously upheld the arrest of three passengers in an automobile where drugs were found.

The Court held that the Telecommunications Act of 1996 had not modified the Sherman Act's framework, preserving claims meeting established antitrust standards without creating new ones, and it refused to extend the essential facilities doctrine.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Fourth Amendment permits the police to use a roadblock to investigate a traffic incident.

In a 5–4 decision, the Supreme Court found the EPA has authority to overrule state agency decisions under the Clean Air Act that a company is using the "best available controlling technology" to prevent pollution.
The court held that a search warrant that does not state the items to be seized is unreasonable by default, and the officer is not entitled to qualified immunity for executing such a warrant.

The Court's 6–3 decision determined that the latter interpretation was correct; as a result, it will be more difficult for a plaintiff to prevail as he or she must now prove both a violation and some damages before being entitled to recovery.
Reformulated the standard for determining when the admission of hearsay statements in criminal cases is permitted under the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment.
The Court held that customs agents may remove the gas tank from a vehicle crossing the international border in an effort to look for contraband.
The Court decided sand and gravel are not "valuable minerals" reserved to the United States Government under the Pittman Underground Water Act of 1919.
The Court held that both the United States and a Native American (Indian) tribe could prosecute an Indian for the same acts that constituted crimes in both jurisdictions.
The Court, in a plurality opinion, upheld the District Court's ruling for the appellees that the alleged political gerrymandering in the redistricting was not unconstitutional.

In a Chapter 13 bankruptcy cramdown dispute over a loan's value, the Court, with no majority opinion, approved a 9.5 percent rate that adjusted the national average loan rate for the risk of non-payment.
The court held that a party's post-filing change in citizenship cannot cure a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction that existed at the time of filing in a diversity action.

The Court held that when a police officer makes a lawful custodial arrest of an automobile's occupant, the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution allows the officer to search the vehicle's passenger compartment as a contemporaneous incident of arrest.
The court held unanimously that an appeal of proposed execution procedures is different from a habeas corpus petition because it is not an appeal of a conviction or sentence.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, or FSIA, applies retroactively to acts prior to its enactment in 1976.

The court held that, because FMCSA lacks discretion to prevent cross-border operations of Mexican motor carriers, neither NEPA nor the CAA requires FMCSA to evaluate the environmental effects of such operations.

In a challenge to the words "under God" in the Pledge of Allegiance in schools, the Court held that Newdow, a noncustodial parent, lacked standing to sue on his daughter's behalf, reversing the Ninth Circuit without reaching the constitutional question.
The Court held that although the Administrative Procedure Act says that a person may challenge an agency's failure to act, this provision essentially just carries forward the writ of mandamus.

The Court ruled that a federal criminal defendant who did not alert the district court to a possible Rule 11 violation must show on appeal that the violation affirmatively affected his rights to obtain reversal of his guilty plea conviction.
The court held that the Tax Injunction Act does not prevent a person from bringing a prospective challenge to the constitutionality of a tax credit assessed for other people.
The court held that an employer may be liable for a Title VII violation under a constructive discharge theory.

The Court held that where price-fixing significantly harmed customers both abroad and in the United States, but the foreign harm was independent of any domestic harm, neither the FTAIA exception nor the Sherman Act applied to a claim based solely on the foreign harm.

The Court held that a statute requiring suspects to disclose their names during a valid Terry stop did not violate the Fourth Amendment if it first required reasonable suspicion, nor the Fifth Amendment absent any allegation that the name could incriminate.
The Court limited the scope of the Texas Healthcare Liability Act (THCLA).
The Supreme Court held that not considering a defendant's low IQ would breach his Eighth Amendment rights and constitute a cruel and unusual punishment.

The Court held, 5–4, that in the context of mandatory sentencing guidelines under state law, the Sixth Amendment right to a jury trial prohibited judges from enhancing criminal sentences based on facts other than those decided by the jury or admitted by the defendant.
The United States Supreme Court held that its prior holding in Ring v. Arizona did not apply retroactively in collateral federal habeas corpus proceedings.

In a case over a U.S. citizen's military detention as an "unlawful combatant," the Court did not decide the detention-authority issue and held that the habeas corpus petition had been improperly filed.
The Court held that foreign nationals held in the Guantanamo Bay detention camp could petition federal courts for writs of habeas corpus to review the legality of their detention.

The Court recognized the power of the U.S. government to detain enemy combatants, including U.S. citizens, but ruled that detainees who are U.S. citizens must have the rights of due process, and the ability to challenge their enemy combatant status before an impartial authority.
The Court struck down the police practice of first obtaining an inadmissible confession without giving Miranda warnings, then issuing the warnings, and then obtaining a second confession.
The Court ruled that the Child Online Protection Act was unconstitutional because it violated the First Amendment's guarantee of freedom of speech.

The Court held that aliens may not be deported after being convicted of DUI if the DUI statute that defines the offense does not contain a mens rea element or otherwise allows a conviction for merely negligent conduct.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that Congress's 1995 amendment of the Truth in Lending Act (TILA) left unaltered the prior minimum and maximum limits of $100 and $1,000 prescribed for statutory damages awarded to plaintiffs in TILA violation suits involving personal-property loans.
The court held that the defendant in a trademark infringement action may raise a fair use defense without proving that there is no likelihood of confusing the marks.
The court held that attorneys lack third-party standing to assert the rights of indigent defendants denied their constitutional right to have appointed appellate counsel.

The Court ruled that even if an officer wrongly arrests a suspect for one crime, the arrest may still be "reasonable" if there is objectively probable cause to believe that the suspect is involved in a different crime.
The court held that a private party can seek contribution under CERCLA's §113(f) only after being sued under §106 or §107(a).

The court held that defense counsel's failure to obtain the defendant's express consent to a strategy of conceding guilt in a capital trial does not automatically render counsel's performance deficient.

The court held that the forced accompaniment statute described under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(e) is not limited to cases where the victim was forced to accompany the robber (or attempted robber) over a "substantial" distance.

In a criminal sentencing case, the Court ruled that the Sixth Amendment requires that, apart from prior convictions, only facts admitted by the defendant or proved to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt may be used to calculate a sentence above the statutory maximum.
The court held that 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(2)(E)(iv) permits a non-citizen to be deported to a country without the advance consent of that country's government.
The Court ended the detention of people denied refugee status who were held in prison awaiting deportation even though they could not actually be deported because of a political stalemate with Cuba.

The Court held that the use of a drug-sniffing police dog during a routine traffic stop does not violate the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, even if the initial infraction is unrelated to drug offenses.
The Supreme Court held when a taxpayer's recovery constitutes income, the taxpayer's income includes the portion of the recovery paid to the attorney as a contingent fee.

The court held that submitting a count to the jury after the judge has granted a mid-trial acquittal subjects a defendant to further factfinding proceedings going to guilt or innocence and violates the Double Jeopardy Clause.
The court held that a dredge is a "vessel" under the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act.
The court held that a prison system's policy of segregating new residents by race for the purpose of inhibiting gang violence is subject to strict scrutiny analysis.
The Court held that it is unconstitutional to impose capital punishment for crimes committed while under the age of 18.
The Court held that a contract with the Federal Government to reimburse the tribe for health care costs was binding, despite the failure of Congress to appropriate funds for those costs.
The court ruled unanimously that spies (those recruited for espionage by the Central Intelligence Agency) cannot sue the CIA or the United States government to enforce an espionage contract.

The Court held that the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution allows detention of an occupant in handcuffs while a search is being conducted, and that it does not require officers to have an independent reasonable suspicion before questioning a subject about their immigration status.
The United States Supreme Court held that the Telecommunications Act (TCA) precluded damages under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 because it provided a comprehensive remedial scheme.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that repurchase of traditional tribal lands did not restore tribal sovereignty to that land.

In a case under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Court held that the disparate impact theory applies under the ADEA, but that the Act is narrower because it permits actions based on reasonable factors other than age.
The Court held that Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) qualify for certain exemptions under Title 11 of the United States Code.
The Court held that an inflated purchase price will not by itself constitute or proximately cause the relevant economic loss needed to allege and prove "loss causation."
The Court held that a plot to defraud a foreign government of tax revenue violates the federal wire fraud statute.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) did not preempt state law claims, brought by a group of Texas farmers, alleging that one of Dow's pesticides damaged their peanut crop.
The Court ruled that New York and Michigan laws letting in-state wineries ship wine directly to consumers while barring out-of-state wineries from doing so were unconstitutional.
The Court expressly overruled precedent created in Agins v. City of Tiburon.
The court held that, when a check-off funds government speech, the government cannot be sued under the First Amendment for compelled speech.

In a 7–2 opinion delivered by Justice Breyer, the court held that it is against due process, a right prescribed by the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, to shackle a defendant in the sentencing portion of a trial unless the shackling relates to a specific defendant and certain state interests.
The Court unanimously overturned accounting firm Arthur Andersen's conviction of obstruction of justice in the fraudulent activities and subsequent collapse of Enron.

The Court held that, under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA), facilities that accept federal funds cannot deny prisoners accommodations that are necessary to engage in activities for the practice of their own religious beliefs.
The Court ruled that, under the Commerce Clause, Congress may criminalize the production and use of homegrown cannabis even where state law allows its use for medicinal purposes.
The Court determined (in a 6–3 decision) that the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) applies to foreign cruise ships in American waters.

The court held that a defendant satisfies the first step of Batson v. Kentucky by producing evidence sufficient to permit the trial judge to draw an inference that discrimination has occurred, and a state cannot adopt a "more likely than not" standard for this step.

The Court held, in a dispute over the FDA safe harbor patent exemption, that basic research without intent to develop a particular drug is not covered, but the exemption does not categorically exclude experimentation on drugs not ultimately submitted to the FDA.

The Court held that while the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment gives rise to a liberty interest in not being placed in a Supermax prison, Ohio's procedures for determining which prisoners should be placed there satisfied the requirements of due process.

The Court held that a convicted murderer received ineffective assistance of counsel because his lawyer failed to adequately investigate evidence the prosecution would likely use, reversing the Third Circuit and overturning his death sentence.

The Court held, 5–4, that the use of eminent domain to transfer land from one private owner to another private owner to further economic development does not violate the Takings Clause of the Fifth Amendment.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that 28 U.S.C. § 1367 permits supplemental jurisdiction over joined claims that do not individually meet the amount-in-controversy requirements of § 1332, provided that at least one claim meets the amount-in-controversy requirements.
The Court held that a Michigan law denying public counsel to defendants appealing a conviction based on a plea violated the equal protection and due process clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
The Court ruled that a display of the Ten Commandments on a monument given to the government at the Texas State Capitol did not violate the Establishment Clause, holding the display constitutional.

The Court ruled, 7–2, that a town and its police department could not be sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for refusing to enforce a restraining order, even though the refusal led to the murders of a woman's three children by her estranged husband.
The Court ruled that Ten Commandments displays at two Kentucky county courthouses, challenged under the Establishment Clause, were unconstitutional.

The Court ruled unanimously that the defendants, peer-to-peer file sharing companies Grokster and Streamcast (maker of Morpheus), could be held liable for inducing copyright infringement by users of their file sharing software.

The court held that decisions by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on how to regulate Internet service providers are eligible for Chevron deference, in which the judiciary defers to an administrative agency's expertise under its governing statutes.

The court held that under the Federal Tort Claims Act, the United States waives sovereign immunity only where local law would make a "private person" liable in tort, not where local law would make "a state or municipal entity" liable.
The Court determined that the burden of proof belonged to whoever challenged an Individualized Education Program (IEP).

The court held that defendants may remove an action on the basis of diversity of citizenship when there is complete diversity between all named plaintiffs and all named defendants and when no defendant is a citizen of the forum state.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a state's non-discriminatory fuel tax imposed on off-reservation distributors does not pose an affront to a tribe's sovereignty.
The court held that, absent unusual circumstances, attorney's fees should not be awarded under 28 U.S.C. §1447(c) when the removing party has an objectively reasonable basis for removal.
In a unanimous decision, the Court affirmed the lower court's decision that allowed the offset by the government.

The Court decided that the protection of Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA), passed by the U.S. Congress, extends to persons held in a state prison and protects prison inmates from discrimination on the basis of disability by prison personnel.

The court held that a manufacturer may not be held liable for secondary-line price discrimination under the Robinson-Patman Act in the absence of a showing that the manufacturer discriminated between dealers competing to resell its product to the same retail customer.

The Court held that, absent clear direction from the state supreme court on the timeliness of habeas filings, a federal appellate court must itself examine the delay in each case and determine what the state courts would have held about timeliness.

The Court ruled that the United States Attorney General cannot enforce the federal Controlled Substances Act against physicians who prescribed drugs, in compliance with Oregon state law, to terminally ill patients seeking to end their lives, commonly referred to as assisted suicide.
The court held that a national bank, for 28 U.S.C. §1348 purposes, is a citizen of the state in which its main office, as set forth in its articles of association, is located.

In a facial challenge to a state parental notification abortion law, the Court vacated the First Circuit's judgment and remanded, holding only on remedy that invalidating a statute entirely is not always necessary because lower courts may render narrower relief.
The court held that a refusal to apply the Federal Tort Claims Act's judgment bar is not open to collateral appeal.
The Court held that the Bankruptcy Clause of the Constitution abrogates state sovereign immunity.

The Court held that, under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, the government had failed to show a compelling interest in prosecuting religious adherents for drinking a sacramental tea containing a Schedule I controlled substance.

In a case about racial discrimination claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1981, the Court ruled unanimously that agents of contracting parties lack personal rights under those contracts and so cannot state a section 1981 claim.

The Court ruled that an exception to the FTCA that barred liability for the "negligent transmission of mail" did not apply to a claim for injuries caused when someone tripped over mail left by a USPS employee.

In a Title VII employment discrimination case, the Court ruled that the fifteen-employee numerosity requirement was not a limit on courts' jurisdiction but a substantive element of the claim, which a defendant must raise before verdict or waive.

The Court ruled that the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution does not grant criminal defendants facing the death penalty the right to introduce new evidence of their innocence during sentencing that was not introduced during trial.

The Court ruled unanimously that the joint venture's unified price for the two companies' brands of gasoline was not a price-fixing scheme between competitors in violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act.

The Court ruled unanimously that there is not a presumption of market power under the Sherman Antitrust Act when the sale of a patented product is conditioned on the sale of a second product in a tying arrangement.

The Court ruled that the federal government, under the Solomon Amendment, could constitutionally withhold funding from universities if they refuse to give military recruiters access to school resources.

The Court unanimously ruled that SLUSA barred state law securities fraud class action "holder" claims, based on losses from retaining stock due to fraud, even though federal securities laws gave a private cause of action only to purchasers or sellers.

The Court ruled that anticipatory search warrants, issued in advance of a "triggering condition" that makes them executable, are constitutional under the Fourth Amendment and need not describe that condition on their face.
The U.S. Supreme Court held that without a search warrant, police had no constitutional right to search a house where one resident consents to the search while another resident objects.
The Court ruled unanimously that the county had no basis for claiming immunity because it was not acting as an "arm of the state."

In a 5–4 decision, the court held that, when the government unintentionally failed to object to the filing of a petition after the AEDPA limitations period has expired, it is not an abuse of discretion for a district court to dismiss sua sponte (on its own initiative) the petition on that basis.

The Court ruled, 5-3, that after a mailed notice was returned unclaimed, a state was required by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to take additional reasonable steps to notify the owner before the sale could proceed.

The Court ruled that a plaintiff claiming a prosecution was brought in retaliation for First Amendment speech against postal policy must allege and prove that the criminal charges were brought without probable cause.

The Court ruled unanimously that a federal statutory prohibition against liens on personal property to recover Medicaid expenditures applied to settlements, so that only the portion of the settlement that represented payment for past medical expenses could be claimed by the state.
The United States Supreme Court held that a federal district court had equal or concurrent jurisdiction with state probate (will) courts over tort claims under state common law.

The Court unanimously vacated a South Carolina rape and murder conviction, ruling that excluding the defendant's evidence of a third party's guilt because the prosecution's forensic evidence seemed strong violated his right to present a complete defense.

The Court unanimously ruled that state taxpayers did not have standing under Article III of the United States Constitution to challenge state tax or spending decisions simply by virtue of their status as taxpayers.
The Court ruled unanimously that ERISA permitted the fiduciary to recover costs from the settlement proceeds a beneficiary received in a personal injury lawsuit.

In a dispute over Clean Water Act licensing requirements, the Court ruled unanimously that hydroelectric dams were subject to section 401, since the simple flowing of water from a dam qualified as a "discharge" under its ordinary meaning.

The Supreme Court of the United States unanimously determined that an injunction should not be automatically issued based on a finding of patent infringement, but also that an injunction should not be denied simply on the basis that the plaintiff does not practice the patented invention.
The Court ruled that police may enter a home without a warrant if they have an objectively reasonable basis for believing that an occupant is or is about to be seriously injured.

The Court ruled, in a 5–4 decision, that because his statements were made pursuant to his position as a public employee, rather than as a private citizen, his speech had no First Amendment protection.

In a dispute over standing under the civil RICO provision, the Court held that a plaintiff must show he or she was the direct victim of the defendant's RICO violation, so a business could not sue a competitor that gained an advantage by not paying taxes.
In a case about the right to a speedy trial, the Court unanimously ruled that a defendant cannot prospectively waive the protections of the Speedy Trial Act.
The Court found that admitting new DNA evidence was in line with Schlup v. Delo (1995), which allows cases to be reopened in light of new evidence.

The Court ruled unanimously that an Eighth Amendment challenge to the method of execution properly raised a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which provides a cause of action for civil rights violations, rather than under the habeas corpus provisions.

The Court held that a violation of the Fourth Amendment's knock-and-announce requirement for police entering a private residence does not require suppression of the evidence obtained in the ensuing search.

The court held that a federal district court's decision to send a case back to state court because its removal to federal court was not required by the Security Litigation Uniform Standards Act cannot be reviewed under 28 U.S.C. 1447(d).
The court held that a creditor cannot seek priority status in a bankruptcy case to recover unpaid premiums owed for legally-required workers' compensation insurance.

The Court affirmed the Second Circuit's ruling against a health insurer that sought reimbursement of benefits paid to a deceased federal employee from his wife's settlement with third parties who allegedly caused his injuries.

The Court affirmed the California Court of Appeal's ruling that suspicionless searches of parolees are lawful under California law and that the search in this case was reasonable under the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution because it was not arbitrary, capricious, or harassing.

The Court held that the reinstatement provision in §241(a)(5) applied to immigrants who illegally reentered the U.S. before IIRIRA's effective date, and that applying it to a man deported after reentering in 1982 was not impermissibly retroactive.

In a case about when prison litigation may be commenced in federal court, the Court ruled that prisoners must exhaust all state-court remedies in accordance with the rules thereof before filing claims in federal court.
The Court held that a Kansas death penalty statute was consistent with the United States Constitution.
In a case where a defendant's sentence was enhanced for being armed with a firearm though the jury had not found that, the Court held that a Blakely error could be considered harmless.
The court ruled that Vermont's law, the strictest in the nation, unconstitutionally hindered the citizens' First Amendment right to free speech.
In a case about experts' fees under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, the Court ruled that the Act does not authorize payment of the prevailing parents' experts' fees.
The United States Supreme Court held that a state court did not have to exclude evidence that was admitted into court in violation of Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations.
The Court ruled that only District 23 of the 2003 Texas redistricting violated the Voting Rights Act.

The Court held that military commissions set up by the Bush administration to try Guantanamo Bay detainees violated both the Uniform Code of Military Justice and the Geneva Conventions ratified by the U.S.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of the insanity defense used by Arizona.

The Court held that a catch-all jury instruction allowing consideration of any circumstance extenuating the gravity of the crime permitted jurors to consider post-crime evidence and was consistent with the right to present mitigating evidence in death-penalty sentencing.

The Court held that an "aggravated felony" includes only conduct punishable as a felony under the federal Controlled Substances Act, regardless of whether state law classifies such conduct as a felony or a misdemeanor.
The Supreme Court ruled that the state court did not unreasonably apply clearly established federal law when it upheld the conviction.

The Court unanimously ruled that a statute of limitations on government actions for contract claims did not apply to a federal administrative agency's actions to recover royalties on federal oil and gas leases.
The court held that an indictment alleging attempted reentry under 8 U.S.C §1326(a) need not specifically allege a particular overt act or any other component part of the offense.
The court held that the same causation standard applies to railroad negligence under Section 1 of the Federal Employers' Liability Act to employee contributory negligence under Section 3.
The court held that the term "theft offense" in the Immigration and Nationality Act includes the crime of "aiding and abetting" a theft offense.

The court held that, although 28 U.S.C. § 1447(d) generally prevents appeals of decisions to remand removed cases back to state court, that statute does not apply to cases removed under the Westfall Act.
The Court held, 6–3, that the sentencing standard set forward in Apprendi v. New Jersey (2000) applies to California's determinate sentencing law.
The Court held that the Court's decision in Brooke Group Ltd. v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. did not apply in predatory purchasing cases.

The court held that the statute of limitations for seeking federal habeas relief from a state decision is not tolled while a certiorari petition is pending with the United States Supreme Court because it is tolled only during review by state courts.
The Court held that the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment limits punitive damages, and it ordered a lower court to reconsider its damages awards on that basis.

In a §1983 suit seeking damages for a false arrest followed by criminal proceedings, the Court held that the statute of limitations begins to run when the claimant is detained pursuant to legal process, not when the charges are dropped.
The court held that the interpretation of the Confrontation Clause that it announced in Crawford v. Washington (2006) does not apply retroactively.
The court held a United States district court has discretion to respond at once to a defendant's forum non conveniens plea, and need not take up first any other threshold objection.

The Court examined the original-source exception to the False Claims Act's public-disclosure bar and held that the original-source requirement is jurisdictional and that "information on which the allegations are based" refers to the relator's own allegations.

In a dispute over whether the Guam Organic Act's debt ceiling should be calculated using real market value or tax assessed value of property, the Court reversed the Guam Supreme Court and found for the Attorney General's office.

In a suit by Massachusetts, other states and cities to force the EPA to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Clean Air Act, the Court ruled for the plaintiffs, finding that greenhouse gases qualify as air pollutants.
The Court held that while a term may be used more than once in a statute, an agency has the discretion to interpret each use of the term in a different way based on the context.

The Court held that a nationally chartered bank's mortgage business, whether conducted by the bank or its operating subsidiary, is subject to the Comptroller of the Currency's superintendence rather than to state licensing, reporting, and visitorial regimes.
The court held that payphone operators have a private right to sue telephone carriers for failure to pay reimbursement required by the FCC under the Communications Act of 1934.

The Court held that the statute authorizing the Federal Impact Aid Program permitted the Secretary of Education to identify districts to be disregarded by considering both the number of pupils and the size of expenditures per pupil.
In a challenge to the Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act of 2003, the Court upheld the federal ban, holding that it did not impose an undue burden on women's due process right to obtain an abortion.

The Court held that attempted burglary could serve as a predicate felony under the federal Armed Career Criminal Act, which required a mandatory minimum 15-year term for felons in possession of firearms with three prior qualifying convictions.
The Court held that New York county ordinances forcing private waste management companies to deliver waste to a public facility did not discriminate against interstate commerce.

The Court ruled for the deputy in a qualified immunity and excessive force suit by a motorist paralyzed after being run off the road in a chase, finding his actions objectively reasonable because videotape showed the motorist endangered public safety.
The court held that a trust that has missed 26 U.S.C. §7426(a)(1)’s deadline for challenging a levy may not bring the challenge as a tax refund claim under 28 U.S.C. §1346(a)(1).

The Supreme Court reversed a previous decision by the Federal Circuit and ruled in favor of Microsoft, holding that Microsoft was not liable for infringement on AT&T's patent under 35 U.S.C. § 271(f).

The Court held that the District Court did not abuse its discretion in refusing an evidentiary hearing to a convicted murderer who had told his counsel not to present mitigation evidence at sentencing, reversing the Ninth Circuit's en banc ruling.
The court held that the Tax Court is the exclusive forum for judicial review of claims about interest abatement under the Internal Revenue Code.

The court held that it did not have jurisdiction under the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 to review a wrongful termination suit brought against United States Senator Mark Dayton, where the lower courts did not rule on the constitutionality of the Act.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that appeals courts must defer to a trial judge's decision on whether a potential juror would be able to overcome demur about the death penalty and be open to voting to impose a death sentence.
The court held that where "willfulness" is a statutory condition of civil liability, it generally includes both knowing violations of a standard and reckless violations.

The court held that a party who achieves a preliminary injunction in a Section 1983 case is not a prevailing party for the purposes of an attorney fee award if that preliminary injunction expires and is not converted into a permanent injunction.

The court held that an employer that sponsors and administers a single-employer defined-benefit pension plan does not have a fiduciary obligation under ERISA to consider a merger with a multi-employer plan as a method of terminating the plan.
