In AEDPA proceedings, the Court held that a federal court must assess the prejudicial impact of constitutional error in a state criminal trial under the "substantial and injurious effect" standard, whether or not the state appellate court reviewed it for harmlessness.

The court held that, because the CERCLA's Section 107(a)(4)(B) allows a potentially responsible party (PRP) to recover costs from other PRPs, the statute provides a private cause of action to achieve that result with a lawsuit.

The court held that the fact that a federal agency directs, supervises, and monitors a company's activities in considerable detail does not bring that company within the scope of the statute permitting removal jurisdiction for actions against federal officers.

The Court held that it does not violate the First Amendment for a state to require its public-sector unions to receive affirmative authorization from a non-member before spending that nonmember's agency fees for election-related purposes.
The Court determined that the federal courts of appeals lack jurisdiction to hear habeas appeals that are filed late, even if the district court said the petitioner had additional time to file.
The Court held that all occupants of a car are "seized" for purposes of the Fourth Amendment during a traffic stop, not just the driver.
The Court held that the securities markets were exempt from the scope of antitrust laws.
The Court held that a statewide association's rule prohibiting high-school football coaches from contacting middle-school prospects did not violate the First Amendment.
The Court ruled on the interpretation of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995's requirement of scienter in a civil action in apply to Tellabs and Makor Issues & Rights.

The Court held, 5–4, that the First Amendment does not prevent educators from prohibiting or punishing student speech that is reasonably viewed as promoting illegal drug use at a school-sanctioned event.
The Court held that issue ads may not be banned from the months preceding a primary or general election.

In a case on the scope of qualified immunity for Bureau of Land Management officials, the Court held that BLM employees could not be liable for an alleged retaliation claim by a farm owner because other avenues for relief were available.
The Court ruled that taxpayers do not have the right to challenge the constitutionality of expenditures by the executive branch of the government.

The Court held that Section 7 of the Endangered Species Act applies only to federal agency actions involving agency discretion or control, so the EPA did not need to apply additional criteria when evaluating a transfer of Clean Water Act pollution control jurisdiction.

The Court found it unconstitutional for a school district to use race as a factor in assigning students to schools to match the district's overall racial composition, unless it was remedying a prior history of de jure segregation.

The United States Supreme Court overruled Dr. Miles Medical Co. v. John D. Park & Sons Co. Dr Miles had ruled that vertical price restraints were illegal per se under Section 1 of the Sherman Antitrust Act.

The Court ruled that death-sentenced defendants may not be executed if they do not understand the reason for their imminent execution, and that once an execution date is set they may litigate their competency in habeas corpus proceedings.

In a dispute under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act over tuition reimbursement, the Court ruled in favor of the student, affirming the appellate court's decision by an evenly divided 4–4 vote.

The Court held that the Railroad Revitalization and Regulatory Reform Act of 1976 allows a railroad to try to show that state methods of valuing railroad property result in a discriminatory determination of true market value.

The court held that the "civil rights restored" exemption of convictions for sentence-enhancement purposes did not extend to a defendant who retained his civil rights at all times, and whose post-conviction legal status remained in all respects unaltered by any state dispensation.
The Court held that the federal appeals courts may not presume that a sentence falling outside the range recommended by the Federal Sentencing Guidelines is unreasonable.

The Court held that a person who receives a firearm in exchange for drugs does not "use" a firearm during and in relation to a drug trafficking crime under the federal statute, unlike one who gives a gun for drugs.

The Court confirmed that federal district judges utilize, in an advisory (not as law) fashion, Federal Sentencing Guidelines, in cases involving conduct related to possession, distribution, and manufacture of crack cocaine.
The Court held that an action in the United States Court of Claims must always be timely, even if the government has waived timeliness.

In a 5-3 decision authored by Justice Anthony M. Kennedy, the Court held that "aiders and abettors" of fraud cannot be held secondarily liable under the private right of action authorized by §10(b) of the Exchange Act.
The court held that investment advisory fees generally are subject to the 2% tax-deductibility floor when incurred by a trust.

The Court rejected a constitutional challenge to New York's judicial election law, which was alleged to unfairly block candidates' ballot access, and held that it did not infringe candidates' First Amendment associational rights.

The Court held that ERISA gives no remedy for individual injuries distinct from plan injuries, but does let a person with a retirement account recover from a manager whose fiduciary breaches impaired the value of plan assets in that person's individual account.

The Court held that state courts can retroactively apply a new constitutional rule of criminal procedure in post-conviction proceedings by applying state law retroactivity standards that are broader than the Teague v. Lane standard.

The Court held that the pre-emption clause of the Medical Device Amendment bars state common-law claims that challenge the effectiveness or safety of a medical device marketed in a form that received premarket approval from the Food and Drug Administration.
The Court held, 8–1, that the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) overrules state laws declaring that certain disputes must be resolved by a state administrative agency.
The court held that federal law preempts state law that would control the commercial delivery of tobacco and other products harmful to children.

In an individual age discrimination case, the Court held that the relevance of co-workers' "me too" evidence is fact based and depends on many factors, so reviewing courts may not apply per se rules of admissibility or inadmissibility.

The Court held that a distributee accused of criminal tax evasion may claim return-of-capital treatment without producing evidence that, when the distribution occurred, either they or the corporation intended to return the capital.
The Court held that Washington's top-two primary system does not infringe upon smaller political parties' associational rights.

In a death penalty case about racial issues in jury selection, the Court ruled that the prosecutor's use of peremptory strikes to remove African American jurors violated its earlier holding in Batson v. Kentucky.

The Court held that state and federal courts cannot, on a motion to vacate or to modify an arbitration award, expand the limited scope of judicial review specified in 9 U.S.C. §§ 10 and 11, including terms that were agreed upon by the parties.
Concerns refunds for a tax that was levied and subsequently found to be unconstitutional.
The Court upheld the constitutionality of a particular method of lethal injection used for capital punishment.
The court held that the definition of "serious drug felony" for the purposes of sentencing an individual as having a prior drug conviction is taken from 21 U.S. Code § 802(44) and not § 802(13).
The Court held that felony driving while intoxicated is not a "violent felony" for purposes of the Armed Career Criminal Act.
Addresses use of evidence obtained by police in a search incident to an arrest if that arrest is later found to be unlawful.
The Court held that an Indiana law requiring voters to provide photographic identification did not violate the United States Constitution.
The court held that the right to have a district judge preside over jury selection can be waived by counsel, allowing a magistrate judge to serve as a substitute.

The court held that an person who possessed explosives "during" the commission of another crime is eligible for a mandatory 10-year sentence on top of any other sentence even if the explosives were not related to the crime they committed.
The Court upheld a Kentucky law that provides a preferential tax break to Kentucky residents who invest in bonds issued by the state and its municipalities (municipal bonds).

In a case interpreting the Armed Career Criminal Act, the Court ruled that although a crime's elements may not be considered "serious," sentence enhancements related to a defendant's prior record bear on how that determination is made.
The court held that a court's order resolving liability without addressing a plaintiff's requests for relief is not a final judgment.
The Court ruled that the petitioner, Hedrick Humphries, was unfairly retaliated against by CBOCS West Inc. for complaining to managers about the dismissal of another black employee for race reasons.
The Court held that federal employees can assert claims for retaliation resulting from filing an age discrimination complaint.
The court held that the rule of lenity requires that the federal money-laundering statute's use of the inherently-ambiguous term "proceeds" be read in the light favorable to the accused.

The court held that the federal money-laundering statute contains no "legitimate wealth" requirement, and mere proof that the defendant was attempting to conceal the money is not enough to uphold a conviction.

In a dispute over attorney's fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act, the Court held that a prevailing party may be reimbursed for paralegal services at prevailing market rates rather than at the cost to the law firm.
The court held that the class-of-one theory of equal protection does not apply in the public employment context.
The court held that a RICO plaintiff asserting a claim predicated on mail fraud does not need to show that that plaintiff relied on the defendant's alleged misrepresentations.

The Court held that plaintiffs under the False Claims Act must prove that the false claim was made with the specific intent of inducing the government to pay or approve payment of a false or fraudulent claim, rather than merely defrauding a contractor.

The court unanimously concluded that the habeas corpus statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241(c)(1), extends to U.S. citizens held overseas by American forces subject to an American chain of command, even if acting as part of a multinational coalition.
The court held that Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 32(h) does not apply to a variance from a recommended Federal Sentencing Guidelines range; that rule applies only to "departures."

The Court, in a case brought by a Guantanamo detainee, held that the detainees had a constitutional right to habeas corpus and that the Military Commissions Act of 2006 was an unconstitutional suspension of that right.

The Court clarified the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure as regards money damages sought by a foreign government, the Republic of the Philippines, via its Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG).
The Court held that a "virtually represented" non-party cannot be bound by a judgment.
The court held that a non-citizen must be permitted an opportunity to withdraw a motion for voluntary departure, provided the request is made before expiration of the departure period.
The court held that the Bankruptcy Code's section authorizing an exemption from stamp taxes can only be used in relation to a Chapter 11 plan that has been confirmed.

The Court decided that an employer bears both the burden of production and burden of persuasion when defending a disparate impact claim using the "reasonable factors" defense under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA).
The court held that a company that both administers and funds a benefit plan operates under a conflict of interest that must be considered when a court reviews its claim denials.

The court held that Kentucky's retirement system does not amount to age discrimination under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act when granting pensions to disabled persons who had not yet reached the permitted retirement age of 55.
The Court held that the standard for competency to stand trial was not linked to the standard for competency to represent oneself.

The Court held that a criminal defendant's initial appearance before a magistrate judge, where he learns the charge against him and his liberty is subject to restriction, marks the initiation of adversary judicial proceedings that trigger attachment of the Sixth Amendment right to counsel.
The Court held that a federal appeals court may not sua sponte increase a defendant's sentence unless the government first files a notice of appeal.

The court held that an assignee of a legal claim for money owed has standing to pursue that claim in federal court even when the assignee has promised to remit the proceeds of the litigation to the assignor.
The Court held that a tribal court had no jurisdiction to hear a case for discrimination against an Indian in the sale of non-Indian fee land located on a reservation.
The Court held that for testimonial statements to be admissible under the forfeiture exception to hearsay, the defendant must have intended to make the witness unavailable for trial.

The Court held that the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause prohibits the imposition of the death penalty for a crime in which the victim did not die and the victim's death was not intended.
The Court ruled in a 5-3 decision that the punitive damages awarded to the victims of the Exxon Valdez oil spill should be reduced from $2.5 billion to $500 million.

The court held that the Mobile–Sierra presumption that a negotiated rate is "just and reasonable" applies to all contract rates even if it was not actually reviewed for reasonableness, and the presumption applies regardless of whether the rate is considered too high or too low.

The Court ruled that the Second Amendment protects an individual's right to keep and bear arms for lawful purposes such as self-defense at home, and that the District of Columbia's handgun ban and trigger-lock requirement violated it.
The Court held that a state law prohibiting deceptive tobacco advertising was not preempted by a federal law regulating cigarette advertising.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(d)(1)(A), the conviction of a state defendant is not "final" if a state court grants an "out-of-time" appeal and the defendant has not yet filed a federal habeas petition.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that failing to report for incarceration does not qualify as a "violent felony" for the purposes of the Armed Career Criminal Act.

The court decided that the good-faith exception to the exclusionary rule applies when a police officer makes an arrest based on an outstanding warrant in another jurisdiction, but the information regarding that warrant is later found to be incorrect because of a negligent error by that agency.

In a case over sentencing for multiple offenses, the Court held that the Sixth Amendment does not prevent states from having judges, rather than juries, find the facts needed to impose consecutive rather than concurrent sentences.

The Court considered a driver's second-degree murder conviction for a gang-related shooting involving high school students and held that he was tried with due process and should not have been granted federal habeas corpus relief.

The Court held that the Constitution permits a local labor union chapter to charge non-members a service fee covering non-local litigation expenses if they are appropriately related to collective bargaining and the local and national unions have a reciprocal relationship.
The Court took to the unusual step of asking the parties to argue whether past precedent should be overturned.
The United States Supreme Court held that parents could sue a school committee under grounds of the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment.
The Court unanimously ruled that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 protects an employee who opposes unlawful sexual harassment, but does not report the harassment themself.

The court held that because a divorcee did not attempt to direct her interest in the SIP benefits to the Estate or any other potential beneficiary, her waiver did not constitute an assignment or alienation rendered void under ERISA.

The court held that when a statute delegates an interpretive decision to an administrative agency in the first instance, the agency's interpretation governs in the absence of unambiguous statutory language to the contrary or an unreasonable resolution of ambiguous language.

The Court held, by unanimous decision, that police may conduct a Terry-stop patdown of a passenger in an automobile that has been lawfully stopped for a minor traffic violation, provided that the police reasonably suspect that the passenger is armed and dangerous.

The court held that prosecutors are absolutely immune from suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 based on management tasks such as their supervision or training of subordinates and their information-system organization.
The court held that a state ban on political payroll deductions for contributions by public employees to their union's political action committee does not infringe the unions' First Amendment rights.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the federal government could not take land into trust that was acquired by the Narragansett Tribe in the late 20th century, as it was not federally recognized until 1983.

The Court held that a domestic relationship is not necessarily a defining element of the predicate offense to support a conviction for possession of a firearm by a person previously convicted of a misdemeanor crime of domestic violence.

The Court unanimously held that Pacific Bell d/b/a AT&T did not violate the Sherman Antitrust Act when it charged other Internet providers a high fee to buy space on its phone lines to deliver an Internet connection.
The Court ruled on the U.S. Constitution's prohibition on a government establishment of religion specifically with respect to monuments (e.g., statues) on public land.

The Court rejected the environmental groups' argument that they still had standing to challenge the Forest Service's exemption process generally, after their dispute over salvage timber sales on 238 acres was settled.

The Court held that the Board of Immigration Appeals and the Fifth Circuit erred in an asylum case by presuming that an applicant's claimed coercion to participate in persecution was immaterial to whether the persecutor bar applies.
The Court held that Federal regulatory approval of a medication does not shield the manufacturer from liability under state law.

A plurality of the Court held that a minority group must constitute a numerical majority of the voting-age population in an area before section 2 of the Voting Rights Act requires the creation of a legislative district to prevent dilution of that group's votes.

The Court held that a federal court may look at the underlying controversy of a Federal Arbitration Act §4 petition to decide whether it "arises under" federal law, but that controversy must satisfy the well-pleaded complaint rule for jurisdiction.

The Court held that trial delay caused by a criminal defendant's public defender should be attributed to the defense rather than the government, and so did not violate the Speedy Trial Clause of the Sixth Amendment.
The court held that habeas relief may only be granted if the state court decision unreasonably applied the ineffective-assistance-of-counsel standard established by Strickland v. Washington.

The court held that Rule 52(b)'s plain error test applies to challenges of whether the prosecutor failed to follow through on a plea bargain, so those challenges generally cannot be made for the first time on appeal.
The Court, in an opinion by Justice Samuel Alito, ruled unanimously that the state had the power to sell the lands free of encumbrances.
The Court held that the due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment limits punitive damages, and it ordered a lower court to reconsider its damages awards on that basis.

The Court held that federal law gave indigent death row inmates the right to federally appointed counsel to represent them in post-conviction state clemency proceedings, when the state has declined to do so.

In a dispute over EPA Clean Water Act rules on power plant cooling water intakes, the Court reversed the lower court and upheld as reasonable the EPA's decision to allow cost–benefit analysis in determining the best technology available.

The Court decided that when a union contract clearly and unmistakably requires age discrimination claims under the ADEA to be arbitrated, employees covered by that contract cannot bring those claims in court.
The court held that 18 U. S. C. §3501 modified the McNabb–Mallory doctrine but did not supplant it.

The Court held that the Fourth Amendment requires officers to show an actual and continuing threat to their safety from an arrestee, or a need to preserve evidence of the crime of arrest, to justify a warrantless vehicle search incident to arrest after occupants are secured.
The court held that the Federal Circuit's review of claims decisions made by the Department of Veterans Affairs must use the same harmless-error framework used in other civil cases.

The court held that immigrants who are contesting their impending deportation may request stays using the ordinary standards, but they cannot claim that they will be irreparably injured by wrongful deportation.

The United States Supreme Court held that a defendant was entitled to a hearing to determine whether prosecutors in his 1982 death penalty trial violated his right to due process by withholding exculpatory evidence.

The Court upheld regulations of the Federal Communications Commission that ban "fleeting expletives" on television broadcasts, finding they were not arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.
The court held that a statement collected in violation of the Sixth Amendment may be admissible to impeach inconsistent testimony at trial.
The court held that to be an "arranger" under CERCLA requires the specific intent to dispose toxic waste.
The court held that the Federal Arbitration Act does not alter state contract law regarding the scope of agreements, including arbitration agreements.

The court held that a federal district court's order remanding a case to state court after declining to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state-law claims is not a remand for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
The Court held that the law enhancing the sentence for identity theft requires proof that an individual knew that the identity card or number he had used belonged to another, actual person.
The Court held that a plaintiff in a civil law case must plead a claim in a "plausible" manner.
The Court held that maternity leave taken before the passage of the 1978 Pregnancy Discrimination Act needed not to be considered in calculating employee pension benefits.

The Court held that a New York law preventing state trial courts from hearing claims for money damages against prison employees whether based on federal or state law violated the Supremacy Clause of the United States Constitution.
The Court overruled the Court's decision in Michigan v. Jackson.

The Court held that a defendant who used a cellphone for the misdemeanor purchase of cocaine could not be charged with a felony for using a "communication facility" to facilitate the distribution of an illegal drug under 21 U.S.C. § 843(b).
The court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not bar a courts from conducting a full hearing on a convicted defendant's mental capacity to determine if they are eligible for the death penalty.
The court held that the Emergency Wartime Supplemental Appropriations Act gave the president the authority to restore the sovereign immunity of Iraq.

The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires judges to recuse themselves not only for actual bias or an economic interest in the case, but also when "extreme facts" create a "probability of bias."
The court held that the military appellate courts have jurisdiction to hear a request for a writ of coram nobis.

The Court held that where the Government has not intervened or actively participated, private plaintiffs under the False Claims Act must file an appeal within 30 days of the judgment or order being appealed, according to the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
The Court, in a 7-2 opinion, held that any group convened to carry out a crime meets the definition of an enterprise, even if it was only created for that purpose.

The court held that, for deportation purposes, fraud is an aggravated felony when the loss to the victims exceeds $10,000, and that refers to the particular circumstances in which an offender committed fraud on a particular occasion.
The United States Supreme Court decided that the Constitution's Due Process Clause does not require states to turn over DNA evidence to a party seeking a civil suit under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

The Court held that, even when a jury's acquittals on some counts seem inconsistent with its failure to return a verdict on other counts, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars the government from relitigating facts necessarily decided by the acquittals.

The court held that a bankruptcy settlement that immunizes a third party from liability based on events relevant to the bankruptcy is enforceable and cannot be challenged after the Bankruptcy Court approves the settlement with those terms.

In a case over the Voting Rights Act's Section 5 preclearance requirement, the Court held the utility district was eligible to seek a bailout under Section 4(a) and declined to rule on the provision's constitutionality, citing constitutional avoidance.

The Court held that the IDEA authorizes reimbursement for private special education services when a public school fails to provide a free appropriate public education and the private placement is appropriate, even if the child had not previously received public special education services.
Was decided in favor of Coeur Alaska's permit to dump mine waste in a lake.
The Court held that it was a violation of the Sixth Amendment right of confrontation for a prosecutor to submit a chemical drug test report without the testimony of the person who performed the test.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a strip search of a middle school student by school officials violated the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures.
The Court held that a seaman may recover punitive damages from his employer for failure to pay maintenance and cure.

The United States Supreme Court remanded the case to determine whether Arizona's general education funding budget supports Equal Educational Opportunities Act of 1974 (EEOA)-compliant English Language Learner (ELL) programming.
In a 5–4 decision, the court determined that a federal banking regulation did not pre-empt the ability of states to enforce their own fair-lending laws.

In a dispute over a city's decision to discard firefighter promotion test results because no black candidates scored high enough, the Court held that ignoring the results violated Title VII because the city lacked a "strong basis in evidence."
The Court held that disclosure orders adverse to attorney–client privilege do not qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine.
In a case about the Chicago Police Department's seizure of property, the Court declared the case moot because the parties agreed there was no longer any contention over the seized property.

The Court held that, because nothing in the Railway Labor Act made the obligation to conference minor disputes or prove conferencing jurisdictional, the act's limited grounds for relief should not be treated as a constitutional due process issue.
The court held that the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act cannot be used by a city to collect damages against out-of-state internet vendors who fail to pay city cigarette taxes.

The Court held that the state court's conclusion that the petitioner's counsel made a strategic decision not to pursue or present evidence of his mental deficiencies was not an unreasonable determination of the facts.
By a 5–4 vote, the Court held that an interstate water authority and the Duke Energy Corporation could intervene, while ruling unanimously that the city of Charlotte, North Carolina, could not.

The Court held that the statute that makes certain discretionary determinations of the attorney general immune to judicial review does not allow the attorney general to declare determinations discretionary and immune to review via regulations.
The court held that the Mobile–Sierra presumption does not depend on the identity of the complainant who seeks Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) investigation.

The Court held that police may re-open questioning of a suspect who has asked for counsel (thereby under Edwards v. Arizona ending questioning) if there has been a 14-day or more break in Miranda custody.

The Court held that for the purposes of diversity jurisdiction, a corporation's principal place of business is its "nerve center": the state in which its high-level executives work and direct the corporation.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled on the language requirements for Miranda warnings.

The court held that a franchisee cannot recover for constructive termination under the Petroleum Marketing Practices Act (PMPA) if the franchisor’s allegedly wrongful conduct did not compel the franchisee to abandon its franchise.

The Court held that failure to register a copyright under Section 411 (a) of the United States Copyright Act does not limit a Federal Court's jurisdiction over claims of infringement regarding unregistered works.
The court held that attorneys who provide bankruptcy assistance to assisted persons are debt relief agencies under the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005.
The court held that the time granted to prepare pretrial motions is not automatically excludable from the Speedy Trial Act's 70-day limit for bringing a case to trial.
The Court held that a federal district court sitting in a state with competing rules must apply a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure if the Rule is "arguably procedural."
The United States Supreme Court decided that criminal defense attorneys must advise noncitizen clients about the deportation risks of a guilty plea.

In a dispute where investors claimed their investment advisor's fees were too steep, the Court held that courts may regulate mutual fund advisers' fees under the Investment Company Act of 1940 when the fees are excessive and breach fiduciary duty.

The Court ruled that a Michigan jury selection system resulting in low representation of African Americans in Kent County did not violate the Sixth Amendment, because the statistical disparity did not satisfy the Duren test.
The court held that state "administrative" disclosures trigger the public disclosure bar within the False Claims Act.

The court held that, although a Bankruptcy Court is not supposed to discharge a person's student loan debt without finding whether they meet the "undue hardship" requirement, the Bankruptcy Court may enter a binding order without doing so.

The court held that the immunity provided by the Federal Tort Claims Act precludes Bivens actions against individual PHS officers or employees for harms arising out of constitutional violations committed while acting within the scope of their office or employment.
The court held that the trial court's decision in this case was not unreasonable under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996.
In a dispute over a Latin cross placed on a rock outcropping in the Mojave National Preserve to honor war dead, the Court ruled that the cross may stay but sent the case back to a lower court.
The court held that class action arbitration is permitted under the Federal Arbitration Act only if all parties specifically agree to it.

The court held that the time for a plaintiff to file a federal securities fraud lawsuit begins to run when the plaintiff discovers or reasonably should have discovered that the defendant knew that the defendant's statement was false.
The court held that a debt collector's ignorance of the law does not qualify as a good-faith mistake for the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act's bona fide error defense.
The court held that a federal court can award larger-than-usual attorney's fees for excellent performance in a civil rights case, but only in extraordinary circumstances.

The court held that the administrator of an ERISA plan is entitled to deference in matters of interpretation, even when the administrator had previously adopted a different interpretation that a court found erroneous.

The Court ruled that 18 U.S.C. § 48, a federal statute criminalizing the commercial production, sale, or possession of depictions of cruelty to animals, was an unconstitutional abridgment of the First Amendment right to freedom of speech.

The Court held that a parent's ne exeat right (in this case: the right to prevent a child to leave the country) is a "right to custody" under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction and the US International Child Abduction Remedies Act.
The Court held that juvenile offenders cannot be sentenced to life imprisonment without parole for non-homicide offenses.
The Court held that the federal government has authority under the Necessary and Proper Clause to require the civil commitment of individuals already in Federal custody.
The court held that employers can be sued any time they use results from employment-eligibility tests that rule out disproportionate numbers of marginalized groups.

The court held that, when used by the prosecution to obtain a mandatory minimum sentence, the fact that a firearm was a machine gun is an element to be proved to the jury beyond a reasonable doubt, not a sentencing factor to be proved to the judge at sentencing.
The court held that a fee claimant need not be a "prevailing party" to be eligible for an attorney's fees award under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974.

The court held that an appellate court may reverse a conviction based on a plain error raised for the first time on appeal when there is a reasonable probability that the error affected the trial's outcome.
The court held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act's immunity for a "foreign state" does not include an official acting on behalf of that state.

The Court held that, unless and until a criminal suspect explicitly states that they are relying on their right to remain silent, their voluntary statements may be used in court and police may continue to question them.

The court held that, under the comity doctrine, a taxpayer's complaint of allegedly discriminatory state taxation must proceed originally in state court even when the complaint is framed as a request to increase a competitor's tax burden.

The court held that the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act, which criminalizes interstate travel for sex offenders who do not register as a sex offender in the other state, does not apply to sex offenders whose interstate travel occurred before SORNA's effective date.

The Court held that incarcerated people in federal prison accrue good time credits at the end of each year of actual incarceration, not an amount allocated based on the total number of years of incarceration prescribed at their sentencing.

The court held that when a bankruptcy court calculates a debtor's projected disposable income, the court may account for changes in the debtor's income or expenses that are known or virtually certain at the time of confirmation.

The court held that relation back under Rule 15(c)(1)(C) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure depends on what the party to be added knew or should have known, not on the amending party's knowledge or timeliness in seeking to amend the pleading.
The court held that the term "aggravated felonies" in 8 U.S.C. §1101(a)(43) does not mean "any conduct punishable as a felony."
The court held that the government can reduce the fee award due to a person who has successfully sued the government to cover that person's preexisting debts to the government.

The court held that a sentencing court that misses the 90-day deadline nonetheless retains the power to order restitution where that court made clear prior to the deadline's expiration that it would order restitution.
The Court held that the statute of limitations for filing a habeas petition under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act is subject to equitable tolling in appropriate cases.
The Court held that the National Labor Relations Board could not make decisions without at least three members on a panel.

The Court held that the Florida Supreme Court did not effect an unconstitutional taking of littoral property owners' rights to future accretions and to contact the water by upholding Florida's beach renourishment program.
The Court unanimously held that the audit was work-related and thus did not violate the Fourth Amendment's protections against unreasonable search and seizure.

The Court held that when a debtor claims an exemption of a dollar value for specific property, claiming its full anticipated value did not exempt the property from seizure if its true value was greater, and the trustee did not need to object.

The Court held that when a defendant received a resentencing hearing after the Sentencing Guidelines changed in the defendant's favor, the updated Guidelines were binding on the district court, though they could be merely advisory at a first sentencing.

The Court ruled against a group that wanted to help designated foreign terrorist organizations learn to resolve conflicts peacefully, holding that the Patriot Act's ban on providing material support, including training and expert advice, covered such assistance.

The Court held that under the Federal Arbitration Act, when an arbitration agreement delegates enforceability questions to the arbitrator, a challenge to that specific agreement goes to the district court, but a challenge to the whole agreement goes to the arbitrator.

The Court held that, when a cargo shipment begins overseas, portions of the trip when the goods are traveling over land by train are governed by the Carriage of Goods by Sea Act, not the Carmack Amendment to the Interstate Commerce Act.

The Court reversed the lower court's decision barring partial deregulation of Monsanto's genetically modified Roundup-ready alfalfa pending completion of an environmental impact statement, finding the district court abused its discretion in enjoining it.
The Court holds that the disclosure of signatures on a referendum does not violate the Petition Clause of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court held that courts, not arbitrators, determine whether and when arbitration contracts are formed when the decision affects whether parties intended to submit an issue to arbitration.

The Court held that, when a state prisoner obtains federal habeas corpus relief and is re-sentenced, a habeas application challenging the new judgment is not a "second or successive" challenge even if the prisoner could have challenged the original sentence on the same ground.
The Court found the statute vague, meaning it was written in a manner that almost anyone could be convicted of the statute by engaging in most legal activities.

The Court ruled that laws insulating inferior officers from Presidential removal with two levels of "for cause" removal, as for Public Company Accounting Oversight Board officers under Sarbanes–Oxley, violated Article Two of the Constitution.

The Court held that the machine-or-transformation test is not the sole test for determining the patent eligibility of a process, but rather "a useful and important clue, an investigative tool, for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under § 101."

The Court upheld, against a First Amendment challenge, the policy of the University of California, Hastings College of the Law, governing official recognition of student groups, which required the groups to accept all students regardless of their status or beliefs in order to obtain recognition.

The Court found that the right of an individual to "keep and bear arms", as protected under the Second Amendment, is incorporated by the Fourteenth Amendment and is thereby enforceable against the states.
The Court found the statute vague, meaning it was written in a manner that almost anyone could be convicted of the statute by engaging in most legal activities.

The Court ruled that the five-year minimum sentence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) for using or possessing a deadly weapon in drug trafficking or violent crimes was added to any other mandatory sentence, including for the underlying offense.
In a Section 1983 suit over municipal liability, the Court ruled that the "policy or custom" requirement from Monell applied regardless of whether the relief sought was monetary or prospective.

In a copyright dispute over unauthorized sale of authentic, imported watches bearing a registered design, the court held that the first-sale doctrine was not a defense to claims of infringing distribution and importation.
The Court upheld a Treasury Department regulation on the grounds that the courts should defer to government agencies in tax cases in absence of an unreasonable decision on the part of the agency.

In a dispute over the Chapter 13 bankruptcy means test, the Court ruled that the car-ownership cost allowance was available only to debtors who made loan or lease payments on a vehicle, affirming the Ninth Circuit.

The court held that the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996's standard for federal habeas relief applies even when a state court does not issue an opinion explaining the basis of its decision.

In a unanimous ruling, the court held that habeas relief may not be granted with respect to any claim that a state-court has found on the merits unless the state-court decision denying relief involves an "unreasonable application" of "clearly established federal law, as determined by" the Court.
The Court held that NASA's background checks of contract employees did not violate any constitutional privacy right.

The court held that, before August 2009, Regulation Z did not require banks to provide credit-card holders with a change-in-terms notice before raising their interest rate after a delinquency or default.
The Court held that a party may not appeal a denial of summary judgment after a district court has conducted a full trial on the merits.
The Court held that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act protects a worker from retaliation when the worker's fiancé files a workplace grievance.
The Court decided whether a section of the Vaccine Act of 1986 preempts all vaccine design defect claims against vaccine manufacturers.

The Court held that a railroad could challenge a state's sales and use taxes as discriminatory under the Railroad Revitalization and Regulatory Reform Act of 1976 when the tax was imposed on railroads but not their main competitors.

The court held that a state's rule requiring state habeas petitions to be filed "as promptly as the circumstances allow" constitutes an independent state ground that is adequate to bar habeas relief in federal court.

The Court unanimously held that Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard 208, promulgated by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, does not federally preempt state tort lawsuits against auto manufacturers from injuries caused by a defective lack of certain types of seat belts.

The Court held that the exemption from Freedom of Information Act disclosure requirements for law enforcement records which "could reasonably be expected to constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy" does not protect information related to corporate privacy.

The Court held that an employer may be liable for employment discrimination under USERRA if a biased supervisor's actions proximately caused an adverse employment action, even if the ultimate decision-maker was not personally biased.
The Court held that the deadline for filing a notice of appeal with the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims does not have jurisdictional consequences.

The Court held that speech made in a public place on a matter of public concern cannot be the basis of liability for a tort of emotional distress, even if the speech is viewed as offensive or outrageous.

The Court considered whether a district court properly handled the sentencing of a former methamphetamine dealer whose sentence was raised to 65 months after remands, and it ruled in favor of the defendant.

The court held that it is proper to toll the time available for a habeas petition upon a properly filed application for state post-conviction or other collateral review with respect to the pertinent judgment or claim.
The court held that the Freedom of Information Act's Exemption 2 only allows the government to withhold records relating to employee relations and human resources issues.

In a dispute over whether a prisoner seeking biological DNA material for testing to challenge his conviction must use a civil rights suit or a habeas corpus petition, the Court held that the civil rights path was appropriate.

The court held that the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 prohibits retaliation against workers for complaints related to violations of the act without regard to whether the complaints are oral or written.

In a securities fraud class action over a drugmaker's failure to disclose adverse event reports lacking statistically significant evidence of causation, the Court affirmed the Ninth Circuit and held the plaintiffs had stated a claim under §10(b) and Rule 10b-5.

In a case over a man's wrongful conviction after prosecutors suppressed exculpatory evidence, the Court reversed a $14 million jury award, holding a district attorney's office cannot be liable under Section 1983 for failure to train based on a single Brady violation.
The court held that medical providers, as third-party beneficiaries, may not sue drug manufacturers for selling drugs at prices higher than the discounted price required by Medicaid.

The case concerned Arizona taxpayers who challenged a state tax credit for donations to school tuition organizations funding private or religious schools, and the Court ruled that the taxpayers lacked standing to sue.

The Court held that in federal habeas proceedings under § 2254(d)(1), only evidence presented to the state court that adjudicated the claim on the merits could be considered, and that the respondent was not entitled to the habeas relief the Ninth Circuit had granted.

The majority decision, written by Justice Clarence Thomas, held that the petitioner could not sue Texas state officials in their official capacity for damages under the RLUIPA, affirming a lower court ruling.
The court held that Ex parte Young allows a federal court to hear a lawsuit for prospective relief against state officials brought by another agency of the same state.
Was decided by the United States Supreme Court.

The court held that a plaintiff cannot bring a suit in the Court of Federal Claims when they have another active suit based on substantially the same operative facts, regardless of any difference in the requested relief.
The court held that a federal agency's written response to a Freedom of Information Act request for records constitutes a "report" within the meaning of the False Claims Act's public disclosure bar.
The court held that the federal district court did not have authority under Section 502(a)(1)(B) of ERISA to reform CIGNA's pension plan, but Section 502(a)(3) did give the court that authority.

The Court held that warrantless searches conducted in police-created exigent circumstances do not violate the Fourth Amendment as long as the police did not create the exigency by violating or threatening to violate the Fourth Amendment.
The Court held that a court-mandated population limit was necessary to remedy a violation of prisoners’ Eighth Amendment constitutional rights.
The Court upheld an Arizona state law suspending or revoking business licenses of businesses that hire illegal aliens.

The court held that, under the Speedy Trial Act of 1974, the speedy trial clock stops whenever a pretrial motion is filed, regardless of whether the trial process is actually delayed by the motion or expected to be delayed.

The court held that when someone is charged of a killing under the federal witness-tampering statute, the state must prove a violation by showing there was a reasonable likelihood that a relevant communication would have been made to a federal officer.
The Court held that government officials who won on qualified immunity grounds could still appeal the lower court's underlying ruling that their seizure of a schoolchild was unconstitutional.

The Court held that inducing patent infringement requires knowledge of the infringement, but affirmed the Federal Circuit's judgment against the petitioners under the doctrine of willful blindness, given their knowledge of a related infringement lawsuit.

The Court held that U.S. Attorney General John D. Ashcroft could not be personally sued for his involvement in the detention of a U.S. citizen in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks in the United States.
The Court held that reasonable fees may be granted to the defendant in a suit that involves both frivolous and non-frivolous claims, but only for costs resulting from the frivolous claims.

The Court held that that, regarding whether an offense under State law is a serious drug offense for purposes of federal sentencing, courts must consult the maximum term of imprisonment for the offense at the time of conviction.
The Court held that title in a patented invention vests first in the inventor, even if the inventor is a researcher at a federally funded lab subject to the 1980 Bayh–Dole Act.
The Court held that "securities fraud plaintiffs need not prove loss causation in order to obtain class certification."
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the use of the term "cocaine base" in 21 U.S.C. § 841(b)(1) refers to cocaine in its chemically basic form.

The Court held that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had advanced a reasonable interpretation of its regulations in a dispute with AT&T. The case was consolidated with Isiogu v. Michigan Bell Telephone Co.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that felony vehicle flight, as proscribed by Indiana law, is a violent felony for purposes of the residual clause of the Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA).

Addressed the precedent set by Nguyen v. INS, 533 U.S. 53 (2001), which upheld a law imposing different requirements in situations regarding children born out of wedlock to U.S. citizen fathers versus U.S. citizen mothers.
The Court held that the fiduciary exception to attorney–client privilege does not apply to the general trust relationship between the United States and Indian tribes.
The Court held that a service provider cannot be held liable in a private action under SEC Rule 10b-5.
The court held that the Nevada Ethics in Government Law, which required government officials recuse in cases involving a conflict of interest, is not unconstitutionally overbroad.
The court held that people, just like states, may have standing to raise Tenth Amendment challenges to a federal law.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that age and mental status are relevant when determining police custody for Miranda purposes, overturning its prior ruling from seven years before.
The court held that federal courts cannot issue orders to prevent state courts from issuing class certifications.
The Court held that a federal court cannot give a criminal defendant a longer sentence to promote rehabilitation.
The Court ruled that a group of roughly 1.5 million women could not be certified as a valid class of plaintiffs in a class action for employment discrimination against Walmart.

The Court, in an 8–0 decision, held that corporations cannot be sued for greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) under federal common law, primarily because the Clean Air Act (CAA) delegates the management of carbon dioxide and other GHG emissions to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
Was decided by the United States Supreme Court on June 20, 2011, relating to the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment.

The court held that the Federal Employers Liability Act makes a railroad liable if the railroad's negligence plays any part in bringing about the injury; it does not follow proximate-cause standards developed by courts outside of statutory contexts.

The Court considered whether the Confrontation Clause allows a supervisor to testify about lab results transcribed by a non-testifying analyst, and held that a surrogate analyst could not testify about the certifying analyst's testimonial forensic report.
The court held that federal regulations govern what gets put on drug labels for generic drugs, so generic drug manufacturers cannot be sued for damages under state laws that punish a failure to warn.
The Court held that a Vermont statute that restricted the sale, disclosure, and use of records that revealed the prescribing practices of individual doctors violated the First Amendment.

A plurality of the court held that when a criminal defendant pleads guilty under a plea deal and the judge imposes the recommended sentence under the Sentencing Guidelines, the defendant is eligible to have their sentence reduced if the Guidelines later change.

The Court held that a bankruptcy court, as a non-Article III court, lacked constitutional authority under Article III to enter a final judgment on a state law counterclaim not resolved in ruling on a creditor's proof of claim, despite Congress's statutory grant.
The Court held that the connection between Goodyear and its subsidiaries with the state of North Carolina was not strong enough to establish general personal jurisdiction over the companies.

The Court held that a court may not exercise jurisdiction over a defendant that has not purposefully availed itself of doing business in the jurisdiction or placed goods in the stream of commerce in the expectation they would be purchased in the jurisdiction.
The Court struck down a 2005 California law banning the sale of certain violent video games to children without parental supervision.

In a habeas case under AEDPA, the Court unanimously ruled that "clearly established Federal law" does not include Supreme Court decisions announced after the last state-court adjudication on the merits but before the conviction became final.
The court held that Section 2253(c)(3) of the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 is a mandatory but nonjurisdictional rule.
The court held that, when state tort law authorizes adequate alternative damages actions—providing both significant deterrence and compensation—no Bivens remedy can be implied.

The court held that because the Credit Repair Organizations Act is silent on whether claims can proceed in an arbitrable forum, the Federal Arbitration Act requires the arbitration agreement to be enforced according to its terms.
The court held that a witness's statements are "plainly material" under Brady v. Maryland when they are the only evidence linking the defendant to the crime.

The court held that the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act extends coverage for injury occurring as the result of operations conducted on the Outer Continental Shelf to an employee who can establish a substantial nexus between his injury and his employer's extractive operations on the Shelf.

The Court unanimously invalidated the Board of Immigration Appeals' "comparable-grounds rule," used to decide whether certain long-term resident aliens facing deportation over a prior conviction could seek relief, as arbitrary and capricious.
The court held that federal and state courts have concurrent jurisdiction over private suits arising under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991.
The Court held that the "limited time" language of the United States Constitution's Copyright Clause does not preclude the extension of copyright protections to works previously in the public domain.

The Court ruled 7–2 that Cory R. Maples, who had been convicted of murdering two people and faced a possible death sentence, should get another opportunity in court because his lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell had abandoned him.
The court held that Pre-SORNA sex offenders are not obligated to register unless the Attorney General specifies applicability.
The court held that the Federal Meat Inspection Act preempts a California statute relating to non-ambulatory animals.
The court held that installing a Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking device on a vehicle and using the device to monitor the vehicle's movements constitutes a search under the Fourth Amendment.

The Court held that "filing a false tax return in violation of 26 U.S.C. Section 7206 qualifies as an aggravated felony under the Immigration and Nationality Act when the Government's revenue loss exceeds $10,000."

The court held that state officers are entitled to qualified immunity after seizing unrelated evidence from someone who was not under investigation when the error was not immediately apparent based on the text of the search warrant.

The court held that the equal-footing doctrine gives a state title to a segment of a river if that segment was navigable at the time the state enters the union; else, it remained in control of the federal government and could be sold by the government.

The Court, faced with plaintiffs claiming a Supremacy Clause right to sue to enforce federal Medicaid law against a conflicting state law, declined a firm decision and remanded to the Ninth Circuit because circumstances had changed during the appeal.

The Court held that a railroad worker's state-law design-defect and failure-to-warn claims over asbestos exposure from locomotive parts fell within the field of locomotive-equipment regulation preempted by the Locomotive Inspection Act.
The court held that when evaluating motions to substitute counsel in capital cases, courts should employ the same "interests of justice" standard that applies in non-capital cases.
Created a small exception to a previous ruling, Coleman v. Thompson.
The court held that suits under the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993's self-care provision are barred by sovereign immunity.

The court held that an employee is "newly awarded compensation" when they first become disabled and thereby become statutorily entitled to benefits, no matter whether, or when, a compensation order issues on their behalf.

Unanimously held that claims directed to a method of giving a drug to a patient, measuring metabolites of that drug, and with a known threshold for efficacy in mind, deciding whether to increase or decrease the dosage of the drug, were not patent-eligible subject matter.
The court ruled in an 8-0 unanimous opinion that the limitation period was subject to traditional equitable tolling.
The Court held that a dispute about passport regulation was not a political question and thus resolvable by the US court system.

The Court ruled that when a lawyer's ineffective assistance leads to the rejection of a plea agreement, a defendant is entitled to relief if the outcome of the plea process would have been different with competent advice.
The United States Supreme Court ruled that attorneys of criminal defendants have the duty to communicate plea bargains offered to the accused.
The Court ruled that, because the Environmental Protection Agency's orders constitute "final agency action" under the Administrative Procedure Act, federal courts may hear appeals from its orders.
The court held that a federal district court has discretion to order that a defendant's federal sentence run consecutively to an anticipated state sentence that has not yet been imposed.

The Court held that the enforcement of a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 was applied retroactively to Panagis Vartelas and was thus unconstitutional.
The Court held that "actual damages" under the Privacy Act of 1974 is not clear enough to allow damages for suits for mental and emotional distress.
The court held that a witness in a grand-jury proceeding is entitled to the same absolute immunity from suit under Section 1983 as a witness who testifies at trial.

The court held that officials may strip-search people who have been arrested for any crime before admitting the people to jail, even if there is no reason to suspect that the person is carrying contraband.

The court held that a generic manufacturer may employ the counterclaim provision of the Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act of 1984 to force correction of a use code that inaccurately describes the brand's patent as covering a particular method of using a drug.
The Court held that a private contractor temporarily retained by the government to carry out its work is entitled to seek qualified immunity from suit under Section 1983.
The Court held the Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA), 28 U.S.C. § 1350 note, applies exclusively to natural persons and does not impose liability against any organizational entity.

The Court held that there are no limitations on a plaintiff's ability to introduce new evidence in a §145 proceeding other than those in the Federal Rules of Evidence and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
The court held that a court abuses its discretion if it raises a timeliness objection on its own after the State deliberately waived a statute of limitations defense.

The court held that overstating the value of property sold in order to understate the profit made from the sale does not trigger the extended statute of limitations for the IRS to challenge the seller's tax forms.

The court held that the federal income tax liability resulting from a post-petition farm sale is not "incurred by the estate" under §503(b) of the Bankruptcy Code and thus is neither collectible nor dischargeable in a Chapter 12 bankruptcy plan.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that children conceived after a parent's death are not entitled to Social Security Survivors benefits if the laws in the state that the parent's will was signed in forbid it.
The court held that a person who wins their case and is awarded legal costs cannot be awarded costs for document translation under the Court Interpreters Act.

The Court held that the Board of Immigration Appeals permissibly construed the statute in requiring a non-citizen seeking cancellation of a deportation order to individually satisfy lawful permanent resident requirements, rather than relying on a parent's years of status.

The Supreme Court held that the Double Jeopardy Clause does not bar retrial of counts that a jury had previously unanimously voted to acquit on, when a mistrial is declared after the jury deadlocked on a lesser included offense.
The court held that to establish a violation of 12 U.S.C. § 2607(b), a plaintiff must demonstrate that a charge for settlement services was divided between two or more persons.
The court held that a Chapter 11 cramdown plan may not be confirmed if it provides for the sale of collateral free and clear of a bank's lien but does not permit the bank to credit-bid at the sale.

The court held that police officers are entitled to qualified immunity from civil suit for allegedly violating a constitutional right if, at the time of an arrest, it was not clearly established that an arrest supported by probable cause could give rise to the alleged rights violation.

The court held that declining to refund people who had paid a lump sum instead of installments into a city program was rationally related to lowering administrative costs, so it did not violate the Equal Protection Clause.
The Court ruled that the Civil Service Reform Act of 1978 (CSRA) gives exclusive jurisdiction for claims under the Act to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
The court held that the United States waived sovereign immunity from the Native American nation's action under the Quiet Title Act.

The Court held that the United States government, when it enters into a contract with a Native American Indian tribe for services, must pay contracts in full, even if Congress has not appropriated enough money to pay all tribal contractors.
The Court held that pharmaceutical sales representatives were not eligible for overtime pay.

It was ruled that having an expert witness testify on behalf of a third-party lab analyst does not violate the Sixth Amendment's Confrontation Clause as long as the results were not directed to prove guilt.
The Court extended the Apprendi rule, that certain non-conviction elements of a crime must be proved to a jury, to criminal penalties.

The United States Supreme Court held in a 7–2 decision that Dianne Knox and other non-members of the Service Employees International Union did not receive the required notice of a $12 million assessment the union charged them to raise money for the union's political fund.

The Court held that reduced mandatory minimum sentences for "crack cocaine" under the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010 does apply to defendants who committed a crime before the Act went into effect but who were sentenced after that date.
The Supreme Court excused the broadcasters from paying fines levied for what the FCC had determined indecency, in a majority opinion delivered by Justice Anthony Kennedy.
The Court held that mandatory sentences of life imprisonment without the possibility of parole are unconstitutional for juvenile offenders.

The Court ruled that sections 3, 5(C), and 6 of S. B. 1070 were preempted by federal law but left other parts of the law intact, including a provision that allowed law enforcement to investigate a person's immigration status.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled that the Stolen Valor Act of 2005 was unconstitutional.

The Court upheld Congress's power to enact most provisions of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), commonly called Obamacare, and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 (HCERA), including a requirement for most Americans to pay a penalty for forgoing health insurance by 2014.

The Court held that it was possible for government-induced, temporary flooding to constitute a "taking" of property under the Fifth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, such that compensation could be owed to the owner of the flooded property.

The Court held that the Little Tucker Act, which provides jurisdiction to federal courts for certain claims brought against the federal government, does not apply to lawsuits brought under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA).

In a dispute over where "mixed case" appeals involving wrongful termination and discrimination claims go from the Merit Systems Protection Board, the Court unanimously held that the statute clearly provided for appeal to a federal district court.

The court held that an unconditional and irrevocable commitment not to enforce a trademark against the defendant in an action moots that action over the defendant's objection that the trademark is invalid.

The Court unanimously reversed and remanded the Ninth Circuit, holding that water flowing from an improved portion of a navigable waterway into an unimproved portion of it is not a "discharge of a pollutant" under the Clean Water Act.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that a defendant on death row did not need to be held competent during federal habeas corpus proceedings.
The Court held that a vessel in admiralty law is something that a reasonable observer would consider designed for water transportation.
The court held that the 180-day statute of limitations for a hospital to appeal a final Medicare reimbursement is not jurisdictional, but it is also not subject to equitable tolling.
The Court held the appeal of a district court's decision to return a child to his country of residence is not precluded by the child's departure from the United States.
A 6–3 decision reversed the weapons conviction of a Long Island man who had been detained when police followed his vehicle after he left his apartment just before it was to be searched.

The court held that state-action immunity does not apply when the state has not clearly articulated and affirmatively expressed that its plan to enter the market will substantially lessen competition.

The Court, addressing whether a drug-detection dog's training or certification suffices to establish probable cause for a vehicle search, unanimously held that certification by a bona fide organization after reliability testing in a controlled setting supports such reliability.

The Court held regardless of whether a legal question was settled or unsettled at the time of trial, an error is "plain" within the meaning of Rule 52(b) of Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure so long as the error was plain at the time of appellate review.

The Court held that under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act, when a state court rejects some of a defendant's claims but does not expressly address a federal claim, a federal habeas court must presume, subject to rebuttal, that the claim was adjudicated on the merits.

The Court held that if a person accused of a crime receives a directed acquittal, the Double Jeopardy Clause bars a second trial of that person for the same crime, even if the person was acquitted in error.

The Court determined that the ruling in Padilla v. Commonwealth of Kentucky could not be applied retroactively, because the Padilla case applied a new rule to the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The court held that the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act did not modify Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1).

The Court held that Amnesty International USA and others lacked standing to challenge section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (50 U.S.C. § 1881a), as amended by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 Amendments Act of 2008.
The Court ruled that the statute of limitations for filing civil penalty actions initiates when the offending act is committed or finished.
The court held that proof of materiality is not a prerequisite to certification of a securities-fraud class action.

The court held that the Gonzalez Act abrogates the Federal Tort Claims Act's intentional tort exception and therefore permits a suit against the United States alleging medical battery by a Navy doctor acting within the scope of his employment.
The Court held, 6–3, that the first-sale doctrine exhausts copyright of the works lawfully made or purchased abroad.
The court held that a class-action plaintiff cannot defeat federal court jurisdiction by stipulating that they will not seek damages above the amount-in-controversy requirement.

The Court held that a Clean Water Act provision governing challenges to EPA actions did not bar a citizen suit against an alleged violator seeking to enforce CWA obligations, and that the case was not moot despite interim regulations.
The court held that the federal Medicaid statute's anti-lien provision preempts a state's irrebuttable statutory presumption that one-third of a tort recovery is attributable to medical expenses.

In a unanimous ruling, the United States Supreme Court decided that federal laws granting exclusive jurisdiction to cases involving patents does not preclude the ability of state courts to hear cases related to but not involving patents.

The Court ruled that police use of a trained detection dog to sniff for narcotics on the front porch of a private home is a "search" within the meaning of the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution, and therefore, without consent, requires both probable cause and a search warrant.
The court held that courts certifying classes must thoroughly vet prospective classes for all four requirements even if the court's analysis touches on the merits of the claim.
The Court holds that the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) waives the sovereign immunity of the United States for certain intentional torts committed by law enforcement officers.

The court held that, because the respondent had no personal interest in representing putative, unnamed claimants nor any other continuing interest that would preserve her suit from mootness, her suit was appropriately dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
The court held that when someone seeks equitable relief to enforce an ERISA plan, the terms of the plans govern but equitable doctrines can fill gaps in the terms.
The court found that the presumption against extraterritoriality applies to claims under the Alien Tort Statute (ATS).

The United States Supreme Court ruled that police must generally obtain a warrant before subjecting a drunken-driving suspect to a blood test, and that the natural metabolism of blood alcohol does not establish a per se exigency that would justify a blood draw without consent.
The court ruled in a 7–2 decision that "social sharing of a small amount of marijuana" by a legal immigrant does not constitute aggravated felony and so does not require mandatory deportation.
The Court upheld Virginia's and all states' right to restrict citizen requests for state government documents to citizens of that state.
The Court held that federal laws deregulating the transportation industry do not invalidate corresponding state provisions that regulate the seizure, storage, and sale of cars by towing companies.

The court held that the term "defalcation" in the Bankruptcy Code includes a scienter requirement involving knowledge of, or gross recklessness in respect to, the improper nature of the fiduciary behavior.

The Court unanimously affirmed the decision of the Federal Circuit that the patent exhaustion doctrine does not permit a farmer to plant and grow saved, patented seeds without the patent owner's permission.

The court held that courts must apply the Chevron framework to an agency's interpretation of a statutory ambiguity that concerns the scope of the agency's statutory authority (i.e., its jurisdiction).
The court held that a foreign tax is creditable against United States income taxes when the tax would be an income, war profits, or excess profits tax if it had been enacted in the United States.
The court held that the Michigan Court of Appeals' rejection of a due-process habeas claim was not an unreasonable application of the Supreme Court's criminal retroactivity case law.
The court held that an untimely National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act petition may qualify for an award of attorney's fees if it is filed in good faith and there is a reasonable basis for its claim.
The Court held that judges may review new evidence of actual innocence presented after AEDPA's one-year statute of limitations.

The Court held that, because Texas procedures did not afford a meaningful opportunity to raise ineffective assistance of counsel claims on direct appeal, such claims first raised in a federal habeas petition were not barred by procedural default.
The Court held that a buccal swab to harvest an arrestee's DNA is comparable to fingerprinting and, therefore, a legal police booking procedure that is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment.
The court unanimously ruled that a Virginia statute revoking beneficiary status for spouses whose marital status has changed was pre-empted by the Federal Employees’ Group Life Insurance Act (1954).

In a dispute over a rule requiring farmers to keep part of their raisin crops off the market, the Court held that the farmer had standing to sue under the Takings Clause and that the National Raisin Reserve violated the Takings Clause.

The Court held that the Ex Post Facto Clause is violated when a defendant is sentenced under a later version of the Federal Sentencing Guidelines that provides a higher sentencing range than the version in place at the time of the offense.

The court held that, under the limited judicial review allowed for decisions from binding arbitration, the sole question is whether the arbitrator arguably interpreted the parties' contract, not whether the arbitrator erred.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that certain regulations imposed by City of Los Angeles on trucking companies were preempted by federal law.
The Court held that Oklahoma statutes forbidding the export of water from the state are not preempted or forbidden by the Red River Compact.

The Court held that, when a federal judge participates in the plea process in violation of Rule 11(c) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, a guilty plea need not be vacated if the record shows prejudice to the decision to plea due to Rule 11(h).
The Court decided that "a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated."
The Court held that the FTC could make an antitrust challenge under the rule of reason against a so-called pay-for-delay agreement, also referred to as a reverse payment patent settlement.

The Court decided that, in line with Apprendi v. New Jersey (2000), all facts that increase a mandatory minimum sentence for a criminal offense must be submitted to and found true by a jury, not merely determined to be true at a judge's discretion.
The Court held that an attorney's solicitation of clients is not a permissible purpose covered by the "litigation exception" to the federal Driver's Privacy Protection Act.
In a 7–2 decision, the Supreme Court held that Arizona's registration requirements were unlawful because they were preempted by federal voting laws.
The Court ruled that conditions imposed on recipients of certain federal grants restricted freedom of speech and violated the First Amendment.

In a case about evaluating prior offenses under the Armed Career Criminal Act, the Court held that judges may only look at a crime's statutory elements, not the underlying facts, when the conviction crime has a single, indivisible set of elements.
The Court's ruling in Fisher took Grutter and Bakke as given and did not directly revisit the constitutionality of using race as a factor in college admissions.

The Court held that generic drug manufactures cannot be held liable under state law for not adequately labeling medication when federal law prohibits them from changing the label from the original brand name drug.
