The Supreme Court upheld the Seventh Circuit's decision in a 5–4 opinion written by Samuel Alito, rejecting the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's interpretation of who counts as a supervisor.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Sex Offender Notification and Registration Act (SORNA) was constitutional under the Necessary and Proper Clause.

The Court held that while Title VII applies a mixed motive discrimination framework to claims of discrimination on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, or national origin (see 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2), that framework did not apply to claims of retaliation under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-3.

In a challenge to provisions of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the Court ruled that the Section 4(b) coverage formula was unconstitutional because it relied on data over 40 years old, though it did not strike down Section 5.

In a dispute over conditions on development permits, the Court held that land-use agencies must meet the nexus and rough proportionality standards even when the condition is a payment of money or the permit is denied for refusing the condition.
The Court held that several sections of the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) do not apply to Native American biological fathers who are not custodians of a Native American child.

In a challenge to California's ballot initiative banning same-sex marriage, the Court held that the initiative's official sponsors lacked Article III standing to appeal an adverse federal court ruling.

The Court held that Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which denied federal recognition of same-sex marriages, was a violation of the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court held that when a state court makes a factual determination the federal courts must defer to its judgment so long as it is reasonable.
The court held unanimously that a district court has jurisdiction in the application of the Internal Revenues Service Code to a partnership-level proceeding when it is applied to that partnership.
A unanimous Court held that federal court abstention under the Younger v. Harris doctrine is not in order simply because a pending state-court proceeding involves the same subject matter.
A unanimous Court held that the Fifth Amendment does not prevent the prosecution from introducing psychiatric evidence to rebut psychiatric evidence presented by the defense.

The Court considered when the agreed-upon limitations period for challenging a long-term disability denial began, and unanimously ruled that the period was not too short, no statute prevented it, and courts must enforce it and its start date as written in the plan.

The Court considered whether a U.S. court may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign company because its subsidiary acts for it in the forum state, and held that American courts lacked jurisdiction over claims based on conduct outside the United States.
The Court determined whether a class-action suit was properly removed to federal district court as a mass action under the Class Action Fairness Act.
The court held that any judgment on the merits is a final decision, even if there are outstanding questions about the accounting of a compensatory award or attorney's fees.
The Court held that when a patent licensee seeks a declaration that its products do not infringe the licensed patent, the patentee retains the burden of proving infringement.

In a case about penalty enhancement under the Controlled Substances Act, the Court unanimously held that a defendant cannot be liable for the enhancement unless the drug use was a but-for cause of the death or injury, at least when it was not an independently sufficient cause.

The court held that time spent donning and doffing protective gear is time spent "changing clothes," so the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 allows unions and employers to agree that workers will not be paid for that time.

The court held that, under the Aviation and Transportation Security Act, airlines and their employees are immune from civil liability for reporting suspicious behavior so long as the reporting statements are "materially true."

The court held that a criminal defendant who has been indicted is not constitutionally entitled to contest a grand jury's determination of probable cause to believe the defendant committed the crimes charged when challenging the legality of a pre-trial asset seizure.
The Court held that when an objecting co-resident is removed for objectively reasonable purposes, such as a lawful arrest, the remaining resident may validly consent to a search of the dwelling.

The court held that for a state to exercise personal jurisdiction over a defendant, its relationship with the defendant must arise out of contacts that the defendant created with the forum; the plaintiff cannot be the only link between the defendant and the forum.
The court held that the Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act does not preclude civil class actions under state law.

The Court held that, in deciding whether someone trespassed after being ordered to leave by a commanding officer, a "military installation" covers the commander's entire area of responsibility, including base areas the public may visit through easements.
The court held that the Sarbanes–Oxley Act grants whistleblower protection to employees of public companies and also to employees of a public company's private contractors and subcontractors.

The court held that the one-year period in which the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction provides a parent with an automatic return remedy cannot be equitably tolled.

The court held that a court of the United States that is reviewing an arbitration award made under a treaty should interpret and apply "threshold" provisions concerning arbitration using the framework developed for interpreting similar provisions in ordinary contracts.
The court held that convicting someone for aiding and abetting requires the prosecution to prove conduct extending to some part of the crime and intent extending to the whole crime.
The Court held that a railroad right-of-way granted under the General Railroad Right-of-Way Act of 1875 is an easement.
The Court unanimously affirmed the Sixth Circuit's ruling that a toner cartridge component maker had standing under the Lanham Act to sue printer company Lexmark for false advertising.
The court held that severance payments to employees who are involuntarily terminated during a Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceeding are taxable wages under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act.

In a case about a federal statute barring firearm possession by those convicted of a "misdemeanor crime of domestic violence," the Court held that the underlying conviction need not involve violent force, only force sufficient for common-law battery.

The Court held unconstitutional a provision of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 that limited the total contributions an individual could make over a two-year period to all national party and federal candidate committees.

The court held that the Airline Deregulation Act of 1978 preempts a state-law claim for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing if it seeks to enlarge the contractual obligations that the parties voluntarily adopt.
In a 6-2 decision, the court held that the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause does not prevent states from enacting bans on affirmative action in education.

The Court held that a 911 call reporting a recklessly driving pickup truck was reliable, and that officers did not need to personally observe criminal activity before conducting a traffic stop based on it.

The Court held that rejecting the requested jury instruction was not objectively unreasonable or contrary to clearly established law, so the defendant did not meet the requirements for habeas relief under AEDPA.

The United States Supreme Court ruled that to recover restitution under 18 U.S.C. § 2259, the government or the victim must establish a causal relationship between the defendant's conduct and the victim's harm or damages.

The court held that the Clean Air Act does not require that states be given a second opportunity to file a state implementation plan after the Environmental Protection Agency has quantified interstate pollution obligations under a reasonable interpretation of the Good Neighbor Provision.
The Court decided that the Town of Greece, New York may permit volunteer chaplains to open each legislative session with a prayer.
The United States Supreme Court held in a unanimous decision that restitution in cases involving mortgage fraud is determined by the actual money lent not the value of the property.
The Court held 6-3 that the equitable defense of laches is not available to copyright defendants in claims for damages.

The Court held that a bright-line IQ threshold requirement for determining whether someone has an intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation) is unconstitutional in deciding whether they are eligible for the death penalty.
The Court held that secret service officers who moved protesters away from the president were protected by qualified immunity.
In a 5–4 decision, the Court held that the State of Michigan's suit against Bay Mills is barred by tribal immunity.

The Court held that it had jurisdiction and that police officers who fired shots at a driver during a high-speed car chase did not violate the Fourth Amendment's prohibition on unreasonable searches and seizures.

The Court, addressing the requirement that a patent particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention, held unanimously that a patent fails it when its claims fail to inform those skilled in the art about the invention's scope with reasonable certainty.
The Court found that a woman's attack on her friend using dangerous toxicants was not use of a chemical weapon under section 229(a)(1) of the Chemical Weapons Convention Implementation Act.

The Court held that north Carolina’s statute of repose is not preempted by the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, which instead only preempts state statutes of limitations on bringing state-law environmental tort cases.

The Court held that, under Stern v. Marshall, when a bankruptcy court does not have subject matter jurisdiction over a proceeding, the bankruptcy court may still hear the case and issue proposed findings to be reviewed de novo by a federal district court.

The court held that lawful residents in the United States who turned twenty-one while their visa applications were being processed could not retain their original application date after "aging out" of eligibility for child-visas.
The Court held that a statutory private right of action under the Lanham Act is not precluded by regulatory provisions of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.

The Court held that funds held in inherited Individual Retirement Accounts are not "retirement funds" within the meaning of 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(c) and therefore not exempt from the bankruptcy estate.
The Court found that Argentina, after defaulting on its debt and losing a federal collection action, had no foreign sovereign immunity shielding its foreign assets from discovery.
The Court found that making arrangements for a straw purchase of a gun is in violation of the Gun Control Act of 1968, and is different from re-selling or gifting a previously purchased gun.
In a case about the EPA's regulation of air pollution under the Clean Air Act, the Court, in a divided decision, largely upheld the EPA's ability to regulate greenhouse emissions.

The Court held that a conviction of the crime of knowingly executing a scheme to obtain property owned by, or under the custody of, a bank "by means of false or fraudulent pretenses," does not require the government to prove that a defendant intended to defraud a financial institution.
The court ruled that the warrantless search and seizure of the digital contents of a cell phone during an arrest is unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment.

The court found Employee stockownership (ESOP) fiduciaries have the same prudential duties as non-ESOP fiduciaries, as set by ERISA, except that they are not required to diversify their investments beyond shares of the employer's stock.
The Court ruled that the service provided by Aereo, which allowed subscribers to view live and time-shifted streams of over-the-air television on Internet-connected devices, violated copyright laws.
The Court unanimously held that the law violated the First Amendment to the United States Constitution, as applied to Massachusetts through the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Court unanimously ruled that the president of the United States cannot use their authority under the Recess Appointment Clause of the United States Constitution to appoint public officials unless the United States Senate is in recess and not able to transact Senate business.

The Court ruled that privately held for-profit corporations with religious objections could be exempt from the contraceptive mandate under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, and struck down the mandate as applied to such companies.
The Court allowed a union security agreement.

The Court held that a taxpayer who wants to question Internal Revenue Service agents about their motives for issuing a summons may do so if they can point to "specific facts or circumstances plausibly raising an inference of bad faith."
The Court delivered its ruling on December 15, 2014.

The Court unanimously ruled that an Arkansas prison policy which prohibited a Muslim prisoner from growing a short beard in accordance with his religious beliefs violated the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA).

In a dispute over removing a class action over oil and gas lease revenue from Kansas state court to federal court, the Court held that a notice of removal did not need to include evidence of the amount in controversy.
The Court delivered their ruling on December 9, 2014.
The Court delivered its ruling on December 9, 2014.
The court held that, when a state knowingly fails to comply with an interstate compact, the Supreme Court may order that state to disgorge its profits from the violation or pay damages.

The Supreme Court held that a state occupational licensing board that was primarily composed of persons active in the market it regulates has immunity from antitrust law only when it is actively supervised by the state.

The Court held that, when reviewing a district court's resolution of subsidiary factual matters made in the course of its construction of a patent claim, the Federal Circuit must apply a "clear error," not a de novo, standard of review.

In a federal habeas proceeding, the Court held that a criminal defendant may defend the district court's judgment on alternative grounds without a cross-appeal or certificate of appealability, unless doing so would enlarge the defendant's rights under the judgment.

The Court held that the president, as head of the executive branch, has exclusive power to recognize formally a foreign sovereign and its territorial boundaries; as such, Congress may not require the State Department to indicate in passports that Jerusalem is part of Israel.
The court held that, under the Securities Act of 1933, the issuer of a security is not liable for a statement of opinion simply because the stated opinion ultimately proves incorrect.

The court held that a whistleblower disclosure that is specifically prohibited by a rule or regulation is permitted because the disclosure is not "specifically prohibited by law" within the meaning of the statute protecting whistleblowers.
The Court held that the Truth in Lending Act does not require borrowers to file a lawsuit to rescind loans and that sending written notice is sufficient to effectuate rescission.
The Court ruled the Residual Clause of the Armed Career Criminal Act was unconstitutionally vague and in violation of due process.
The Court overturned a federal district court decision that had upheld Alabama's 2012 redrawing of its electoral districts.
The court held that the interpretation of collective-bargaining agreements must follow ordinary contract principles when that interpretation does not conflict with federal labor policy.
The Court ruled that railroads like CSX can compare their tax treatment to competing transportation companies under federal law.

The Court held that a state income-tax scheme taxing residents on in-state and out-of-state income violated the Dormant Commerce Clause when it did not give residents full credit for income taxes paid to other states.

The Court held that the D.C. Circuit's Paralyzed Veterans doctrine is contrary to a clear reading of the Administrative Procedure Act and "improperly imposes on agencies an obligation beyond the Act's maximum procedural requirements."
The court held that Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) adjudications of trademark infringement can preclude issues for district courts.

The court held that the forced accompaniment statute described under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(e) is not limited to cases where the victim was forced to accompany the robber (or attempted robber) over a "substantial" distance.

In a case on disparate treatment claims under the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, the Court held that a pregnant employee must show the employer refused accommodations but later provided them to other employees with similar restrictions, and remanded.
The court held that whether two trademarks may be tacked for purposes of determining priority is a question for the jury.

The Court held that a lawsuit by the Direct Marketing Association trade group about a Colorado law regarding reporting the state's tax requirements to customers and to the Colorado Department of Revenue is not barred by the Tax Injunction Act.
The Court held "for purposes of determining the validity of the metrics and standards, Amtrak is a governmental entity."

The court held that when multiple claims are consolidated into one proceeding, the dismissal of one of the claims is a final decision that may be appealed without waiting for final decisions on all claims.
The court held that the statutes of limitations within the Federal Tort Claims Act are subject to equitable tolling because they have not been expressly tagged by Congress as jurisdictional.
In a unanimous opinion written by Associate Justice Samuel Alito, the Court held that Wartime Suspension of Limitations Act only applies to criminal offenses.

The Court reversed the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit on the matter of whether Tunisian national Moones Mellouli should be deported after being convicted for driving under the influence.

The Court held that a town's sign ordinance, which put stricter limits on signs advertising religious services than on political or ideological signs, imposed content-based restrictions that did not survive strict scrutiny.
The court held that bankruptcy courts may adjudicate Stern claims with the parties' knowing and voluntary consent.
The court held that the Supremacy Clause does not confer a private right of action.

The Court held that disparate impact claims are cognizable under the Fair Housing Act, because Congress intended to include them, but that a plaintiff must prove the defendant's policies cause the disparity.
In a 6–3 opinion, the Court held that officers may not extend the length of a traffic stop to conduct a dog sniff unrelated to the original purpose of the stop.

The Court held a court-ordered transfer of a felon's lawfully owned firearms from government custody to a third party is not barred by §922(g) if the court is satisfied that the recipient will not give the felon control over the firearms, so that he could either use them or direct their use.

The Court held that because a fiduciary has a continuing duty to monitor investments and remove imprudent ones, a plaintiff may claim a breach of the duty of prudence, and the claim is timely if filed within six years of the alleged breach.
The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 8–1 in Elauf's favor on June 1, 2015.
The Court held that Section 330(a)(1) of the Bankruptcy Code does not permit bankruptcy courts to award attorney's fees for work performed while defending fee applications.
The Court upheld the right of Arizona voters to remove the authority to draw election districts from the Arizona State Legislature and vest it in an independent redistricting commission.
The Court narrowed the standard set in Crawford v. Washington for determining whether hearsay statements in criminal cases are permitted under the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment.

The Court held that a Los Angeles law, Municipal Code § 41.49, requiring hotel operators to retain records about guests for a 90-day period, is facially unconstitutional under the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution because it does not allow for pre-compliance review.
The United States Supreme Court upheld a death sentence of a Hispanic defendant despite the fact that all Blacks and Hispanics were rejected from the jury during the defendant's trial.

In a dispute over Affordable Care Act provisions, the Court upheld the payment of premium tax credits to qualifying persons in all states, including those with exchanges established by the Department of Health and Human Services rather than by a state.

The court held that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission can submit a sworn affidavit to show that it has completed the required conciliation process before suing for employment discrimination.

The court held that the Natural Gas Act does not preempt state-law antitrust claims against entities controlling natural-gas pipelines because the act does not occupy the field of controlling retail prices and curbing other unfair business practices.

The Court held that the First Amendment did not prohibit states from barring judges and judicial candidates from personally soliciting campaign funds, because the restriction was narrowly tailored to serve the compelling interest of keeping the judiciary impartial.

The court held that the Telecommunications Act of 1996 requires a locality that denies an application to build cell-phone tower to state its reasons for denial with sufficient clarity in a written record issued essentially contemporaneously with the denial.
The Court held that license plates are government speech and are consequently more easily regulated/subjected to content restrictions than private speech under the First Amendment.

The court held that police officers who entered the home of a mentally-ill woman and shot her were entitled to qualified immunity because there was no clearly established law requiring them to accommodate mental illness.
In a bankruptcy case, the Court held that a Chapter 7 debtor could not void a junior mortgage under 11 U.S.C. § 506(d) when the senior mortgage debt exceeded the property's current market value.

The Court held that the EPA must consider costs, and that it interpreted the Clean Air Act unreasonably when it decided it did not need to consider costs in finding that regulation was "necessary and appropriate."
The Court held that because Brumfield satisfied 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d)(2)’s requirements, he was entitled to have his Atkins v. Virginia claim considered on the merits in federal court.

The Court, in a case on the standard for induced patent infringement, held that induced infringement requires showing the defendant knew it was engaging in infringing conduct, and that a belief that the patent is invalid is not a defense.
The Court unanimously held that a debtor who earns money after filing Chapter 13 bankruptcy and converts to Chapter 7 before the money is sent to creditors is permitted to keep those funds.
The court held that an order from a bankruptcy court denying a debtor's confirmation of a proposed repayment cannot be immediately appealed, as it is not a final order.

The Court held that section 841 of the Controlled Substances Act requires the government to prove that to be in criminal violation, a defendant must be aware that an analogue defined by the Controlled Substance Analogue Enforcement Act with which he was dealing was a controlled substance.

The Court held in a 5–4 decision that a pretrial detainee must prove only that force used by police is excessive according to an objective standard, not that a police officer was subjectively aware that the force used was unreasonable.

In a dispute over a rule requiring farmers to keep part of their raisin crops off the market, the Court held that the farmer had standing to sue under the Takings Clause and that the National Raisin Reserve violated the Takings Clause.

The Court ruled that the fundamental right to marry is guaranteed to same-sex couples by both the Due Process Clause and the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Court held, 5–4, that lethal injections using midazolam to kill prisoners convicted of capital crimes do not constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution.
The Court ruled that the federal courts of appeals have jurisdiction to review the orders of the Board of Immigration Appeals to reject motions to reopen.
The Court held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act barred a California resident from bringing suit against an Austrian railroad in federal district court.

The Court held that a conspiracy to violate the Hobbs Act can occur when an individual obtains property from another conspirator, in a case involving a police officer in a kickback scheme with an auto repair shop.
In a 6–3 opinion written by Justice Stephen Breyer, the Court reversed a decision by the California Court of Appeal that refused to enforce an arbitration agreement between DIRECTV and its customers.

In a case on sentencing procedures in capital cases, the Court held that judges need not affirmatively instruct juries on the burden of proof for mitigating evidence, and that joint trials of capital defendants are often preferable.

The Court held that its previous ruling in Miller v. Alabama (2012), that a mandatory life sentence without parole should not apply to persons convicted of murder committed as juveniles, should be applied retroactively.

The Court, in an 8–1 ruling, applied the rule of Ring v. Arizona to the Florida capital sentencing scheme, holding that the Sixth Amendment requires a jury to find the aggravating factors necessary for imposing the death penalty.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission had the authority to regulate demand response transactions.

The Court vacated and remanded a ruling by United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on the basis that the Ninth Circuit had not properly determined whether the plaintiff has suffered an "injury-in-fact" when analyzing whether he had standing to bring his case in federal court.
The Court held that the state law doctrine of res judicata does not preclude a Batson challenge against peremptory challenges if new evidence has emerged.

The Court interpreted a federal statute imposing a 10-year minimum sentence for child pornography possession after certain prior state convictions, holding that "involving a minor or ward" modifies only the last item in the series, and upheld the sentence.
The Court decided the interpretation of section 1101(a)(43) of the federal Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which includes "aggravated felony" as a possible reason for deporting a non-citizen.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Antonin Scalia, the Court ruled that federal district courts are required to refer cases to a three-judge panel when plaintiffs challenge the constitutionality of the apportionment of congressional districts.

The Court held that healthcare plan fiduciaries cannot demand reimbursement for medical benefits from a plan member's general assets if the beneficiary's general assets cannot be traced back to the original payment from the fiduciary.

The Court held that the Department of Veterans Affairs must apply the "Rule of Two" when considering and awarding contracts under the Veterans Benefits, Health Care, and Information Technology Act of 2006.
The Court affirmed the decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, which held that representative evidence could be used to support the claims of the class.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that the Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution prohibits the pre-trial restraint of assets needed to retain a defendant's counsel of choice when those assets have not been used in conjunction with criminal activity.

The Court unanimously held that when reviewing a claim of insufficient evidence for a criminal offense, an appellate court should assess the elements of the alleged crime rather than the elements described in the jury instructions.
The Court held that when filing a workplace discrimination complaint under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the filing period begins only after an employee resigns.
The Court held, 8–0, that the jurisdictional test established by §27 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 is the same as 28 U.S.C. § 1331's test for deciding if a case "arises under" a federal law.

In a case about when litigants may receive equitable tolling of a statute of limitations, the Court unanimously held the plaintiff was not entitled to tolling because it did not show "extraordinary circumstances" prevented timely filing.

The Court held that a Vermont state law requiring the disclosure of certain information relating to health care services was preempted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA) to the extent that the state law applied to ERISA plans.

In a dispute over whether a tribal court could hear a civil case against a non-Indian operating a Dollar General store on tribal land, the Court was equally divided and thereby affirmed the Fifth Circuit's holding that the tribal court had jurisdiction.

The Court held that the Nevada rule that does not extend the same immunities to agencies of other states as it does to its own is effectively a "policy of hostility", which is unconstitutional under the Full Faith and Credit Clause.

The Court held that the one person, one vote principle under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment allows a state's redistricting commission slight variances in drawing of legislative districts provided that the variance does not exceed 10 percent.

The Court held that the one person, one vote principle under the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment allows states to use total population, not just total voting-eligible population, to draw legislative districts.
The Court held that the Fifth Circuit had correctly found that the University of Texas at Austin's race-conscious undergraduate admissions policy survived strict scrutiny.

The Court held that the United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit's reliance on a requirement that defendants show "additional evidence" to show substantial harm arising from incorrect sentencing guidelines is impermissible.

The Court found that a law which only applied to a specific case, identified by docket number, and eliminated all of the defenses one party had raised does not violate the separation of powers in the United States Constitution between the legislative (Congress) and judicial branches of government.

The Court, in a criminal case asking whether Puerto Rico and the federal government are separate sovereigns under the Double Jeopardy Clause, affirmed that the Clause bars both from successively prosecuting the same person for the same conduct under equivalent criminal laws.

In a case about a police detective disciplined for apparently supporting a mayoral challenger, the Court held that a public employee's constitutional rights might be violated when an employer disciplines them over a mistaken belief that they engaged in protected speech.
The Supreme Court of the United States clarified rules for determining whether a federal court may exercise diversity jurisdiction in cases involving unincorporated organizations.
The Court held that Congress's 1882 Act did not diminish the Omaha Indian Reservation.

In disputes over National Park Service authority in Alaska under ANILCA, the Court ruled the Service may regulate only "public" lands, and later unanimously held navigable waters are "non-public" lands exempt from its regulations.
The Court limited the scope of the Fourth Amendment's exclusionary rule.
The Court held that in a federal criminal prosecution under the Hobbs Act, the government is not required to prove an interstate commerce element beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Court held that the two-part Seagate test, used to determine when a district court may increase damages for patent infringement, is not consistent with Section 284 of the Patent Act.
The court held that state regulation of the energy market is preempted if it conflicts with requirements set by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, including rates.
The Court held that the Domestic Violence Offender Gun Ban in U.S. federal law extends to those convicted of reckless domestic violence.
The court held that a prosecutor involved in seeking the death penalty for a defendant should recuse himself if asked to judge an appeal in the capital case.
The Court held that the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act (SORNA) does not require an individual to update his registration after departing a state.

The court held that the term "actual fraud" in the discharge exceptions of Chapter 7 of the Bankruptcy Code encompasses fraudulent conveyance schemes even when those schemes do not involve a false representation.
The Court ruled 5–3 that Texas cannot place restrictions on the delivery of abortion services that create an undue burden for women seeking an abortion.
The Court held that the appellants lacked standing under Article III of the United States Constitution to pursue their appeal.

The Court held that the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act has certain extraterritorial applications, but that plaintiffs must prove injuries within the United States for the Act to apply.
The court held that state officials may still be liable for conduct that the state is immune to under exceptions within the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA).
The Court held that the right to a speedy trial does not guarantee the right to speedy sentencing.

The Court held that the use of the Ohio Attorney General's letterhead, as its direction, was permissible and not a false, deceptive, or misleading representation under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

The Court held that "special circumstances" cannot excuse an inmate's failure to exhaust administrative remedies before filing a lawsuit under the Prison Litigation Reform Act of 1995, but clarified that inmates are required to exhaust only administrative remedies that are genuinely available.
The Court ruled that the decision in Johnson v. United States announced a substantive rule change and is therefore retroactive.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a Clean Water Act jurisdictional determination issued by the United States Army Corps of Engineers is reviewable under the Administrative Procedure Act because jurisdictional determinations constitute "final agency action".

The Court held that Chapters 9 and 11 of the Federal Bankruptcy Code preempted the corresponding sections of Puerto Rico's Public Corporation Debt Enforcement and Recovery Act, because states may not enact municipal bankruptcy laws and Puerto Rico is usually treated as a "state."

In a dispute over whether religious institutions other than churches should be exempt from the ACA contraceptive mandate, the Court vacated the appeals court ruling and the six consolidated cases and sent them back to the courts of appeals for reconsideration.

In a unanimous decision authored by Associate Justice Anthony Kennedy, the Court held that a defendant need not succeed on the merits in order to be the prevailing party for the purposes of seeking attorney fees.
In a challenge to the constitutionality of the Deferred Action for Parents of Americans program, the Court, equally divided, affirmed the lower-court injunction blocking President Obama's program.
The Court held that tribal-court convictions from proceedings that complied with Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 may be used as predicate offenses in subsequent prosecution.

The Court held that the implied false certification theory can be a basis for False Claims Act liability when a claim makes specific representations but fails to disclose noncompliance with material requirements that make them misleading.
The Supreme Court of the United States held that the search incident to arrest doctrine permits law enforcement to conduct warrantless breath tests but not blood tests on suspected drunk drivers.

The Court, in a dispute over whether automotive service advisors were eligible for overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act, reversed the Ninth Circuit's ruling that the exemption did not include service advisors.

The Court held that when deciding whether to award attorney's fees under the Copyright Act's fee-shifting provision, a district court should give substantial weight to the objective reasonableness of the losing party's position while considering all other relevant circumstances.
The Court held that the Patent Office's inter partes review process is constitutional.

The Court held that if a state law defines a crime more broadly than the common understanding of that crime, a conviction under that state law cannot be used as a sentencing enhancement under the federal Armed Career Criminal Act.
The Court held that a federal district court may rescind a discharge order and recall jurors for further service in the same case.
The court held that a defendant wishing to appeal an order imposing restitution in a deferred restitution case must file a notice of appeal from that order.
The Court held that gifts of confidential information without any compensation to relatives for the purposes of insider trading are a violation of securities laws.

The Court held that the Handicapped Children's Protection Act of 1986 did not require exhaustion of IDEA's state-level administrative remedies when the gravamen of the lawsuit was not the denial of a free appropriate public education.

In a dispute between two cheerleading uniform makers, the Court rejected the argument that the designs were uncopyrightable because of their utilitarian purpose and held that the aesthetic elements of the clothing designs could be copyrightable.
The court held that bankruptcy courts may not approve structured dismissals that provide for distributions that do not follow ordinary priority rules without the consent of affected creditors.
The court held that laches is not an appropriate defense against a claim for damages brought within a statute of limitations period.
In a 6–2 decision, the Court affirmed the judgment of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Sonia Sotomayor, the Court held that plaintiffs may file lawsuits against Fannie Mae in any state or federal court that is "already endowed with subject-matter jurisdiction over the suit."

The Court unanimously found that the Immigration and Nationality Act's longer physical presence requirements for unwed fathers than for unwed mothers, for conveying citizenship to a foreign-born child, violated equal protection and due process.

In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the Court held that the government may re-try criminal defendants after a jury returns irreconcilable verdicts when the conviction is later vacated because of a procedural error that is unrelated to the inconsistency.
In a unanimous opinion written by Justice Anthony Kennedy, the Court held that a violation of the False Claim Act's seal requirement does not require the dismissal of a complaint.

The Court considered whether the residual clause in the advisory Sentencing Guidelines was unconstitutionally vague, and it unanimously affirmed the lower court, holding the advisory Guidelines are not subject to vagueness challenges under the Due Process Clause.

In a death penalty case involving intellectual disability, the Court held that contemporary clinical standards determine what counts as an intellectual disability, and that even milder forms may bar a death sentence under the Eighth Amendment.
The Court ruled 5–3 that the North Carolina General Assembly used race too heavily in re-drawing two Congressional districts following the 2010 Census.

The Court, in a case about selling components of patented inventions in foreign markets, held that supplying a single component abroad is not a substantial portion of the components that can give rise to liability under the Patent Act of 1952.
In a 7-1 decision written by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the Court held that a state has no right to keep fines and other money collected based on an invalid conviction.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 8–0 that tribal sovereign immunity does not apply in a suit against a tribal employee in his individual capacity, and an indemnification provision cannot extend tribal sovereign immunity to cases in which it would otherwise not apply.

The Court held that price controls, when used to prohibit the communication of prices of goods with regard to a surcharge, was a regulation of speech and required an analysis of the First Amendment's protections for freedom of speech.

The court held that when a court sanctions bad-faith conduct by ordering a litigant to pay the other side’s legal fees, the award is limited to the fees the innocent party incurred solely because of the bad-faith misconduct.

The Court held that the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act ("IDEA"), required schools to provide students an education that is "reasonably calculated to enable a child to make progress appropriate in light of the child’s circumstances."

The court held that the filing of a bankruptcy proof of claim that is obviously time-barred is not a false, deceptive, misleading, unfair, or unconscionable debt-collection practice within the meaning of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act.

The Court unanimously affirmed the Federal Circuit's judgment that the Lanham Act provisions barring registration of trademarks that may "disparage" persons, institutions, beliefs, or national symbols violated the First Amendment.

The Court determined, by a vote of 4–2, that non-U.S. citizens detained in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks cannot recover monetary damages from high level federal officials for the conditions of their confinement.

The court held that a scheme to defraud customers also deprives the bank of money in which the bank held a "property right"; therefore, criminal defendants may be convicted under the federal bank-fraud statute for schemes to defraud bank customers.
The Court held, in a case over a U.S. Border Patrol agent's shooting of a Mexican teenager across the border, that the Bivens precedent did not extend to claims based on cross-border shootings.

The court held that the FAA preempts any state rule that discriminates on its face against arbitration or that covertly accomplishes the same objective by disfavoring contracts that have the defining features of arbitration agreements.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a North Carolina statute that prohibited registered sex offenders from using social media websites was unconstitutional because it violated the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, which protects freedom of speech.

The Supreme Court of the United States ruled 8–0 that in the context of statutory rape offenses that criminalize sexual intercourse based solely on the ages of the participants, the generic federal definition of "sexual abuse of a minor" requires the age of the victim to be less than 16.

The court held that Section 924(c), which provides mandatory minimum sentences for the use of a firearm during certain crimes, does not prevent a sentencing court from considering a mandatory minimum imposed under that provision when calculating an appropriate sentence for the predicate offense.
The court held that federal laws governing federal employees' health insurance preempt state laws affecting contractual subrogation and reimbursement prescriptions.
The court held that the reviewing court was correct to analyze the lot owners' property as a single unit in assessing the effect of a governmental action challenged as a regulatory taking.

The court held that a state court may not order a veteran to indemnify a divorced spouse for the loss in the divorced spouse's portion of the veteran's retirement pay caused by the veteran's waiver of retirement pay to receive service-related disability benefits.
The Court held that Federal courts of appeals lack jurisdiction to review a denial of class certification after plaintiffs have voluntarily dismissed their claims with prejudice.

In a patent suit over refilled and resold ink cartridges, the Court held that under the exhaustion doctrine a patent holder cannot sue for infringement over further use of an item after selling it, reversing the Federal Circuit.

The Court decided that the Hague Service Convention permits service of judicial process abroad by mail, provided that the country in which the service takes place has not objected to service by mail, and service by mail is authorized in the country where the litigation is pending.
The court held that a plan maintained by a principal-purpose organization qualifies as a "church plan," regardless of who established it.

In a dispute over where patent infringement suits could be brought, the Court unanimously ruled for the petitioner, upholding its 1957 decision that patent infringement cases must be heard in the district where the defendant is incorporated.

The court held that evidence withheld by the prosecution is only Brady material if there is a reasonable probability that the result of the proceeding would have been different, considering the context of the entire record.
The court held that there is no joint and several liability for forfeitures in federal conspiracy judgments when a party did not personally benefit from the crime.
The court held that the proper review forum when the Merit Systems Protection Board dismisses a mixed case on jurisdictional grounds is district court.

The court held that a litigant seeking to intervene as of right under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 24(a)(2) must meet the requirements of Article III standing if the intervenor wishes to pursue relief not requested by a plaintiff.

The court held that, because SEC disgorgement is a punitive measure rather than a compensatory one, any claim for disgorgement in an SEC enforcement action must be commenced within five years of the date the claim accrued.
The Court held that a company is not a "debt collector" under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) if it purchased that debt and then attempts to collect from the debtor.

The Supreme Court of the United States held that a Missouri program that denied a grant to a religious school for playground resurfacing, while providing grants to similarly situated non-religious groups, violated the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The court held that in the context of a public-trial violation during jury selection, where the error is neither preserved nor raised on direct review but is raised later via an ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim, the defendant must demonstrate prejudice to secure a new trial.

The Court held that when the conditions of Ake v. Oklahoma are met, the state must give a defendant access to a mental health expert who is sufficiently available and independent from the prosecution to examine and assist the defense.
The court held that the ineffective assistance of postconviction counsel does not provide cause to excuse the procedural default of ineffective-assistance-of-appellate-counsel claims.

The Court held that California courts lacked personal jurisdiction over the defendant on claims brought by plaintiffs who are not California residents and did not suffer their alleged injury in California.

The Court held that Montana courts lacked personal jurisdiction over a railroad that was neither incorporated nor headquartered in Montana, even though it had over 2,000 miles of track and 2,000 employees there.
The court held that Section 262(l)(2)(A) of the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 is not enforceable by injunction under federal law.
The Court held that the government cannot revoke the citizenship of a naturalized U.S. citizen based on an immaterial false statement made by the citizen in their naturalization application.

The United States Supreme Court reversed the death sentence of the defendant Duane Buck after the defendant's attorney introduced evidence that suggested the defendant would be more likely to commit violent acts in the future because he was black.
The Court held that 18 U.S.C. § 16(b), a statute defining certain "aggravated felonies" for immigration purposes, is unconstitutionally vague.

In a 5–4 decision issued in May 2018, the Court ruled that arbitration agreements requiring individual arbitration and prohibiting class action lawsuits are enforceable under the FAA, regardless of allowances set out within the NLRA.
The Court held that detained immigrants do not have a statutory right to periodic bond hearings.

In a challenge to Wisconsin's redistricting plan as a partisan gerrymander, the Court remanded the case to the lower courts, finding that the plaintiffs had not demonstrated standing because they had not shown harm.
The Court held that police officers had probable cause to arrest those attending a party in Washington, D.C.
The court held that Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(5)(C)'s limitation on extensions of time to file a notice of appeal is a court-made rule and not jurisdictional.
The court held that challenges to the Environmental Protection Agency's Waters of the United States (WOTUS) Rule must be filed in federal district courts.
In a suit alleging a bank facilitated terrorist attacks by transferring funds, the Court held that foreign corporations cannot be sued under the Alien Tort Statute.
The Court held that an ex parte decision by a judge can still be judicial in nature.

The court held that a federal court sitting in a habeas corpus proceeding should "look through" an unexplained, summary ruling to the last related state-court decision that provides a relevant rationale and presume that the unexplained decision adopted the same reasoning.
The court held that clear error is the proper standard for review of a determination that a purchaser was not a non-statutory insider for purposes of approving a cramdown plan of reorganization.
The court held that the limitations period for state claims filed in federal court is suspended while such claims are pending in federal court and for 30 days after dismissal by the federal court.
The court held that the only relevant transfer for purposes of the Bankruptcy Code's Section 546(e) safe harbor is the transfer that the trustee seeks to avoid.
The Court upheld a federal act that barred federal courts from hearing lawsuits involving a particular parcel of land, with a plurality holding that it did not violate Article III.

The Court ruled that Ohio's voter list-maintenance process, which used voter inactivity to trigger a confirmation notice before removal from the rolls, did not violate federal voter registration laws.

The Court held the Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act of 1998 did not strip state courts of jurisdiction to adjudicate class actions alleging only 1933 Securities Act violations; nor did it authorize removing such suits from state to federal court.

The Court, in a case over a bakery's refusal to make a custom wedding cake for a gay couple, ruled that the Commission showed hostility toward the owner's religious objections, violated his free exercise rights, and reversed its decision.

The Court held that government entities violate the Fourth Amendment to the United States Constitution when accessing historical CSLI records containing the physical locations of cellphones without a search warrant.

In a challenge by New Jersey to the federal Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, the Court reversed the lower courts, held that the law violated the anticommandeering principle, and declared the entire law unconstitutional.

The Court unanimously upheld the judgment that ancient Persian artifacts owned by Iran could not be seized by families of bombing victims, ruling that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act exceptions did not apply.

The Court held that the inter partes review process granted by Congress to the United States Patent and Trademark Office for challenging the validity of patents, rather than a jury trial, is constitutional and did not violate either Article III of the Constitution nor the Seventh Amendment.
The Court held the United States Patent and Trademark Office, when conducting an inter partes review, must make judgement on all patent claims contested by the petitioner.
The court held that an incarcerated person who is awarded attorney's fees in connection to their successful civil rights case must contribute up to 25% of their own winnings to paying that award.

The court held that, to convict a defendant under the Internal Revenue Code's Omnibus Clause, the Government must prove the defendant was aware of a pending tax-related proceeding, such as a particular investigation or audit, or could reasonably foresee that such a proceeding would commence.

The Court ruled that "whistleblower" status and associated protections as defined by Sarbanes-Oxley and Dodd-Frank only apply in cases where the whistleblower has reported malfeasance directly to the Securities and Exchange Commission.
In a dispute over water allocation in the ACF River Basin, the Court ruled that the special master had not properly considered Florida's argument and remanded the case to be reheard and reviewed.

The Court considered the question of whether the U.S. federal government had a legal right to join litigation against New Mexico; the Court ruled that the federal government was within its rights when it did so.
The Court held that drivers of rental cars have rights protecting them from unconstitutional searches by police, even if the drivers are not listed on the rental agreement.

The Court held that within consolidated cases under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 42(a), the losing party has the immediate right to appeal when one of the consolidated cases is finally decided, even if other cases remain pending.

The Court determined that it had jurisdiction to rule on appeals from the USCAAF, even though that court was created by Congress via Article I of the United States Constitution and is not an Article III court.

The Court held the Sixth Amendment guarantees a defendant the right to decide that the objective of his defense is to maintain innocence at all costs, even when counsel believes that admitting guilt offers the defendant the best chance to avoid the death penalty.

The Court, in a dispute over whether automotive service advisors were eligible for overtime pay under the Fair Labor Standards Act, reversed the Ninth Circuit's ruling that the exemption did not include service advisors.
The Court ruled that California's FACT Act notices, required of crisis pregnancy centers, likely violated the First Amendment by targeting speakers rather than speech.
The court held that if a criminal defendant consents to sever their case into multiple trials, they waive issue preclusion in the subsequent trials.

The Court ruled that a century-old Minnesota law barring voters from wearing political clothing or items at polling places was overbroad, violated free speech rights under the First Amendment, and was therefore unconstitutional.

In a dispute over credit card anti-steering provisions that barred merchants from steering customers to cards with lower fees, the Court affirmed the Appeals Court's ruling that the provisions did not violate antitrust laws.

The Court ruled that fees collected by labor unions from non-members in the public sector violate the First Amendment right to free speech, overruling its 1977 decision in Abood v. Detroit Board of Education.

The court held that a miscalculation of a Guidelines sentencing range that has been determined to be plain and to affect a defendant's substantial rights calls for a court of appeals to exercise its discretion to vacate the defendant's sentence in the ordinary case.

In a dispute over whether a Stored Communications Act warrant could compel production of emails stored in Ireland, the Court held the case moot after the CLOUD Act and a new warrant, and vacated the Second Circuit's decision.

The United States Supreme Court decided that the mere existence of probable cause for an arrest did not bar the plaintiff's First Amendment retaliatory arrest claim, but deferred consideration of the broader question of when it might.

The court held that because the wiretap orders did not lack any information that the statute required them to include and would have been sufficient absent the superfluous language authorizing interception outside the court's territorial jurisdiction, the orders were not facially insufficient.
The court held that employee stock options are not taxable "compensation" under the Railroad Retirement Tax Act because they are not "money remuneration".

The court held that awarding lost profits over patent-infringing goods assembled outside of the United States with components manufactured in the United States was a permissible domestic application of Section 284 of the Patent Act.

The Court held that states may charge tax on purchases from out-of-state sellers even without a physical presence in the taxing state, overturning its earlier decision that had barred such collection requirements under the Dormant Commerce Clause.

The court held that a debtor's statement about a single asset can be a "statement respecting the debtor’s financial condition" under the Bankruptcy Code's exceptions to discharge; therefore, debt associated with a single-asset statement that is not in writing may be discharged.

The court held that the words "investigation" and "proceedings" in the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 are limited to government investigations and criminal proceedings and do not include private investigations and civil or bankruptcy proceedings.
The U.S. Supreme Court decided whether a Minnesota law violated the Contract Clause of the Constitution of the United States.
The court held that Yakima County v. Yakima Nation did not address the scope of tribal sovereign immunity for in rem lawsuits.

The Court held that there is no analog to class actions under the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, and there is no "capable of repetition yet evading review" exception for mootness where repetition would require the defendant to be charged with a crime in the future.

The Court held that upon denial of class certification, a putative class member may not, in lieu of promptly joining an existing suit or promptly filing an individual action, commence a class action anew beyond the time allowed by the applicable statute of limitations.

The court held that a sentence imposed pursuant to a plea agreement under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(c)(1)(C) is "based on" the defendant's Guidelines range so long as that range was part of the framework the district court relied on in imposing the sentence or accepting the agreement.

The court held that a person who has been sentenced based on a mandatory minimum sentence with a statutory justification for a longer sentence, rather a justification within the Guidelines, is not entitled to sentence reductions under subsequent amendments to the Guidelines.

The Court held that they are considered inferior officers of the United States and so are subject to the Appointments Clause and must be appointed through the President or other delegated officer of the United States, rather than hired.

In an immigration case, the Court reversed the lower court, holding that a Notice to Appear that does not tell a noncitizen when and where to appear for removal proceedings is not valid and does not trigger the stop-time rule.

The court held that when the record as a whole demonstrates the judge had a reasoned basis for his decision, the judge's use of generic boilerplate to explain their choice of a sentence reduction under the Guidelines is adequate.

The court held that the Texas court erred in requiring the state to show that the 2013 Legislature purged the "taint" that the court attributed to the defunct and never-used plans enacted by a prior legislature in 2011.

In a price-fixing suit where a Chinese company claimed Chinese law required its conduct, the Court unanimously reversed the Second Circuit, holding that a foreign government's statements about its law get respectful consideration but not conclusive effect.

The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, ruling that challengers to the presidential travel restriction proclamation were unlikely to succeed on their INA or Establishment Clause claims, and vacated the injunction and remanded.

In a Fourth Amendment search and seizure dispute over a warrantless search of a vehicle parked a few feet from a house, the Court ruled that the automobile exception does not apply to vehicles parked within a home or its curtilage.
The court held that, under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967, state and local governments are covered employers regardless of the number of employees they have.

The Court, in a unanimous decision, vacated the 5th Circuit's ruling that upheld the designation of private land in Louisiana as critical habitat for the dusky gopher frog and sent the case back for further review.

In a dispute over classifying workers hired as contractors under the Federal Arbitration Act's arbitration exceptions, the Court unanimously ruled that the exceptions, such as for interstate commerce workers like truck drivers, apply to contractors as to regular employees.

The court held that state robbery offenses that involve overcoming victim resistance count as "violent felonies" under the definition of that term under the Armed Career Criminal Act of 1984, even when only 'slight force' is required.
The court held that the term "burglary" in the Armed Career Criminal Act includes burglary of a structure or vehicle that has been adapted or is customarily used for overnight accommodation.

The Court held that, in maritime tort cases, a manufacturer has a duty to warn when its product requires incorporation of a part, it knows or has reason to know the integrated product is likely dangerous, and it has no reason to believe users will realize the danger.

In a 5–4 vote, the Court ruled that the government has the power to detain, at any time, immigrants that have committed certain crimes that could lead to their deportation, even if they were not detained by immigration authorities upon release from criminal custody.
In a 5–4 decision, the Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's decision and held that arbitration on a classwide basis could not be compelled based on the provision's ambiguous language.

The Court unanimously held that the "wholly groundless" exception to arbitrability violated the Federal Arbitration Act, so a valid delegation of arbitrability to an arbitrator must be honored even if a court thinks the argument for arbitration is wholly groundless.
The Court held that the Yakama Nation Treaty of 1855 preempts the state law which the State purported to be able to tax fuel purchased by a tribal corporation for sale to tribal members.
The Court held that the presumption of prejudice for Sixth Amendment purposes applies regardless of whether a defendant has waived the right to appeal.
In a class action case about cy pres settlements, the Court remanded to the Ninth Circuit to address the plaintiffs' standing in light of Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins.

The Court ruled that international organizations, such as the International Finance Corporation, could be sued in US federal courts for conduct arising from their commercial activities, sharing the same immunity as foreign governments.
The Court held that Virginia's ban on uranium mining did not conflict with the Atomic Energy Act, and it let the ban stand.

In disputes over National Park Service authority in Alaska under ANILCA, the Court ruled the Service may regulate only "public" lands, and later unanimously held navigable waters are "non-public" lands exempt from its regulations.
The court held that a railroad's payment to an employee for working time lost due to an on-the-job injury is taxable "compensation" under the Railroad Retirement Tax Act.

In a challenge to a state's method of execution under the Eighth Amendment, the Court held that a death-sentenced convict claiming excessive pain must show that alternative methods exist and would clearly cause less pain than the state's method.

The court held that the Social Security Act's 25% cap on awards of attorney's fees applies only to fees for court representation, not to the aggregate fees awarded for representation before the agency and before the court.

The Court held that civil service of a lawsuit against the government of Sudan was invalid because the civil complaints and summons had been sent to the Embassy of Sudan in Washington, D.C. rather than to the Sudanese Foreign Minister in Khartoum.

In a dispute over whether consumers could bring antitrust claims over Apple's App Store practices, the Court ruled that because consumers bought apps directly from Apple, they had standing under Illinois Brick to sue.

The court held that whether a state-law failure-to-warn claim was pre-empted in light of "clear evidence" that the FDA would not have approved a change to a drug's label is a question of law to be decided by a judge.

The court held that a state violates the intergovernmental tax immunity doctrine when it treats retired state employees more favorably than retired federal employees and no significant differences between the two classes justify the differential treatment.

The Court held that Wyoming's statehood did not void the Crow Tribe's right to hunt on "unoccupied lands of the United States" under an 1868 treaty, and that the Bighorn National Forest did not automatically become "occupied" when the forest was created.
The Court unanimously ruled that a copyright infringement suit must wait until the copyright is successfully registered by the United States Copyright Office.

The Court held that someone who disseminated false statements to potential investors with intent to defraud could be held liable under Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act, even without having drafted the statements.
The Court unanimously ruled that the Eighth Amendment's prohibition of excessive fines is incorporated under the Fourteenth Amendment and so applies to state and local governments.

The court held that Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(f), which provides 14 days for seeking permission to appeal a class certification order, is "a nonjurisdictional claim-processing rule" that is not subject to equitable tolling.

The Supreme Court of the United States decided that probable cause should generally defeat a retaliatory arrest claim brought under the First Amendment, unless officers under the circumstances would typically exercise their discretion not to make an arrest.

The court held that a vocational expert's refusal to provide private market-survey data upon the applicant's request does not categorically preclude the testimony from counting as "substantial evidence."

The court held that a commercial sale of a patent to a third party who is required to keep the invention confidential may place the invention "on sale" under Leahy-Smith America Invents Act, meaning the invention qualifies as prior art that invalidates subsequent patents.
The Court determined that unless they consent, states have sovereign immunity from private suits filed against them in the courts of another state.

The court held that a business engaged in only nonjudicial foreclosure proceedings is not a "debt collector" under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, except for the limited purpose of Section 1692f(6).
The Court determined that a third-party defendant to a counterclaim submitted in a state-court civil action cannot remove its case to federal court.

The Court held the Department of Health and Human Services' new policy to retroactively reduce Medicare payments must be vacated due to the department's failure to uphold its notice-and-comment obligations.
The Supreme Court, in a 6–3 decision, ruled that within context of Leahy-Smith, the government does not constitute a "person".

The court held that a Social Security Administration Appeals Council dismissal on timeliness grounds after a claimant has had an administrative law judge hearing on the merits is a final decision subject to judicial review.

In a copyright infringement dispute, the Court held that the Copyright Act's award of "full costs" to a prevailing party was limited to the taxable costs defined by the Fee Act of 1853, rejecting a broader reading covering other litigation expenses.
The court held that a debtor's rejection of an executory contract under Section 365 of the Bankruptcy Code has the same effect as a breach of that contract outside bankruptcy.

The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the five-year mandatory minimum prison sentence for certain sex offenses committed by federal supervised releases under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(k) as unconstitutional unless the charges are proven to a jury beyond a reasonable doubt.
The Court held that a public access station was not considered a state actor for purposes of evaluating free speech issues in a 5–4 ruling split along ideological lines.

The Court reversed the Fourth Circuit, ruling that a World War I memorial in the shape of a Latin cross on government-owned land did not violate the Establishment Clause since it had stood for decades without controversy.
The Court ruled that a term of supervised release is paused, or tolled, by imprisonment for another offense, in a case where a prisoner on supervised release was later jailed on state-law charges.

In a case over peremptory challenges used to remove black jurors in a black man's murder trials, the Court ruled that the case fell under Batson and that the state inappropriately removed most of the potential black jurors.

The Court held that Tennessee's two-year durational-residency requirement applicable to retail liquor store license applicants violated the Commerce Clause (Dormant Commerce Clause) and was not authorized by the Twenty-first Amendment.

In a dispute over 11 Virginia legislative districts that a district court found to be racial gerrymanders, the Court held that the Virginia House of Delegates lacked standing to appeal, leaving the district court's ruling in place.
The court held that the limitations period for qui tam lawsuits does not change when the Government intervenes in the lawsuit.

The court held that the extent to which the 2006 Federal Communications Commission (FCC) order defining "unsolicited advertisement" binds the lower courts may depend on the resolution of two preliminary sets of questions that were not aired before the Court of Appeals.
The Court held that a plaintiff may not recover punitive damages on a maritime claim of unseaworthiness.

In a challenge to partisan gerrymandering in districting plans, the Court ruled that federal courts cannot review such claims because they present nonjusticiable political questions, even if the practice may be incompatible with democratic principles.

The Court held that the Lanham Act provisions barring registration of "immoral" or "scandalous" trademarks were unconstitutional because they let the Patent & Trademark Office engage in viewpoint discrimination, violating the First Amendment's Free Speech Clause.
The court held that the charge-filing precondition to suit set out in Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 is not a jurisdictional requirement.

The Court held that when a person is charged with possessing a gun while prohibited from doing so under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g), the prosecution must prove both that the accused knew that they possessed a gun and that they knew they held the relevant status.
The Court held that, when a driver is unconscious and cannot be given a breath test, the exigent-circumstances doctrine generally permits a blood test without a warrant.

In a dispute over adding a citizenship question to the 2020 census, the Court held that the Enumeration clause permits such a question but that the administration's explanation for adding it appeared contrived and pretextual.
The court held that state laws can be "applicable and not inconsistent" with federal law under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act only if federal law does not address the relevant issue.

The Court held that the presence of in-state beneficiaries alone does not empower a state to tax trust income that has not been distributed to the beneficiaries where the beneficiaries have no right to demand that income and are uncertain to receive it.
The court held that a statute authorizing enhanced penalties for using a firearm during the commission of a "crime of violence" is unconstitutionally vague.

In a 6–3 ruling, the Court held that the 3-year statute of limitations for a fabrication of evidence civil lawsuit under section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act begins to run when the criminal case ends in the plaintiff's favor.

The Court held that, where commercial or financial information is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner and provided to the government under an assurance of privacy, the information is "confidential" within the meaning of the Freedom of Information Act.
The court held that, when deciding whether a state law is broader than a crime within the scope of the Armed Career Criminals Act, the state law’s "exact definition or label" does not control.
The court held that a court may hold a creditor in civil contempt for violating a discharge order if there is no fair ground of doubt as to whether the order barred the creditor’s conduct.

The justices ruled that the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments of the United States Constitution do not require that states adopt the insanity defense in criminal cases that are based on the defendant's ability to recognize right from wrong.

The Court ruled that the Sixth Amendment requires unanimous guilty verdicts in criminal trials, applied that requirement to the states, and overturned its earlier decisions in Apodaca v. Oregon and Johnson v. Louisiana.

In a unanimous opinion, the Supreme Court ruled that the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) was not entitled to be reimbursed for attorney's fees from patent applicants, who file appeals against USPTO decisions.
The Court held that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 protects employees against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.
The Court held that appointments to the Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico are not subject to the restrictions in the Appointments Clause of the U.S. Constitution.
The Court ruled that the statute of limitations begins one year after the alleged FDCPA violation took place, not one year after the violation was discovered by the plaintiff.
Was decided, by a 5–4 majority, in 2020.

The Court upheld an Eleventh Circuit decision that permanent residents rendered inadmissible for certain crimes committed within their first seven years of continuous residence were ineligible for cancellation of removal.

The Court held that an investigative traffic stop, made after a license plate check showed the registered owner's license was revoked, is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment when the officer lacks information negating the inference that the owner is driving.
The Court held that Congress lacked the authority to abrogate the States' sovereign immunity from copyright infringement suits via the Copyright Remedy Clarification Act of 1990.

In a dispute over who bore the cleanup costs of a 2004 Delaware River oil spill, the Court ruled that the contract language required Citgo to provide a safe berth for the vessel, making Citgo ultimately responsible for the spill.

The Court ruled that under the Clean Water Act, pollutant discharges from a non-point source that reach navigable waters, such as through groundwater, require a permit when they are the "functional equivalent of a direct discharge."
The Court held, in a case over a U.S. Border Patrol agent's shooting of a Mexican teenager across the border, that the Bivens precedent did not extend to claims based on cross-border shootings.

The Court held by a 5–4 vote that a 2017 U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) order to rescind the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) immigration program was "arbitrary and capricious" under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) and reversed the order.

In a bankruptcy case over a motion for relief from an automatic stay, the Court unanimously ruled that a bankruptcy court's unreserved grant or denial of relief is a final order that may be appealed, and it affirmed the court below.

In a unanimous opinion in March 2020, the Court ruled that under the Civil Rights Act, Allen was burdened to show that race was the sole reason Comcast failed to enter into a contract with his network.

The Court ruled that the Official Code of Georgia Annotated could not be copyrighted, because its annotations were authored by an arm of the legislature in the course of its legislative duties and so fell under the government edicts doctrine.

The court held that landowners are "potentially responsible parties" under CERCLA and therefore need approval from the EPA before taking any action to restore their properties related to a Superfund site.

The Court held that, under ERISA's requirement that plaintiffs with "actual knowledge" of a fiduciary breach sue within three years, a plaintiff does not necessarily have actual knowledge of disclosures he received but did not read or cannot recall reading.

The Court held that a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 59(e) motion to alter or amend a habeas court’s judgment is not a second or successive habeas petition under the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act.
The court held that The statutory phrase "questions of law" includes the application of a legal standard to facts when those facts are undisputed.

In a dispute over unpaid Affordable Care Act Risk Corridors payments to unprofitable insurers, the Court ruled that Congress's appropriations riders did not cancel the government's obligation to pay, and that the insurers properly sought relief under the Tucker Act.
