In a case under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, the Court held that a child's habitual residence is determined by the totality of the circumstances, not by categorical requirements such as a parental agreement.
The court held that an appellate court—not a jury—must reweigh the mitigating and aggravating factors in a death-penalty habeas corpus case after an Eddings error is identified.

The Court ruled unanimously that plaintiffs, including victims of the 1998 embassy bombings and their families, could seek punitive damages from foreign nations under the amended Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act for conduct preceding the amendment.

The Court held that participants in a defined-benefit retirement plan, who were guaranteed a fixed monthly payment regardless of the plan's value or investment decisions, lacked Article III standing to sue the plan's fiduciaries under ERISA.

The Court ruled that federal employees suing under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act only had to prove age was a motivating factor to sue, though but-for causation was still needed to determine the appropriate remedy.

The Court held that the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards does not conflict with domestic equitable estoppel doctrines that permit the enforcement of arbitration agreements by nonsignatories to those agreements.

In a case over politically motivated George Washington Bridge lane closures, the Court unanimously overturned the fraud and conspiracy convictions because the scheme did not aim to obtain money or property, and remanded to the lower courts.
The Court held that claim preclusion did not apply to a defense that could have been raised in a previous case between two parties when the "common nucleus of operative fact" was different.
The Court ruled that a state scholarship program providing public funds for students to attend private schools cannot discriminate against religious schools under the Free Exercise Clause.
In a trademark case under the Lanham Act, the Court ruled that a plaintiff in an infringement lawsuit does not have to show the defendant willfully infringed in order to claim lost profit damages.
The Court ruled that a Louisiana state law placing hospital-admission requirements on abortion clinics doctors was unconstitutional.

In a dispute over a Forest Service permit for a pipeline under the Appalachian Trail, the Court ruled that the Trail's assignment to the NPS did not make its lands NPS lands, so the Forest Service could issue the permit.
The Court held that, under the Armed Career Criminal Act of 1984, the definition of “serious drug offense” only requires that the state offense involve the conduct specified in the statute.

The Court unanimously vacated the Ninth Circuit's decision striking down the law criminalizing encouraging illegal immigration, because the panel violated the party presentation principle by raising overbreadth itself, and remanded for reconsideration.

The Court held that Article II and the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution do not categorically preclude or require a heightened standard for the issuance of a state criminal subpoena to a sitting president.

The Court held that the land Congress reserved for the Muscogee Nation in the 19th century was never disestablished and is Indian country under the Major Crimes Act, so Oklahoma could not prosecute American Indians for crimes committed there.

The Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, ruling that under Hosanna-Tabor a person serving an important religious function, even without a religious leader's title or training, falls within the ministerial exception to employment discrimination laws.

In a dispute over new rules exempting groups with religious or moral objections from the ACA's contraceptive mandate, the Court ruled the rules were valid, as the departments had authority to issue them and the process did not violate the APA.
The Court ruled unanimously, by a vote of 9–0, that states have the ability to enforce an elector's pledge in presidential elections.

The Supreme Court, in a complex plurality decision, ruled on July 6, 2020, that the 2015 amendment to the TCPA did unconstitutionally favor debt collection speech over political speech and violated the First Amendment.
The Court ruled on the question of what appeals courts can review when determining whether a noncitizen who has committed a crime in the United States can be deported.

The Court unanimously held that, for a prisoner seeking to proceed in forma pauperis under the "3 strikes" system of 28 U.S.C. § 1915(g), a dismissal without prejudice for failure to state a claim counts as a strike.
The Court ruled that the 1996 immigration law limiting habeas corpus judicial review of immigration officers' decisions did not violate the Suspension Clause of Article One of the U.S. Constitution.
The Court held that the structure of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, with a single director removable only "for cause," violated the constitutional separation of powers principle.
The Court ruled that courts may award the SEC's sought disgorgement for fraudulent activities as equitable relief, but only up to the wrongdoer's net profits and only for victims.

The Court held that courts must consider separation of powers in disputes over congressional subpoenas for the president's personal information, set out four non-exhaustive factors, and vacated the lower court's decision for not properly weighing those concerns.

The Court, in a per curiam decision following McGirt v. Oklahoma, ruled that Congress never disestablished the Muscogee (Creek) Nation reservation, which remained Indian country for purposes of the Major Crimes Act.

The Court held that, because Adams did not show that he was "able and ready" to apply for a judicial vacancy in the imminent future, he failed to show a "personal," "concrete" and "imminent" injury necessary for Article III standing.
The Court unanimously ruled that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act allowed litigants to seek monetary damages, not just injunctive relief, against federal officials for violations of the Act.

The court held that state statutes are only preempted by the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA) if they have an "impermissible connection" to ERISA plans or they "refer to" ERISA plans.

In product liability suits against an out-of-state manufacturer over accidents in Montana and Minnesota, the Court ruled that the claims arose out of or related to Ford's business and marketing activities, supporting the states' specific personal jurisdiction.

In a dispute over Google's use of Java APIs in Android, the Court ruled that Google's use fell within fair use, bypassed the copyrightability question, reversed the Federal Circuit, and remanded the case.

The Court held that the mere retention of estate property after the filing of a bankruptcy petition does not violate 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(3), which operates as a "stay" of "any act" to "exercise control" over the property of the estate.

The Court ruled unanimously that under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, rapes committed between 1986 and 2006 that were "punishable by death" had no statute of limitations, unlike similar civilian crimes.
The Court ruled in a 5–3 decision that the use of physical force with the intent to restrain a person, even if that fails to restrain the person, is considered a seizure.

The Court ruled that a non-citizen seeking cancellation of a removal order did not meet the burden of proving eligibility unless they showed a past conviction was not disqualifying, even when the record was ambiguous under a divisible state statute.

The Court ruled in a 7–2 decision in 2021 that the government does not have to disclose "draft biological opinions" involving potential threats to endangered species, even though the drafts reflect an agency's final proposal.
The court held that the United States Railroad Retirement Board's decision to refuse to reopen the prior, adverse benefits determination of a former railroad worker was subject to judicial review.
In a 5–4 decision in June 2021, the Supreme Court ruled that crimes resulting from reckless conduct should not be considered as a "violent felony" for the purposes of the ACCA.

The Court upheld a juvenile offender's life sentence without parole, ruling that states have discretion to impose such sentences on juveniles without making a separate assessment of their permanent incorrigibility.

The Court held that the City of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania violated First Amendment rights of a Catholic foster care agency by refusing to renew the agency's contract unless it agreed to certify married same-sex couples as foster parents.
The Court held that a dismissal for failure to state a claim under the Federal Tort Claims Act (FTCA) is a judgment on the merits that triggers the FTCA's judgment bar on future actions.
In a 6–3 decision authored by Neil Gorsuch, the Court ruled against the federal government, holding that deportation hearing notices need to be in a single document.

In a challenge to the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate after its tax penalty was reduced to zero, the Court ruled that Texas and the other challenging states lacked standing because they had shown no past or future injury from the provision.

In a case over the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act's definition of "exceeds authorized access," the Court ruled that one exceeds authorized access by accessing off-limit files and information on a computer system they were otherwise authorized to access.
The Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that Ramos did not apply retroactively to earlier cases prior to their verdict in Ramos.

In a suit by former child slave laborers under the Alien Tort Statute against two U.S. companies for aiding and abetting slavery in Ivory Coast, the Court held that the plaintiffs improperly sought extraterritorial application of the statute.
The Court held that a suit to enjoin IRS Notice 2016–66 did not trigger the Anti-Injunction Act even though a violation of the notice may have resulted in a tax penalty.

The Court unanimously held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act did not allow Holocaust survivors' heirs to sue Germany in U.S. court over property taken during the Nazi era, because the sale was an expropriation of property.

In a unanimous decision based on statutory interpretation of the TCPA, the Supreme Court ruled that auto dialers are defined by their function to either store or produce telephone numbers from a random or sequential number generator.

The Court unanimously held that the "wholly groundless" exception to arbitrability violated the Federal Arbitration Act, so a valid delegation of arbitrability to an arbitrator must be honored even if a court thinks the argument for arbitration is wholly groundless.

In a challenge to the structure of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, the Court ruled that restricting the President's removal of the FHFA director was unconstitutional, but dismissed shareholders' lawsuit because the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac was an established agency power.
The Court ruled unanimously that the FTC had misused its authority granted by the Federal Trade Commission Act under Section 13(b) to obtain monetary relief.

The court held that non-citizens subject to reinstated deportation orders are not entitled to bond hearings while seeking to prevent the deportation; their removal orders are "administratively final."

The Court held that in a case about nominal damages for suppressed free speech rights later mooted by intervening circumstances, nominal damages for a past rights violation satisfy Article III's redressability requirement.

The Court vacated the District Court's ruling that had blocked a presidential memo directing the Commerce Department to report estimated counts of illegal immigrants in each state for congressional apportionment purposes.

In a dispute over FCC media ownership rules under the Telecommunications Act of 1996, the Court unanimously ruled that the FCC had not acted arbitrarily and capriciously, reversing the Third Circuit and allowing it to relax cross-media ownership rules.

In a long-running dispute over water in the ACF River Basin, where Florida sought a cap on Georgia's water use, the Court overruled Florida's exceptions to the special master's report and unanimously dismissed the case.

The Court held that the Ninth Circuit violated the Immigration and Nationality Act with its rule that a reviewing court "must treat a noncitizen's testimony as credible and true absent an explicit adverse credibility determination."
The Court ruled unanimously that the warrantless entry into a home by police in pursuit of a misdemeanant is not unequivocally justified.

In a dispute over the Appointments Clause and patent judges on the Patent Trial and Appeal Board, the Court ruled the judges were principal officers, but resolved the problem by making their decisions reviewable by the Director of the Patent Office.
The Supreme Court ruled in a 6–3 decision in July 2021 that neither of Arizona's election policies violated the VRA or had a racially discriminatory purpose.

The court held that a petitioner need not challenge the constitutionality of an agency's structure under the Appointments Clause in an internal agency administrative proceeding in order to present that challenge in court on appeal.

The Court held that a California regulation requiring agricultural employers to let labor organizers regularly access their property for union recruitment was a per se taking under the Fifth Amendment, so it could not be enforced without just compensation.
The court held that defendants bear the burden of persuasion to prove a lack of price impact by a preponderance of the evidence at class certification.
In a class-action dispute over Article III standing against a private defendant, the Court ruled that only those who can show concrete harm have standing to seek damages in federal court.
The Court unanimously affirmed lower court rulings that NCAA restrictions on non-cash, academic-related compensation for college athletes, such as computers and internships, violated antitrust law.

The Court ruled that California's requirement that non-profits disclose their donors' identities to the Attorney General before soliciting donations burdened donors' First Amendment rights, was not narrowly tailored, and was invalid.

The Court ruled for a student who was suspended from cheerleading over an off-campus profane Snapchat post, holding that the school's interest in preventing disruption under Tinker did not overcome her First Amendment rights.

In a unanimous decision, the Court ruled in June 2021 that for immigrants who had entered the U.S. unlawfully, simply having temporary protected status did not make them eligible to apply for permanent resident status.
The Court held that Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 39 does not permit a district court to alter a court of appeals’ allocation of the costs listed in subsection (e) of that rule.

In a dispute over who paid to clean up the Ordot Dump on Guam, the Court ruled unanimously that Guam had timely filed its Superfund suit to recover part of the cleanup costs from the United States, so the case could proceed.
Dealt with the three requirements under which a deportation order may be dismissed, as listed in 8 USC § 1326(d).
In a 6–3 decision, the Supreme Court ruled that by the majority's interpretation of the law, the congressional law did allow for refineries to seek extensions after their exemption period had lapsed.
In a 6–3 decision issued in June 2021, the Court ruled that ANCs were considered to be "Indian tribes" and were eligible to receive the set-aside funds.
The Court unanimously ruled that the First Step Act allows retroactive sentence reductions for pre-2010 drug-possession crimes, but only for those sentenced under minimum sentencing requirements.
The Court held that an unobjected-to failure to instruct the jury that the defendant must have known they were a felon is not structural error requiring reversal.

In a case over state sovereign immunity and eminent domain powers delegated to private companies for a natural gas pipeline right-of-way, the Court ruled that states gave up their sovereign immunity from such delegated federal authority by ratifying the Constitution.

In a unanimous decision, the court ruled that multiple criminal offenses that a person commits during a single criminal episode do not count as separate convictions when considering the number of prior convictions a criminal has under the ACCA.
The Court held that the waters of the Middle Claiborne Aquifer are subject to the judicial remedy of equitable apportionment.

The court held that federal courts can not grant habeas relief when state courts have already ruled on a prisoner's claim, unless the situation satisfies the test laid out in Brecht v. Abrahamson, and the exceptions to the AEDPA's §2254(d) jurisdictional bar.

In a dispute over the state secrets privilege, where an alleged Al Qaeda operative sought testimony from CIA contractors about his torture at a black site and the government blocked it as classified, the Court ruled against him.

The court held that, to demonstrate a favorable termination of a criminal prosecution for malicious prosecution, a plaintiff need not show that the criminal prosecution ended with some affirmative indication of innocence.
The Court held (6-3) that a defendant is entitled to an impartial panel of jurors, not necessarily a panel of jurors who know nothing about the case.

The Court held that civil-service pension payments based on employment as a dual-status military technician are not payments based on "service as a member of a uniformed service" under 42 U.S.C. § 415(1)(7)(A)(III).
The court held that new evidence that was not in the state court's records, based on ineffective assistance of post-conviction counsel, could not be used in an appeal to a federal court.
The Court unanimously held that a local government board member's First Amendment freedom of speech was not abridged when his colleagues verbally censured him.

The Court held that the "look through" approach established by the Court's decision in Vaden v. Discover Bank "does not apply to requests to confirm or vacate arbitral awards under Sections 9 and 10 of the FAA."

In a 6–3 decision issued in June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled that New York's law was unconstitutional and that the ability to bear arms in public was a constitutional right guaranteed by the Second Amendment.
In a case over FBI surveillance and the state secrets privilege, the Court overturned the Ninth Circuit's ruling and held that FISA does not override the state secrets defense.
The Court held that a lack of either factual or legal knowledge can excuse an inaccuracy in a copyright registration.

In a case over excluding U.S. citizens in Puerto Rico from Supplemental Security Income, the Court ruled that Congress's broad power over the territories under Article Four meant the exclusion did not violate the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.

In a 6–3 ruling, the Court ruled that the Austin regulation against off-premise digital signs was content-neutral and thus should be reviewed as a facial challenge rather than a strict scrutiny following from the reasoning in Reed v. Town of Gilbert.

The Court held that Section 1231(a)(6) of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 does not require bond hearings, with the government bearing the burden by clear and convincing evidence, for noncitizens detained for six months.
The court held that the United States Constitution does not confer a right to abortion.
The Court held that the Seventh Circuit erred in relying on the participants' ultimate choice over their investments to excuse allegedly imprudent decisions by respondents.
The Court held that federal courts lack jurisdiction to review factual findings underlying judgments related to discretionary relief in immigration proceedings under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2).

The Court ruled that Maine's restrictions barring school vouchers from paying tuition at religious private schools violated the Free Exercise Clause because they discriminated against religious schools and the parents who chose them.
The Court clarified which patients hospitals are allowed to be reimbursed by Medicare for treating, and at what rate.

The Court held that an attempted Hobbs Act robbery does not qualify as a "crime of violence" under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A) because no element of the offense requires proof that the defendant used, attempted to use, or threatened to use force.

In a challenge to a Texas law banning abortions after six weeks and enforced by private lawsuits, the Court ruled providers could not sue state-court judges, clerks, or the Attorney General, but their claims against state licensing officials could proceed.

The case concerned whether the federal government could sue Texas to stop enforcement of its six-week abortion ban, and the Court ruled per curiam that certiorari was improvidently granted and dismissed the case.
In a unanimous decision by the court, they ruled that 30 day timeline is non-jurisdictional and is protected by equitable tolling.

The Court held that, in a suit raising non-federal claims against a foreign state or instrumentality under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, a court should determine the substantive law by using the same choice-of-law rule applicable in a similar suit against a private party.
In a unanimous 9–0 decision, the Court ruled that the city violated a Christian group's free speech rights when it denied their request to raise a Christian flag over City Hall.

The Supreme Court of the United States struck down section 304 of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act, which limited the amount of money that candidates could be paid on personal loans to their campaign.
The Court held that the double jeopardy clause does not bar successive prosecutions of distinct offenses arising from a single act, even if a single sovereign prosecutes them.

The Court ruled, in a case about whether Texas could control and regulate gambling on Native American reservations, that the Restoration Act bans only gaming activities also banned by the state of Texas.
In a case about the ability of states to defend federal regulations in court, the Court did not resolve the questions presented and instead dismissed review as improvidently granted.

In a dispute over the EPA's Clean Air Act authority to regulate carbon emissions from existing power plants, the Court ruled that Congress did not authorize the EPA to require generation shifting without considering costs, which would have invalidated the Clean Power Plan.

The Court held that the Medicare Secondary Payer statute does not authorize disparate-impact liability, and the Marietta Plan's coverage terms for outpatient dialysis were lawful because those terms applied uniformly to all covered individuals.
In a 5–4 decision issued in June 2022, the Court ruled that state sovereign immunity does not prevent states from being sued under federal law related to the nation's defense.

The Court held that the invalidation of a Department of Veterans Affairs regulation after a veteran's benefits decision becomes final cannot support a claim for collateral relief permitting revision of that decision based on "clear and unmistakable error" under 38 U.S.C. §§ 5109A and 7111.
The Court unanimously held that cargo loaders and ramp supervisors employed at airports are exempt from the Federal Arbitration Act.
The Court held that federal courts may not adopt an arbitration-specific rule conditioning a waiver of the right to arbitrate on a showing of prejudice.

The Court unanimously ruled that a private arbitral tribunal overseas is not a "foreign or international tribunal" under 28 U.S.C. § 1782(a), and also held the same for the investor-state arbitral tribunal in the companion case.

The Court held, 6–3, that the government, while following the Establishment Clause, may not suppress an individual from engaging in personal religious observance, as doing so would violate the Free Speech and Free Exercise Clauses of the First Amendment.

The Court ruled that federal and state authorities held joint jurisdiction to prosecute non-Native Americans for crimes committed on Native American lands in Oklahoma, following the aftermath of McGirt.
The court held that Congress's enactment of a significant fee increase that exempted debtors in two states violated the uniformity requirement of the Bankruptcy Clause.
The Court held, 6–3, that an officer's failure to read Miranda warnings to a suspect in custody does not alone provide basis for a claim of civil liability under Section 1983 of United States Code.
The Court held that the term "mistake" in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b)(1) includes a judge's errors of law.

In a suit by Texas and Missouri over the termination of the "Remain in Mexico" policy, the Court reversed the lower courts and ruled that the Biden administration and DHS legally had the authority to end the program.
The Court held that the Clean Water Act covers only wetlands that have a "continuous surface connection" to "waters of the United States" connected to "traditional interstate navigable waters".
The Court held that 38 U.S.C. § 5110(b)(1), a provision relating to VA disability compensations, is not subject to equitable tolling.
The Court ruled 5–4 that Alabama's districts likely violated the VRA, and maintained an injunction that required Alabama to create an additional majority-minority district.

The court held that, when a prisoner pursues state post-conviction DNA testing through the state-provided litigation process, the statute of limitations for a Section 1983 procedural due process claim begins to run when the state litigation ends.

The Court ruled that a foundation's licensing of Andy Warhol's Prince Series images, based on a photographer's photograph of Prince, was not protected by fair use, as the works shared a similar purpose.
The court held that, regardless of income level, workers are not considered salaried unless the conditions set out in the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 are met.

The Court ruled that race-based affirmative action programs in most college admissions violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, in a suit alleging Harvard's admissions discriminated against Asian Americans.

The court held that the statutory review schemes set out in the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and Federal Trade Commission Act of 1914 do not displace a district court's federal-question jurisdiction over claims challenging as unconstitutional the structure or existence of the SEC or FTC.
The court held that a Pennsylvania law is consistent with Due Process.

In a challenge by Texas, Louisiana, Indiana and individual plaintiffs to the Indian Child Welfare Act, the Court held the Act consistent with congressional powers, rejected the state commandeering claims, and made no ruling on the Fourteenth Amendment claims for lack of standing.
In a 6–3 decision, the Court ruled in favor of a website designer, ruling that the state of Colorado cannot compel the designer to create work that violates her values.
The court held that debts incurred by fraud cannot be discharged in bankruptcy, regardless of whether the debtor committed the fraud.
The Court held that in a qui tam action filed under the False Claims Act, the United States may move to dismiss whenever it has intervened – whether during the seal period or later on.

In a case about the federal honest services fraud statute, the Court held that a private citizen with significant influence over government decision-making cannot be convicted of honest services fraud for actions taken while not holding public office.

In a dispute over public use of an easement road near private properties, the Court reversed and remanded, holding that the Quiet Title Act's 12-year statute of limitations is a non-jurisdictional claims-processing rule.
The Court rejected the "right-to-control" theory as a valid basis for convictions under the federal wire fraud statute, 18 U.S.C. § 1343.

The Court held that Section 363(m) of the Bankruptcy Code, which restricts the effects of certain successful appeals of judicially authorized sales or leases of bankruptcy-estate property, is not a jurisdictional provision.

In a dispute over North Carolina's legislature-drawn congressional districts, the Court ruled that the Elections Clause does not give state legislatures sole power over federal elections, rejecting the independent state legislature theory.

In a labor dispute involving a state National Guard, the Court held that the Federal Labor Relations Authority had jurisdiction because the Guard acts as a federal agency when it hires and supervises dual-status technicians in their civilian role.

In a dispute over an employer's power to sue a labor union for destruction of property following a strike, the Court concluded that the National Labor Relations Act did not preempt the lawsuits against the union, allowing litigation to continue.
The Court held that nothing in the Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act categorically nullified any sovereign immunity the Board enjoyed from legal claims.

The court held that the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act's comprehensive scheme governing claims of sovereign immunity in civil actions against foreign states and their instrumentalities does not cover criminal cases.
The court held that noncitizens are not required to exhaust all possible discretionary appeals offered by the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) before contesting removal orders in federal courts.

The Court held that an ADA lawsuit seeking compensatory damages for denial of a free and appropriate public education could proceed without exhausting IDEA's administrative procedures, because IDEA does not offer compensatory damages.

The case asked whether internet service providers were liable for aiding and abetting a foreign terrorist organization by recommending user-posted content, and the Court unanimously ruled the charges against Twitter and other companies were not permissible under the Antiterrorism Act.
The Supreme Court's ruling was issued on June 30, 2023, ruling 6–3 that the Secretary of Education did not have the power to waive student loans under the HEROES Act.
The Supreme Court's ruling was issued on June 30, 2023, ruling 6–3 that the Secretary of Education did not have the power to waive student loans under the HEROES Act.
The Court held that New Jersey had the right to unilaterally withdraw from the Waterfront Commission of New York Harbor.
The Court determined that the Treaty of Bosque Redondo did not require the U.S. Government to take affirmative steps to secure water for the Navajo Nation.
The Court held that a federal district court must stay its proceedings while an interlocutory appeal on the question of arbitrability is ongoing.
The Court decided whether or not the Act applies to foreign sales.
The court held that, when an alleged infringer uses a trademark as a designation of source for the infringer's own goods, the Rogers test does not apply.
The Court held that Amgen's two patent applications on cholesterol-lowering drugs failed to satisfy the enablement clause of §112 of the Patent Act, 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
The Court held that a provision of one subsection of Title 18 barring concurrent sentences does not govern sentences pursuant to a different part of the same section.
The Court held that a defendant may be retried following a jury trial conducted in the improper venue before a jury drawn from the incorrect district.

The Court held that when the Internal Revenue Service issues a summons in aid of collecting a tax liability, the exception to the notice requirement in 26 U.S.C. § 7609(c)(2)(D)(i) applies even if the delinquent taxpayer has no legal interest in the accounts or records summoned.

The Court unanimously held that to state a claim under Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933, a plaintiff must plead and prove that he purchased "such security" that is "traceable to the allegedly defective registration statement".
The Court held that an offense may "relate to" obstruction of justice under the Immigration and Nationality Act even if the offense does not require that an investigation or proceeding be pending.

In a Title VII religious accommodation dispute, the Court unanimously ruled for the employee, generally upholding Trans World but clarifying that more than de minimis costs do not show undue hardship; employers must show substantial increased costs.

The Court held that the False Claims Act's scienter element, which requires a defendant to "knowingly" give a "false" claim to the government, refers to a defendant's knowledge and subjective beliefs, not refer to what an objectively reasonable person may have known or believed.
By a 7–2 majority, the court decided that statements are not protected if the defendant recklessly disregarded a substantial risk that their statements would be viewed as threatening.
The Court determined that Native Americans Tribes are not immune from the automatic stay of the Bankruptcy Code.
The Court held that a post-trial motion under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50 is not required to preserve for appellate review a purely legal issue resolved at summary judgment.
The Court decided how the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act applied to extraterritorial claims of damage to intangible property.
A unanimous court held that the surplus value is protected by the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause.

The Court held that Texas and Louisiana lacked Article III standing to challenge a Biden administration immigration policy that prioritized apprehending and deporting suspected terrorists, non-citizens who committed crimes, and those recently caught at the border.

The Court ruled that the funding mechanism of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), which is allocated from the Federal Treasury budget rather that through Congressional appropriations, is constitutional under the Appropriations Clause.

In a challenge to South Carolina's 1st congressional district map as a racial gerrymander, the Court held the district court's finding that race predominated was not sufficiently supported by evidence, reversed it as clear error, and remanded.

In a dispute over individuals blocked from a public official's personal social media account, the Court unanimously held that the official's private posts were not state action, so blocking was allowed unless the official had authority to speak for the government and purported to do so.

In a dispute over individuals blocked from a public official's personal social media account, the Court remanded the case to the Ninth Circuit for further consideration in light of a similar case decided the same day, Lindke v. Freed.
The court decided that the provision does not violate the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment.
The Court held that the Fair Credit Reporting Act unequivocally and unambiguously waives the sovereign immunity of the United States.
The Supreme Court reversed the 5th Circuit in an 8–1 ruling and upheld the law.
The Court held that veterans who accrue educational benefits under both the Montgomery and Post-9/11 GI Bills may use either or both, and may use them in any order.
The Court held that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 protects against discriminatory job transfers even where the transfer does not result in a significant disadvantage.

In an administrative law dispute brought by fishing companies challenging a fisheries service rule, the Court overruled Chevron deference and assigned the determination of statutory ambiguity to the courts instead of deferring to agencies.
The Court held that federal courts have the jurisdiction to review the determinations of immigration judges as a mixed question of law.

The Court considered whether the government satisfied its notice obligations when it gave an initial notice to appear without a date and location and a later notice with them, and ruled for the government that the notice was sufficient to justify removal.
The Court held that "Not guilty by reason of insanity" is an acquittal for double jeopardy purposes notwithstanding any inconsistency with the jury's other verdicts.
The Supreme Court upheld the Mandatory Repatriation Tax (MRT).
The justices ruled that the Securities and Exchange Commission violated the Seventh Amendment.
The Supreme Court affirmed both courts of appeals, holding that a state drug conviction counts as an ACCA predicate if it involved a drug on the federal schedules at the time of that conviction.

The Court ruled in a Chapter 11 dispute over a release extinguishing nondebtors' claims against nondebtor third parties without consent, holding that the Bankruptcy Code did not authorize it and blocking the bankruptcy plan.

The Court unanimously held that states could not determine eligibility for federal office, including the presidency, under Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, after Colorado's Supreme Court had rejected Trump's eligibility.
The court held that a complaint about being put on the No Fly List is not moot simply because the government later took the plaintiff off the List.

In a dispute over land-use permit fees under the Takings Clause, the Court unanimously held that such fees must be closely related and roughly proportional to the land use's effects, even when set by legislation rather than individualized assessment.
The court held that prospective parity is the appropriate remedy for the short-lived and small disparity created by the fee statute held unconstitutional in Siegel v. Fitzgerald.

The court held that when an expert conveys an absent analyst's statements in support of the expert's opinion, and the statements provide that support only if true, then the statements come into evidence for their truth.
The Court held that pure omissions are not actionable under the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Rule 10b–5(b).
The Supreme Court of the United States decided on April 16, 2024.
The Supreme Court held, by a 6–3 vote, that the statute of limitations does not start running until the particular plaintiff has been harmed by the agency action.
The Court held that transportation workers do not need to formally work in the transportation industry to be exempt from the Federal Arbitration Act.
The Court held that, assuming the discovery rule applies to copyright infringement, the three-year statute of limitations for an infringement suit does not prevent recovery.
The Court held that a court's failure to enter a preliminary order imposing criminal forfeiture before sentencing does not necessarily bar a judge from ordering forfeiture at sentencing.

In a dispute over whether New York's interest-on-escrow law was preempted as applied to national banks, the Court held that the Second Circuit failed to analyze preemption consistently with the Dodd-Frank Act and Barnett Bank.
In a 6–3 decision, the Supreme Court ruled that bump stocks are not machine guns for purposes of the NFA, vacating the ATF rule and finding that the ATF exceeded its statutory authority.
The Court held that where one contract between parties sends disputes to arbitration and another contract sends disputes to courts, a court must decide which contract governs.

The Court ruled that Missouri and Louisiana lacked standing to sue the federal government over alleged pressure on social media companies to censor content, because they failed to show a substantial risk of redressable injury traceable to government action.

The Court unanimously ruled that if a former New York financial regulator attempted to coerce financial institutions to refrain from doing business with the NRA, that conduct would violate the First Amendment.
The court interpreted a provision of the Federal Rules of Evidence regarding the admissibility of expert witness testimony.

The Court held that an insurer with financial responsibility for bankruptcy claims is a "party in interest" under §1109(b) that "may raise and may appear and be heard on any issue" in a Chapter 11 case.

The court held that plaintiffs alleging retaliatory arrest need only provide evidence that their arrest occurred in circumstances where probable cause exists to arrest, but officers typically exercise discretion and decline to arrest.
The Court denied the States' motion to enter the consent decree because the proposed consent decree would have disposed of the United States' Compact claims without its consent.

The Court determined that the federal government must provide additional funding to cover some third-party administrative costs incurred by Native American tribes that operate their own health-care programs.
The Court held that the 60-day filing deadline for appeals of decisions by the Merit Systems Protection Board is not jurisdictional, so courts have discretion to equitably toll it.

In a challenge to the FDA's approval of the abortion drug mifepristone, the Court unanimously held that the Alliance lacked Article III association standing because no legal injury was shown, and it reversed the lower court decisions.
The Court held that a corporation's contractual obligation to redeem shares is not necessarily a liability that reduces a corporation's value for purposes of the federal estate tax.
The Court held 18 U.S.C. § 666 prohibits bribes to state and local officials but does not make it a crime for those officials to accept gratuities for their past acts.

In a 6–3 opinion by Justice Kagan, the Court held that probable cause for one charge does not categorically defeat a claim that another contemporaneous charge lacked probable cause and caused a seizure.

The Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in June 2024 that the charge only applied when the defendant "impaired the availability or integrity" (attempted or successfully) of a physical document or object used in an official proceeding.
The Court held that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals interpreted and applied Strickland v. Washington incorrectly.
The Court held that local government ordinances with civil and criminal penalties for camping on public land do not constitute cruel and unusual punishment of homeless people.

The Court held that, when a court finds that a lawsuit involves an arbitrable dispute and a party has requested a stay of the court proceeding pending arbitration, Section 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act compels the court to issue a stay, and the court lacks discretion to dismiss the suit.
The Court held that a "citizen does not have a fundamental liberty interest in her noncitizen spouse being admitted to the country."
The Court held in an 8–1 decision that the ordinary four-factor Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council test applies.
The court initially agreed to expedite the appeal and temporarily allowed Idaho to enforce its abortion ban.

The Court held that presidential immunity from criminal prosecution presumptively extends to all of a president's official acts, with absolute immunity for official acts within exclusive presidential authority that Congress cannot regulate.

The Court vacated the lower-court decisions in challenges to Florida and Texas laws limiting online content moderation, because the courts had not fully assessed the laws under the First Amendment, and remanded the cases for further consideration.
The US Supreme Court ruled that visa revocations are left to the discretion of the Homeland Security Department, so they cannot be judicially reviewed.

The Court held that a clause of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act creating a private cause of action for "any person injured in his business or property" did not exempt claims originating from a personal injury.

The Court held that the Food and Drug Administration's denial of authorization to market flavored electronic cigarette products was not arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

The Court held that state laws requiring exhaustion of state administrative remedies are preempted by 42 U.S.C. § 1983 of the federal Ku Klux Klan Act when they prevent a state court from hearing claims challenging delays in the administrative process.

The Court considered a challenge to ATF regulations extending the Gun Control Act's "firearm," "frame," and "receiver" terms to ghost gun kits, and held the rules could not be struck down on a facial challenge because not all applications conflicted with the statute.

The Court held that winning a preliminary injunction under the Civil Rights Attorney's Fees Award Act of 1976 did not make litigants a "prevailing party" entitled to attorney's fees, even when the case became moot after the challenged law was repealed.
The Court decided that, in light of newly disclosed evidence and the state attorney general's confession of error, Richard Glossip should receive a new trial.

The Court ruled in favor of San Francisco in a dispute over whether the Clean Water Act lets the EPA impose generic prohibitions in discharge permits that expose permit-holders to enforcement for violating water quality standards.

The court held that the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims must apply clear error review when reviewing the Department of Veterans Affairs's application of the "benefit-of-the-doubt rule" regarding a veteran's claim to a service-related disability.

The Court held that fraudulent representations made to private administrators of government programs are prosecutable under the False Claims Act of 1863 as long as the disbursed funds at least partially came from the government.

The Court held that Medicare disproportionate share hospital adjustments should only consider patients as "entitled to supplementary security income benefits" if they received such benefits during the month in which they were hospitalized.

Unanimously held that a preponderance of evidence standard applies when an employer argues that an employee is exempt from the minimum wage and overtime pay provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The Court held that voluntary departure deadlines that end on a weekend or public holiday are automatically extended to the following business day for the purposes of filing a post-decision motion to reopen or reconsider immigration removal proceedings.
The Court held that the US Bankruptcy Code's waiver of sovereign immunity does not entitle a bankruptcy trustee to recover a debtor's fraudulent federal tax payments.

The Court held that for plaintiffs to sue a foreign government over illegally seized property, the expropriation exemption of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act requires that the property is directly traceable to transactions with a commercial nexus to the United States.

The Court held that a Tennessee state law banning puberty blockers and hormone therapy for the treatment of gender dysphoria in minors did not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution.

The Court held that a defendant who induces a victim to enter into a transaction under materially false pretenses may be convicted of federal fraud even if the defendant did not seek to cause the victim economic loss.

The Court held that American military reservists are entitled to differential pay whenever they are called to active duty during a national emergency, regardless of whether their service is substantially connected to the emergency.
The Court held that the National Environmental Policy Act only requires the environmental impact statements of government agencies to consider impacts that they have regulatory power over.
The Court held that Lanham Act awards of a "defendant's profits" in trademark infringement cases do not extend to the profits of the defendant's corporate affiliates.

The court held that all first-time 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) offenders who appear for sentencing after the First Step Act's enactment date, including those whose previous § 924(c) sentences have been vacated and who thus need to be resentenced, are subject to the Act's revised penalties.

The Court held that Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act protects only qualified individuals who hold or desire a position, and affirmed dismissal of a retired firefighter's claim over reduced post-employment health benefits.
The Court held that prosecution for making a false statement to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation under 18 U.S.C. § 1014 requires the statement to be false, rather than simply misleading.
The Court held that Rule 60(b) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure empowers federal courts to reverse voluntary dismissals when based on a mistake, among other reasons.
In a 6–3 decision in June 2025, the Supreme Court ruled that Texas's age-verification law passed intermediate scrutiny and only incidentally burdened the protected speech of adults.
The court held that retailers who would sell a new tobacco product if not for the Food and Drug Administration's denial order may seek judicial review of that order.
The court held that the Hobbs Act does not bind district courts in civil enforcement proceedings to an agency's interpretation of a statute.

The Court, in a unanimous decision, reaffirmed the "totality of the circumstances" test for Fourth Amendment excessive force claims and rejected the "moment of the threat" test used by some Circuit Courts as excessively narrow.
The Court held that conflict of interest claims under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 do not need to address exceptions in the initial pleading.
The court held that a person sentenced to death had standing to challenge Texas DNA-testing procedures under the Due Process Clause.

The court held that a district court considering whether to revoke a defendant's term of supervised release may not consider 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)(2)(A), which covers retribution vis-à-vis the defendant’s underlying criminal offense.
The court held that parties are entitled to a jury trial on Prison Litigation Reform Act (PLRA) exhaustion when that issue is intertwined with the merits of a claim.
The Court unanimously held that requiring members of a majority group to show additional "background circumstances" to prove discrimination was at odds with Title VII and could not be used.

In a suit against a foreign state under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, the Court held that personal jurisdiction exists if an immunity exception applies and service is proper, without a minimum contacts analysis, and vacated and remanded the Ninth Circuit's decision.

The court held that relief under Rule 60(b)(6) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure requires extraordinary circumstances, and this standard does not become less demanding when the movant seeks to reopen a case to amend a complaint.
The Court determined that domestic firearm manufacturers cannot be sued by foreign states, if not materially causing the importation of weapons, under the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act.
The court held that only parties to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's licensing proceedings are entitled to obtain judicial review of the Commission's licensing decisions.
The Court held that when the EPA disapproves a state implementation plan (SIP) under the Clean Air Act, that decision is a local or regional action, not a national one.

The court held that the Environmental Protection Agency's denials of small refinery exemption petitions are locally or regionally applicable actions that fall within the "nationwide scope or effect" exception of the Clean Air Act, requiring venue in the D.C. Circuit.
The court held that an order from the Board of Immigration Appeals denying deferral of removal in a withholding only proceeding is not a final order of removal.

In a challenge by ByteDance and TikTok to a law requiring divestment of foreign adversary controlled apps on First Amendment and other grounds, the Court ruled the law constitutional because it satisfied intermediate scrutiny given national security concerns.
The Court held that, after a defendant has removed a case to federal court, a plaintiff can amend the complaint to omit all references to federal law and have the case sent back to state court.
The Supreme Court found that Wisconsin's denial was unconstitutional because it discriminated against religious organizations based on their religious activities.

The court held that once a district court enters its judgment with respect to a first-filed habeas corpus petition, a second-in-time filing qualifies as a "second or successive application" properly subject to the requirements of §2244(b).

The Court held that the personal jurisdiction provision of the Promoting Security and Justice for Victims of Terrorism Act of 2019 (PSJVTA) does not violate the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
The Court held that the Medicaid Act does not give individuals an enforceable right to choose a specific healthcare provider.
The Court held that the structure of the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force does not violate the Constitution's Appointments Clause.
The court held that a litigant who files a notice of appeal after the original appeal deadline but before the court grants reopening need not file a second notice after reopening.
The court held that the United States Tax Court lacks jurisdiction to resolve disputes between a taxpayer and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) when the IRS is no longer pursuing a levy.
The Court held that the school district's policy of not permitting opt-outs violated the parents' right to free exercise of religion under the First Amendment.

The court held that the fuel producers have Article III standing to challenge the Environmental Protection Agency's approval under the Clean Air Act of California regulations requiring automakers to manufacture more electric vehicles and fewer gasoline-powered vehicles.

The court held that the combat-related special compensation (CRSC) statute, 10 U.S.C. § 1413a, confers authority to settle CRSC claims and thus displaces the Barring Act's settlement procedures and limitations period.

The court held that schoolchildren bringing Americans with Disabilities Act and Rehabilitation Act claims related to their education are subject to the same standards that apply in other disability discrimination contexts, rather than a higher standard.
In a suit under the Federal Tort Claims Act over an FBI raid on the wrong house, the Court unanimously vacated the Eleventh Circuit's dismissal and remanded the case for further proceedings.

The Court considered whether lower-court judges could issue universal injunctions blocking nationwide enforcement of policies, and ruled that such injunctions exceed judicial power unless necessary to give the formal plaintiff "complete relief".
The court decided how a jurisdiction stripping provision of the Anti-terrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act applied to the Supreme Court.
The court held that a candidate for federal office has standing to challenge time, place, and manner regulations created by a state that affect the candidate's federal election.

The Court addressed whether police may enter a home without a warrant under the emergency aid exception based on a reasonable belief someone needs help, and held that an objectively reasonable basis suffices, which the officers' entry satisfied.
The Court held that two separate convictions under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(a)(i) and § 924(j) for a single act was not intended by Congress.

In a dispute over whether a party could move to set aside a default judgment as void after several years, the Court unanimously affirmed the Sixth Circuit's decision, which had denied the motion as untimely under Rule 60(c)(1).
The court held that restitution ordered under the Mandatory Victims Restitution Act of 1996 (MVRA) is criminal punishment subject to the constitution's Ex Post Facto Clause.

The court held that a state law requiring an affidavit of merit to be filed with a complaint is unenforceable in federal court because it conflicts with Rule 8 of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
The court held that prohibiting discussion of a defendant's testimony during a mid-testimony overnight recess does not violate the Sixth Amendment's right to counsel.

The Court ruled that the First Amendment requires strict scrutiny of state laws restricting what therapists may say to clients, reversing the lower courts' rulings upholding Colorado's ban on conversion therapy for minors and remanding the case.

The court held that the United States Postal Service is immune to suits for money damages for failure to deliver the mail even when postal employees intentionally and maliciously refuse to deliver the mail.

The Court, in a challenge to Louisiana's new congressional map that created two majority-minority districts, affirmed the district panel's judgment that the map was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander under the Fifteenth Amendment.

In a case about the fugitive-tolling doctrine, the Court held that the Sentencing Reform Act does not authorize a rule automatically extending a defendant's supervised release term when the defendant fails to report to probation.

The court held that a suit in state court based on a military contractor's actions in a war zone is not preempted when the contractor was neither required nor authorized to take the challenged actions.

The court held that, when a federal court cannot cure a jurisdictional defect in a case that is removed from state to federal court, the federal court's decision must be vacated and returned to state court.
The Court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), an economic sanctions law, does not authorize the president to unilaterally set tariffs.
The court held that an order denying a government contractor's claim of derivative sovereign immunity cannot be immediately appealed.

In a case brought under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, the Court held that individuals may not be held personally liable under a Spending Clause statute unless they voluntarily and knowingly consented to answer lawsuits under it.
The Court held the First Step Act's amendments to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) are not retroactively "extraordinary and compelling reasons" for granting compassionate release.

The court held that an incarcerated person who collaterally attacks the validity of his conviction must proceed through 28 U.S.C. §2255, not 18 U.S.C. §3582; the supposed invalidity of a conviction is not among the "extraordinary and compelling reasons" that justify compassionate release.
The court held that, when reviewing an immigration court's decision to deny asylum, a reviewing court must apply a substantial-evidence standard.

In a suit by music labels over an internet service provider's subscribers sharing copyrighted music, the Court held the provider was not contributorily liable for its users' infringement and reversed the Fourth Circuit.

The Court ruled that federal courts can review constitutional challenges to state investigative subpoenas—particularly when those allegedly chill First Amendment rights such as donor association and advocacy.

The court held that a plaintiff can sue the government under Section 1983 to seek wholly prospective relief from a law that they believe is unconstitutional even though they cannot use Section 1983 to challenge a prior conviction.

In a challenge to the president's firing of an FTC commissioner without cause, the Court held that the president had the power to remove independent agency heads at will, overturning Humphrey's Executor.
The Supreme Court held that federal limits in the Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) violated the First Amendment.
The court held that Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act does not impliedly empower private parties to sue for rescission of any contract that allegedly violates the act.
The Court held that schools can provide separate girls' and boys' sports teams defined by biological sex.
The court held that "NJ Transit is not an arm of New Jersey and thus is not entitled to share in New Jersey's interstate sovereign immunity."
The Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that a portion of the law in question was unconstitutional.

The court held that the provisions of ERISA governing the calculation of withdrawal liability do not require the actuarial assumptions underlying that calculation to be selected on or before the measurement date.

In a dispute over President Trump's attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook "for cause," the Court denied the government's application and held that Cook could remain in her job while the removal efforts were litigated.
The court held that the "property which was confiscated" under Title III of the Helms–Burton Act can refer both to the physical property and the plaintiff's interest in that property.

The Court held that the Helms–Burton Act itself abrogated the sovereign immunity of Cuban agencies and instrumentalities, so plaintiffs suing them under the act did not also need to satisfy a Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act exception.
The court held that the 30-day deadline for removing a lawsuit to federal court in 28 U.S.C. §1446(b)(1) cannot be equitably tolled.

The court held that the proper baseline for measuring "just compensation" following a tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property’s hypothetical fair market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the country's history of tax sales.

The Court held that using the federal law banning unlawful drug users from possessing firearms to criminalize gun possession by habitual users, without proof of active intoxication or dangerousness, violated the Second Amendment.

The court held that a claim that one company negligently hired another to transport goods is not preempted by the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act because states retain authority to regulate safety "with respect to motor vehicles" under the act.
The Supreme Court held that it is not the correct venue, striking down the prosecution as unconstitutional.

The court held that the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952 (INA) does not require a border officer to have clear and convincing evidence that a Lawful Permanent Resident has committed a crime involving moral turpitude before deeming the resident an applicant for admission.
The Court held that a geofence warrant is a search subject to the Fourth Amendment, reaffirming and expanding its earlier holding on warrantless access to historical cell site location information.
The court held that courts may not create new rights of action to remedy violations of international law under the Alien Tort Statute.

The Court held that the FCC did not violate the Seventh Amendment by issuing forfeiture orders without a jury trial, because such orders do not definitively resolve legal obligations and the defendant keeps the right to a full de novo jury trial before paying.

The court held that a worker who contributes to the intrastate leg of an interstate journey can qualify for the Federal Arbitration Act's exemption under Section 1 without crossing state lines or interacting with any vehicles that do.
The court held that the necessary inducement element of a patent infringement claim must be clear to the relevant audience and affirmative.

The court held that, after a federal court has stayed claims in a pending action under Section 3 of the Federal Arbitration Act, that court has jurisdiction to confirm or vacate a resulting arbitral award on those claims under Sections 9 and 10 of the act.

The court held that, to determine whether an omission of a claim in the bankruptcy context was inadvertent or mistaken for purposes of judicial estoppel, courts should look to the totality of the circumstances surrounding the omission.

In a dispute over whether state-law cancer warnings for Roundup could be required when the EPA had not identified the product as carcinogenic, the Court ruled for Monsanto, holding that Missouri law could not override the EPA's uniform labeling requirements.

The Court held that a non-citizen arrives in the United States under the Immigration and Nationality Act only upon crossing the border, so the Act neither entitles a non-citizen standing in Mexico to apply for asylum nor requires inspection by an immigration officer.

The court held that, after a prosecutor responds to a Batson challenge by asserting race-neutral reasons for a peremptory strike, the defense counsel must always have an opportunity to argue that the asserted race-neutral reasons were pretextual.
The court held that a showing of pecuniary loss to investors is not required before the Securities and Exchange Commission may obtain a disgorgement award.

In a case concerning the Rooker–Feldman doctrine, the Court held that the doctrine bars federal court review of state court decisions even if those decisions are subject to further review in state court.

The Court held that children born in the United States, including to parents unlawfully or temporarily present, are "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution (1868).
The court ruled that mail-in ballots cast and postmarked by Election Day can be counted if they are received after Election Day.
The court held that an appeal waiver included in a plea bargain is unenforceable when it would result in a miscarriage of justice.

The Court held that the temporary protected status (TPS) statute bars judicial review of non-constitutional claims challenging the second Trump administration's termination of TPS for Haitian and Syrian nationals.
